## Turning observations into goals

For an alliance-captain ambition, compare your expected pre-event capability to the event's strongest robots, then ask whether compatible partners can reach the observed alliance band. For a first/second-pick role, use the actual champion team EPA breakdown and identify the capability the alliance lacked. A robot well below the leading EPA can still be a winning defender, supplier or endgame partner. Conversely, matching the leader's EPA is insufficient if your autonomous conflicts or your architecture collapses under defense.

Set separate goals for the first event, the next improvement interval and DCMP. Use success distributions, not only a best run: acquisition/transfer time, accuracy under contact, successful endgame rate, downtime and repair duration. Recompute when RP thresholds or partner assumptions change. The CSV contains champion member EPAs and phase medians to make these comparisons explicit. In 2026, inspect tower fields separately from late fuel.
methodology:
# Methods and limits

This research edition is a substantial starting corpus. It does **not** satisfy a literal claim that every mechanism, every intermediate robot version and every Einstein tactic has been exhaustively verified. The coverage audit is part of the data, not a footnote. All 125 entries are reference dossiers; none is certified as a complete historical record.

## Team selection

The starting lists are the Statbotics mirror's team-year total-points EPA rankings for 2022–2026, ordered descending. Ties are ordered by team number. Selected dossiers preserve original rank and EPA. Higher-ranked candidates that were not selected remain in `selection_audit.csv`, with a retrieval/scope reason. A skip means this review did not obtain sufficient usable coverage; it does not mean the team published nothing or built an inferior robot.

Substitution makes the sample biased toward teams that publish, English-language interviews and documentation accessible to these tools. High EPA is also an outcome-selected sample. This dataset cannot identify the causal effect of a mechanism across all teams, nor prove the highest-ranked architecture was best for a particular team's resources.

Some selected entries still have important gaps, especially endgame installation and complete season chronology. Those are marked provisional. The user's stricter requirement—25 fully documented accepted entries in each season—remains an open acceptance gate. The database does not pad that gate by calling an unresolved feature absent or treating one interview as proof of every version.

## Source hierarchy

Official game manuals define rules; event-specific rules and updates are necessary for historical thresholds. TBA supplies event/match identities, schedules, divisions and score verification. Numeric bulk data came through the user-supplied public Statbotics mirror API. The package keeps both TBA links and numeric-source URLs. Selected direct TBA/FIRST checks corroborate results; it does not claim every one of the 7,995 scorecards was independently re-entered from TBA.

Team-authored binders, CAD/code releases, build journals and technical interviews support robot summaries. Interview captions can mistranscribe dimensions, materials and team numbers; unresolved transcription is not promoted to fact. A third-party dashboard was used to discover links, not as an authority for robot specifications. Additional bibliography links may be discovery-only; those are separate from reviewed source bundles.

Copyrighted source binders, complete transcripts and forum threads are not redistributed. The deliverable contains concise original summaries, derived data and links. Intermediate downloads and frontend assets are excluded. No API keys or authentication material are included.

## Numeric definitions

`epa` is the snapshot team-year estimate, not a raw individual score. `pre_elim_epa` is the event estimate before elimination play. `event_end_epa` is after that event. The eighth-highest EPA is **not** the eighth qualification seed. Qualification rank 1 is recorded separately. Components may be negative or physically implausible because they are model estimates; they are never treated as literal individual counts.

Clean alliance score means score excluding received foul points. Champion playoff clean-score median/min/max summarize matches attributed to the eventual winning alliance, using at least two continuing lineup members to account for an appearing substitute. The full four-team award roster is not reconstructed when a robot never appeared in the sampled lineups. Selection and winning a district event also depend on partners and opponents; there is no guaranteed “EPA needed to win.”

Event participation is derived from actual matches. This avoids a 2026 Einstein payload metadata problem that listed hundreds of teams. There are 75 events, 7,995 completed match rows, 4,021 appearing team-event rows, 58 benchmark rows and 80 Einstein rows in this snapshot. Some completed matches have missing score components, including disqualification/abnormal cases; these remain null, not invented zeros.

## Einstein analysis

All 80 records have phase/component analysis and source links. Fifty-one have reviewed reported tactics from broadcast captions or first-hand team accounts. None has a completed visual frame-by-frame audit. Other rows retain an explicit pending tactical-review state. Captions do not establish failure causes or player intent, and an aggregate teleop advantage does not prove a named defender's effect.

One mirror video association is demonstrably wrong: the video linked to 2022 semifinal match 2 describes match 15 and is embedded on TBA's match-15 page. The association is rejected for match 2 and used only for match 15. The primary ledger preserves the error flag.

For 2026, the two own-active scoring windows occur at different clock times for red and blue. `endgame_points` includes final-window fuel; tower components are kept separately. This distinction prevents the especially misleading inference that a large endgame score means a high climb.

## Reproducibility and updates

The package includes schema, build scripts, exact input/derived exports and checksums. The compact numeric exports are sufficient to rebuild the database without the original downloaded web pages. Rechecking human interpretation still requires following the primary links. The ranking snapshot is dated 2026-10-25; later EPA models, offseason records, corrected matches or link changes can alter a fresh pull.

To add a source or resolve a gap, preserve the original claim, add the new dated evidence, mark whether the conclusion changed and update coverage. To add a robot version, create a distinct version row with its applicable period; do not silently overwrite the season record with a later mechanism. Architecture recommendations should cite the version actually supporting them.
agentGuide:
# Using this corpus for robot architecture decisions

This is a retrieval corpus and an auditable research edition, not a model trained to recognize every FRC robot from an image. Its 125 robot entries contain substantial primary-source summaries, but unresolved subsystem details and unverified intermediate versions remain. Treat those as unknowns; never fill them with a famous team's usual practice. There are 80 Einstein records, of which 51 have reviewed reported tactics; none has a completed visual audit. Score-only records must not be narrated as observed match strategy.

## Retrieval order

1. Load the dated game rules and field geometry. Extract legal actions, possession, timing, finite resources, access constraints and scoring dependencies.
2. Define the role and event stage: PCH week 3, week 5, DCMP, division contender, or Einstein alliance. Include two hypothetical partners.
3. Estimate the bottleneck in a complete match: acquisition, transport, handoff, alignment, release, recovery, energy, supply or lane occupancy.
4. Retrieve mechanisms by function and failure mode, then by team/year/version. A team number without a year is an ambiguous reference.
5. Compare at least two coherent whole-robot architectures. Use the same match assumptions for both.
6. Return a source-backed recommendation, confidence, unresolved interfaces, and the smallest tests that could falsify it.

Use SQLite for structured filtering and full-text retrieval; use the Markdown chapters and source links for context. Embeddings can supplement this, but should not replace exact year, version, event and metric filters. The JSONL exports make provider-neutral ingestion straightforward. No model API credentials or paid service are required to browse the delivered database.

## Mechanism vocabulary and interface contracts

Store four separate ideas: **function** (acquire fuel), **kinematics** (four-bar, pivoting/slapdown, translating rack), **implementation** (materials, rollers, transmission), and **observed performance** (conditions and date). Treat labels as retrieval hints and inspect actual linkage geometry. For 2910 specifically, the 2026 original and rebuild briefs explicitly distinguish dual four-bars from the later slapdown; do not blend versions.

“Dumper” in the reviewed 2026 sources usually refers to multi-stream/batch shooting through a broad fixed-heading drum. It does not imply a literal gravity dump, a fixed hood, absence of aiming software, or a particular lane count. “Four-wide” should specify usable stream width, not merely the number of visible wheels. DYE Rotor is paintball-loader lineage; a rotating-cone spindexer is a related but different singulation family.

For every proposed combination, explicitly check:

- Intake → hopper: deployed/stowed envelopes, full-load capacity, collision collapse and whether a deformed wall can block retraction.
- Hopper → feeder: floor support, packing pressure, dead zones, bridging, agitation, retained residual pieces and service access.
- Feeder → launcher: compression, incoming velocity/spin, lane width, time of flight, rate distribution and current draw.
- Scorer → chassis: aiming motion, swept volume, cable limits, reaction loads, CG throughout travel, and accessible routes while loaded.
- Climber → everything: capture alignment, partner clearance, removed scoring time, held state after disable, mass margin and actual installed version.

## Required evidence language

Use **official score**, **team-reported measurement**, **broadcast report**, **analyst inference**, **proposed/unfielded**, and **unresolved** as distinct labels. A reported BPS number without fuel condition, accuracy, duration and battery state is not a portable design specification. An automatic score decomposition does not establish defensive effectiveness or individual contribution. A part visible in CAD is not proof it was installed at every event.

EPA is a model estimate of contribution, not an individual scoring ledger. Some component estimates are negative or outside physical probability bounds. Do not convert such outputs to observed ball counts, success rates or hardware absence. Do not add three season-final EPAs to claim the score an alliance will produce in a specific match. Partner interference, defense, rule versions and timing can invalidate that approximation.

The numeric snapshot uses the user-supplied Statbotics mirror consistently, retrieved 2026-10-25. It is not asserted to be bit-identical to every official Statbotics historical model revision. Pre-elimination event EPA is supplied for historical event comparison; it is still an estimate, not a prediction made before kickoff.

## Output format for the eventual agent

Start with a robot role and measurable goals. Then give an architecture sentence with **year and version** on each inspiration. Explain what function each reference solves and why the components fit together. Include two rejected alternatives and the conditions under which either would become preferable. State development burden, maintenance requirements and the next decision-changing prototype.

Example query: “Find 2026 batch scorers with expanding storage, compare a 2910 rebuild intake/hopper arrangement to 1678 and a 254-style preaccelerated drum. Explain which motion/linkage details must be rechecked.” A correct answer retrieves those particular dossiers, distinguishes their interview dates, and declines to invent a universal combination from their labels.

## Evaluation cases

- Ask for 5940's 2022 Worlds climb. The answer must distinguish onseason high-bar from offseason traversal.
- Ask whether 4414 held 110 fuel in 2026. The answer must identify the published 85+/100+ configuration claims and leave 110 unverified.
- Ask which 2026 Einstein finalist had 150 climb points. The answer must reject interpreting endgame fuel as tower points.
- Ask for 2025 week-1 coral-RP requirements. The answer must find the early rule version rather than blindly use the latest manual.
- Ask for the strategy of a score-only Einstein row. The answer must expose the pending tactical review, not invent a defender.
- Ask why 1690's 2025 alliance used a station-fed third robot. The answer must discuss partner interference and preserve attribution to the team account.
- Ask for the best 2022 architecture solely from EPA. The answer must explain outcome-selection and documentation bias, then ask which role/resources the architecture must serve.

Hold back some known robot-year questions when evaluating a retrieval agent. Score source correctness, version correctness, unknown handling, interface reasoning and recommendation quality separately. Fluent use of team numbers is not evidence of sound strategic design.


## Technical review edition

Read `data/binder_audit.jsonl` for all 125 search statuses, `data/binder_sources.jsonl` for reviewed publications, and `data/technical_mechanisms.jsonl` for construction, stated intent, inference, proposed tests and limits. Use `data/technical_parameters.jsonl` for selected published values and source notation. `docs/TECHNICAL_EVIDENCE_GUIDE.md` explains the reasoning standard. A first-pass search is not exhaustive absence evidence.

For 2026, begin with fuel contribution and treat climbing as low priority; use actual tower fields rather than endgame EPA. For 2025, retrieve the 1323/2910/4272 parallel L1-algae/branch case before ranking tasks by height.

contextDocs.title: 1323 in 2025: Aurelia’s value depends on the alliance around it
contextDocs.body:
# 1323 in 2025: Aurelia’s value depends on the alliance around it

The base dossier describes a compact tilting elevator, ground acquisition, a differential end effector and dedicated L1 work. That list does not explain why the package was useful. The deeper story concerns where mass and motion were placed, how transitions were controlled, how the robot was practiced, and how a highly capable scoring robot could rationally spend important matches doing a low-valued task. This supplement combines team replies from the release discussion with attributed match interpretation. It does not certify every configuration or CAD revision.

## Ground acquisition changes the source of the cycle, not only the pickup

The team credits Spectrum’s published funneling prototypes as direct input to its thinking. That is a specific lineage claim by the team, stronger than an observer noticing a resemblance. [Acknowledgment](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/212).

A ground collector becomes strategically powerful only when the rest of the system can exploit it. The human player has to deliver useful coral near the intended work area; the robot has to acquire it in more than one plausible orientation; the handoff must preserve control; and the scoring motion must finish before the next piece is needed. Reducing travel can expose a new bottleneck in transfer or joint motion. The agent should therefore compare complete acquisition-to-next-acquisition cycles rather than assume a floor pickup automatically halves cycle time.

The RoboReplay review ledger preserves a progression from early floor-supplied cycles to widespread field supply, then to L1 placement and algae security. These are dated observations and interpretations, not proof that 1323 invented each tactic first. The recap author explicitly does not claim to know the first inventor. Use that ledger to find the relevant discussion, then use team releases for mechanism construction and official records for scores.

## A differential needs a coordinate system and a recovery plan

In its controls explanation, the team describes two CANcoders and average/difference relationships for pitch and roll, with useful resolution through the range of motion. It also describes pain caused by a poor zeroing arrangement on the practice machine. [Encoder explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/218).

The transferable issue is not the encoder brand. Coupled actuation makes a light moving assembly possible, but makes calibration, limits and fault recovery part of the mechanism. If a team loses one joint reference, it needs to know which physical configurations are still safe. A robot that must disassemble a gearbox or trust an eyeballed pose after every power cycle can spend far more competition time recovering than its nominal mechanism speed saves.

The thread’s belt discussion also keeps packaging costs visible. The team reports more tension than expected and explains the role of belt construction and wrap. A later answer discusses the packaging that reduced wrap and the use of current/velocity when detecting a limit, while suggesting a larger pulley or changed path as a potential improvement. [Belt experience](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/242). [Packaging discussion](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/250). Do not copy a thin, low-mass elevator rendering without the tension, stiffness, bearing loads and reference strategy that support it.

## Mechanically possible motion is not the same as permitted match motion

The team explains an emphasis on continuous joint motion toward useful states rather than a sequence of pauses. It also describes driver overrides for L1 and handoff behavior, a later allowance for algae-intake positioning, and Worlds changes including additional vision for L1 and default stow behavior. These are control-policy changes, not evidence that every physically reachable pose was always exposed to the driver. [Operating policy](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/236).

Another reply describes a superstructure state containing elevator position, elevator pivot and wrist pitch/roll, with a choreographer that builds safe transitions. A separate answer discusses using differential controller support once the mechanics and sensing were correct. [State representation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/283). [Controller/mechanical dependency](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/281).

An agent recommending this architecture should explicitly include that transition layer. A tilting elevator with a versatile wrist can have excellent final poses and still collide with its own intake during the path between them. The architecture should name which motions can overlap, which require a clearance condition, what the operator can interrupt, and where a stalled transition leaves the game piece. This is a reason to study code releases alongside CAD, while preserving their exact commit and event relevance. A public repository’s current default branch is not automatically the version run at a particular event.

## Human control remained part of the successful system

The team describes left/right branch selection relative to the nearest reef location and explains that manual release could be cleaner than a fully automatic release because of mechanism quirks. Driver and operator coordination also helped prevent intake interference with pipes. [Driver interface](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/303).

This avoids a common generalization error: a high-performing robot is not necessarily autonomous in every part of teleop. A deliberately manual action can be a reasonable way to handle ambiguous sensing or preserve operator judgment. The relevant measure is the entire decision-and-execution loop, including its error rate under contact and visual obstruction. The agent should not recommend automatic release merely because the mechanism has accurate joints. It should ask whether the observations needed to release safely are actually available.

## The build history includes abandoned mechanisms

The team’s timeline describes early CAD blocks, a largely functional machine by the following phase, and subsequent redesign. It names claw and hanger work, removal of suction, later mass reduction, a 2910-inspired hanger and Worlds emphasis on robustness and weight. [Development account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/263).

The abandoned suction matters. A database that gathers every impressive prototype and treats all of them as features of the final robot produces an impossible composite. The correct representation is a versioned choice: a concept existed, a later report says it was removed, and the final package must be determined from the dated sources. Similarly, “2910 hanger” is a lineage lead that still needs the year and exact retained principles. It is not permission to assume identical dimensions or identical integration into a different superstructure.

## Practice and material selection are part of the architecture’s cost

The team describes building the practice robot early enough for extensive validation, while the competition machine was completed much closer to its event. It also notes configuration drift between two robots as a cost. [Two-robot account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/267). A later reply gives a rough team estimate about the benefit of their practice time; this is a self-assessment, not a controlled measurement or a universal hours-to-performance equation. [Practice reflection](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/305).

Another reply contrasts inexpensive, quickly iterated practice prints with competition material chosen for confidence, while noting that practice hardware accumulated more hours. [Printing experience](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/327). Material choice therefore has to be read with the test exposure, replacement cadence and failure consequence. A competition material does not by itself explain the success of the mechanism; rapid cheap prototypes may have discovered the load path and geometry that made the final part straightforward.

## Why specializing in L1 can be the correct job for an excellent robot

Once partners can reliably fill the higher branches, an additional robot’s ability to place another L4 has little immediate value unless it frees a partner for a better job. Fast L1 acquisition and controlled placement can instead increase the alliance’s remaining score. Orientation and release geometry affect how densely coral can be arranged near a convenient face, which changes how soon the robot must move to a less convenient face. This is an alliance-dependent marginal-value argument, not a claim that L1 is intrinsically the best task.

The RoboReplay finals analysis attributes importance to 1323’s L1 stacking and 2910’s algae steals. It also interprets score visibility and drive-team decisions; those psychological explanations remain commentary. See the complete review of `SQure1sSDpk` in the RoboReplay ledger for the source, with official Einstein records used for scores. A future agent should preserve the difference between the visible configuration, a measured cycle count, a team statement about its plan and an analyst’s explanation of the result.

## What to borrow and what to test

Retrieve this case for low moving mass, coupled joints, bidirectional scoring, dedicated L1 placement and the distinction between capability and match role. Test the collection/handoff cycle with delivered coral at realistic locations, joints moving simultaneously, contact during acquisition, worn components and an interrupted transition. Validate zeroing and recovery as deliberately as scoring. Pair the case with 2910’s arm architecture and 1690’s low-mass vacuum/differential system to compare where each design puts its complexity. The agent should state which capability your likely PCH partners supply; without that assumption, a recommendation to optimize L1 may copy the visible job while missing the alliance that made it valuable.

contextDocs.title: 1768 in 2026: the rebuild is a sequence of decisions, not one drum photograph
contextDocs.body:
# 1768 in 2026: the rebuild is a sequence of decisions, not one drum photograph

This supplement uses the team’s October CAD-release replies alongside the earlier technical interview. It distinguishes the original Nightshade, the Nightshift rebuild, later onseason adjustments and offseason changes. The source is unusually useful because the team explains why mechanisms and schedule choices were coupled. A successful rebuild should not be reduced to “replace two shooters with a drum,” nor should October performance be assigned to the robot that competed at Worlds.

## The schedule establishes what the team actually proved

The team describes an eleven-day rebuild between URI in week 3 and WPI in week 5, with the new machine operational after nine days. Only the swerve modules and bellypan were retained. The reply’s timeline runs from the original robot’s final match on March 21 through CAD on March 25, stripping the old machine on March 27, mounting major subsystems on March 28 and reaching a practice field on April 2. Those are dated milestones reported by the team, not an inference that another team can repeat the schedule. [Schedule and retained hardware](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/12). [Detailed milestones](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/13).

The distinction matters when borrowing architecture. A mechanism whose drawings can be completed quickly may still consume the entire available interval in wiring, controls, feeding tests and driver learning. Conversely, retaining a technically mediocre but known assembly can preserve enough practice time to win more matches. The relevant rebuild calculation includes the probability of arriving with an integrated machine, not just the predicted performance of the finished CAD. An architecture recommendation should name the existing interfaces that survive, the ones that are replaced and the latest date at which a failed experiment can still be abandoned.

The team’s process reply describes student ownership of deadlines and explicit gates: if a new assembly does not meet a milestone, the original version stays. Older students handled CAD while newer students manufactured early enough to understand assembly. This is evidence about the organization that made a rapid rebuild possible. It is not a universal staffing prescription. [Process account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/21).

For a PCH rebuild, the transferable question is therefore not “can our team also rebuild in eleven days?” It is “which uncertainty can our actual team retire before our next event, with enough time left to integrate and practice?” A new hopper that retains the old collector, floor and mounting interfaces can be a fundamentally different risk from a new collector, hopper and feed path that must all work on their first combined test. The latter may still be justified, but the justification needs an integration plan and a fallback with a real deadline.

## The four-bar is doing more than deploying an intake

The later replies explain that the week-zero machine did not stow under the trench. On the developed machine, the hopper attaches to the lower link of the four-bar. The team describes fitting the trench envelope in both positions, satisfying the starting envelope, folding the kicker and choosing link angles that survive contact. They arrived at the geometry through iteration rather than a single independent constraint calculation. [Envelope discussion](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/15). [Coupled geometry](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/16).

This is exactly why “a 2910-style intake with a Citrus hopper” needs an interface analysis. The intake’s ground contact point and deployed reach are only part of the design. The moving hopper wall changes where stored fuel rests; the lower link’s motion changes the floor slope; the kicker’s folded position changes what can occupy the trench envelope. The mechanism must pass through intermediate positions while full of fuel. A configuration that clears a field element in a static CAD screenshot can still trap fuel, pull a flexible wall into a roller or require a transition that cannot be completed while moving.

The useful inspiration is the constraint-solving strategy: let one linkage carry several compatible motions, then check the consequences as a system. It is not a claim that the same link lengths fit another chassis. A receiving team should record the deployed and retracted volumes, the swept paths of rigid members and flexible walls, the lowest loaded floor point, the expected collision direction and the fuel escape routes. If any of those are unknown, the recommendation should remain an architectural candidate rather than a dimensioned solution.

## Transmission failures need local explanations

One reply separates motor-to-roller belt skipping from roller-to-roller belts that did not skip. The team changed the former to chain after Worlds, then added polycarbonate retaining flanges after the chain came off once. Their explanation involves possible motor or plate flex reducing wrap or tension around a small pulley; it is a team hypothesis about this installation. [Transmission sequence](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/9).

That report does not establish “chain is better than belts.” It suggests tests: watch relative motor and shaft displacement under load; inspect tooth engagement through the entire torque transient; distinguish a belt climbing out of mesh from a shaft or tensioner moving; and check retention after changing the transmission type. A mechanism database should keep the failed condition, the suspected cause, the modification and the observed result as separate fields. Without that separation, an agent may copy the final component while repeating the geometry that caused the original failure.

The sliding flywheel-belt tensioner belongs to an offseason N.E.R.D. update. The team reports that high-speed slack had been damaging the belt, that the tensioner improved reported accuracy and that short testing had not yet revealed issues. They also anticipated possible creep that could be corrected by retensioning. Another reply explains the generous adjustment range and the washer arrangement around the bearing. [Tensioner report](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/8). [Adjustment explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/11). This is promising design evidence with a limited test horizon, not a season-long reliability certification.

## Fabrication and service choices change what is feasible

The team explains choosing live axles because they were quickest to manufacture for this rebuild. They recognize advantages of stubs for width iteration, but that was not the priority. This is a concrete example of a choice that can be strategically correct despite not maximizing every engineering objective. [Axle tradeoff](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/12).

Their hood-rack reply describes printed material supported by aluminum teeth, with print settings chosen to reduce backlash. The lesson is to document the load path and what each material contributes. A screenshot that looks like a printed rack can conceal metal reinforcement; a recommendation to “print the rack” can therefore remove the part that made it survive. [Rack construction](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/17).

## Do not backdate the faster feeder

October replies describe an entry roller using spaced compliant wheels to create lanes, combining the entry roller and floor drive at a 1:1 ratio, and matching feeder surface speed more closely to drum speed. The team reports moving from roughly 23–26 to 28–30 balls per second. These are offseason reports, not measured Worlds match averages. [October feed changes](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/22). [Reported result](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/24).

The architectural implication is broader than the headline firing rate. Fuel must arrive across the useful shooter width with suitable velocity, spacing and compression. Adding lanes can change the stability of that delivery; linking drives can remove one mismatch while introducing another dependency. A team evaluating the change should compare the beginning and end of a full hopper, partly depleted operation, worn fuel, lateral acceleration and recovery after a jam. A clean burst of a few fuel does not test those conditions.

## What an agent should retrieve from this case

Retrieve 1768 when the question involves a compressed rebuild, a moving hopper carried by a four-bar, drum packaging or separating onseason and offseason transmission fixes. Pair it with 254 and 1678 for feed-contact geometry and with 2910 for a different rebuild triggered by unmet performance goals. Do not merge the named configurations into a single idealized robot. The strongest reusable lesson is that an architecture is a set of coordinated constraints, a manufacturing plan and a validated operating sequence. The remaining unresolved endgame and exact drivetrain details in the base dossier remain unresolved; these additional replies do not establish them.

contextDocs.title: 4414 in 2026: storage, a compact turret and an entire operating policy
contextDocs.body:
# 4414 in 2026: storage, a compact turret and an entire operating policy

RIPCURRENT is useful as an architecture case because its components reinforce each other. The low singulator, small turret swept volume, chassis shape, storage walls, net and movable collection system allocate the same scarce interior space. Merely writing “turret with a big hopper” loses the reason the package is interesting. The base dossier and the team’s interactive binder describe the construction; this supplement adds the team’s explanations of calibration, autonomy, geometry and iteration. [Interactive technical binder](https://2026.team4414.com/). [Discussion](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602).

## Preserve the terms before reasoning from them

The relevant singulator reference is DYE Rotor, a paintball-loader family. It should not be parsed as “di-rotor,” an assertion that there are two rotors, or a generic synonym for any spindexer. The architecture has to be identified from its actual feed paths and independent drives. Likewise a turret makes azimuth independent of chassis heading within its usable range; it does not by itself establish accuracy at every location, continuous firing under every acceleration or immunity to defense.

The current reviewed capacity claims in the binder are 85+ fuel in the trench-capable configuration and 100+ with the net over the bump. The user’s 110-fuel example remains unverified in this edition. A 110-inch frame-perimeter reference must not be turned into 110 stored fuel. An additional later measurement could resolve that question, but a persuasive narrative is not a substitute for it. Capacity also needs a defined condition: static fill, retained fuel while moving, fuel actually deliverable to the shooter and a particular net/deployment configuration can all differ.

## The geometry is a system-level choice

The base dossier records the compact turret, the large low rotor, chamfered chassis, offset battery packaging and structural storage walls. The team later describes an early inspiration that changed its thinking from a square machine toward a wider chamfered shape. This is evidence of design lineage, not a claim that the exact inspirational sketch was fabricated. [October reflection](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/157).

A useful agent generalization is that reducing an assembly’s swept volume can be worth more than making its standalone performance better. A smaller turret can leave more storage around it, permit a better floor route and reduce the space needed for wiring. Those gains can increase how long the robot remains useful in a scoring shift. But the tradeoff must be tested: a compact shooter may have poorer compression consistency, less flywheel inertia, more difficult service or a tighter hood path. The geometry only wins if the integrated robot delivers more reliable output under the target conditions.

The published images include separate rotor V1–V10 and shooter V1–V11 asset labels. These are preserved in the gallery. Some filenames mention pre-Ventura, Ventura or Orange County; the other V-numbers should not be assigned to event configurations without further evidence. An image of a prototype is evidence that a design was considered or published, not that it survived qualification, played at Worlds or ran simultaneously with every other pictured part.

## Do not copy the successful calibration story without the empirical part

The team says its shot solver drew from 1690’s 2022 presentation, but searched a region of shots reaching the near and far rim rather than only targeting the center. It chose solutions with tolerance to exit-speed and angle error. The team then measured angle offset and empirically calibrated exit speed against commanded wheel speed; one shooter revision needed a nonlinear lookup. It frames the benefit as reducing tuning effort, while explicitly not claiming the season’s best shot or best shooting on the move. [Shot-model explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/116).

The independent engineering implication is to model uncertainty, not only nominal trajectories. Ball wear, contact state, feeder speed and wheel compression can change actual exit conditions. If an architecture relies on a computed trajectory but cannot measure or repeat the exit state, adding more aerodynamic terms may not solve its dominant error. Conversely, a well-designed mechanism can make a compact empirical calibration useful across many conditions. An agent should recommend an experiment that identifies the dominant uncertainty before recommending a more complicated simulator.

For a different shooter, the transferable goal is a maintainable calibration procedure. That procedure should say what changes when fuel ages, when a wheel is replaced, when the feed geometry is adjusted and when a hood reference drifts. It should also say how the team distinguishes a localization error from an exit-velocity error. Otherwise a driver can lose an entire event chasing the wrong tuning parameter.

## Vision hardware and the hardware that actually worked are different records

The team describes a turret-mounted Limelight using MegaTag 1 and supplementary USB cameras on an Orange Pi. Historical gyro and turret angles are buffered so camera observations can be transformed at their measurement time before filtering and fusion. The team reports no precise absolute turret zero, using a visually approximated starting zero and accepting a small consequence for the gyro reference. It calls that a local prioritization decision. [Vision account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/107).

The team separately says it ran Champs eliminations with only one working camera on the Orange Pi after USB-port failures, with ESD offered as a suspected explanation. This establishes the difference between intended sensor architecture and the functional configuration in an important competition period; it does not prove the electrical failure mechanism. [Functional configuration](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/111).

This case should therefore not become an agent rule that absolute sensing is unnecessary or that any one camera platform is inherently unreliable. The useful lesson is that the target’s tolerance, the observation geometry and the team’s familiarity can change the value of a more rigorous reference system. A different game with narrow placement or multi-target tasks can expose errors that a large hub did not. An architecture recommendation needs both nominal performance and degraded operation when a camera, port or reference fails.

## A lower peak autonomous routine can be a better alliance routine

The team explains testing depot-auto variants and finding that double swipes left insufficient time to fire and reach the desired transition position. It preferred crossing the bump once to improve compatibility and avoid being affected if a partner got stuck. The chosen path also depended on a fuel triangle that did not reliably form without enough robots rushing midfield. [Autonomous tradeoff](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/124).

That dependency should remain attached to the recommendation. A routine optimized for four strong midfield contestants may collect less at a sparse local event or with a different opponent plan. Similarly, a transition endpoint has value because of what the robot can do next, not because “center” is universally optimal. The agent should compare complete auto-plus-transition outcomes under several partner/opponent configurations, including an obstruction and a failed pickup. Scoring more in the first interval can lose more in the next interval if the machine ends in a poor location with an empty hopper.

## Collision recovery is part of useful throughput

The team reports changing the bottom plastic from 1/16 to 1/8 inch after weight became available, and finding that the stiffer sheet helped the robot slide off fuel. The same reply describes an unsuccessful camera-wiring experiment that damaged hardware. Both belong in the record, but neither should be copied as a generic recipe. [Packaging and belly-sheet account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/105).

This matters strategically because a robot with lower nominal firing rate can outperform a faster one if it spends less time stranded, realigning or hunting for a feedable pile. The correct comparison is fuel successfully scored during useful windows, including the time needed to acquire, transfer, aim, recover and return. It should be measured against representative defense and fuel distribution. A claim that this turret “almost outscored the best drums” needs an identified match, the other robots’ roles and the relevant scoring conditions; this edition does not turn that phrase into a universal ranking of mechanism families.

## What a recommendation inspired by RIPCURRENT should contain

Recommend the package when independent aiming, mobile collection and storage preservation match the team’s intended role and development capacity. State the cost in singulator development, calibration, wiring, sensor recovery and service access. Compare it against a braced fixed shooter with a simpler floor and a wide drum under the same supply and defense assumptions. Prototype partially depleted and mixed-load feeding, not just a full static hopper. Keep a dated configuration record for every claimed improvement. The available evidence is strong enough to make RIPCURRENT a useful source of architectural ideas; it is not complete enough to certify every intermediate competition version, the user’s exact 110-fuel number or a guaranteed advantage against any named drum.

contextDocs.title: How to reason about a robot assembled from several historical references
contextDocs.body:
# How to reason about a robot assembled from several historical references

A compound proposal is meaningful because experienced FRC people compress years of context into a few team names. The agent should expand that shorthand into functions, interfaces and conditional advantages. It should then check whether the resulting machine can work as a whole. This chapter uses the user’s proposed 2026 dumper as an example; it does not provide manufacturing dimensions or certify legality of a new design.

## Expand the phrase before judging it

“Dumper” identifies an intended pattern of high-rate batch discharge. It leaves unresolved how the robot acquires, stores, transfers, aims and recovers, and how often it can reach a useful batch. “Four-wide” proposes parallel delivery but does not establish that four lanes will remain fed or that their trajectories are consistent. “254 geometry” should be resolved to the particular year and source that explain contact, acceleration and spin; it should not be treated as a magic wheel ratio.

“2910-style slapdown” proposes a deployed ground-acquisition package. The database should return the documented linkage and protection arrangement for the intended version, while warning that the broad name does not specify kinematics. “Citrus-style expanding hopper” proposes using changing volume and possibly linked motion to store more fuel while meeting an envelope. It says nothing yet about whether the collector’s path and the floor’s path agree.

The first useful response is a precise restatement: a fixed, parallel-stream launcher fed by a controlled floor/tunnel, with a deploying collector and a storage envelope that changes between travel and scoring states. Then name the unresolved degrees of freedom. Is the robot intended to fit the trench full, empty or in a reduced-capacity state? Can it collect and fire simultaneously? Does deployment alter the floor? Is the shooter expected to change range while loaded? Those answers change which historical package is a useful starting point.

## Check the intake-to-storage interface

The collector must deliver fuel into a space that remains open through the deployment motion. A wide roller can move fuel faster than a narrow throat accepts it. A moving hopper wall can improve volume but pinch fuel at the handoff. A robust crash bar can protect the roller while preventing recovery of fuel near a wall. These are not reasons to reject the concept; they are the first places to test whether the chosen mechanisms agree.

Build a representative section with the actual bumper opening, roller position, floor, wall and transfer entry. Test scattered fuel, a dense pile, oblique approach and reversal. Include the deformed states that can plausibly occur in a match. Record retained, feedable fuel rather than only how many entered the robot. If the first test uses an open box with no bumper or moving wall, it has not tested the proposed interface.

## Check the storage-to-feed interface

Large storage creates multiple pressure and contact conditions. A full load can produce bridging or uneven lane fill; a nearly empty load can leave fuel stranded where agitation no longer reaches it. Turning can move the whole pile, and flexible boundaries can change the effective floor area. A feed path should be evaluated over the entire depletion curve.

The 254, 1678, 2910 and 1768 notes offer different ways of accelerating, staging and retaining fuel. Some eliminate a velocity reversal; others retain a geometry that worked in their own comparison. The existence of both is useful evidence against a universal S-path or J-path rule. The agent should state the desired contact history and compression, then explain which source demonstrates a similar condition. It should not choose a path shape solely because the label appears in a champion’s interview.

An important question is where excess fuel goes when one lane slows. If the only response is to compact the pile harder, a brief disturbance can become a full jam. An independently controlled entry, reverse policy, bypass or compliant surface may help, but each adds its own cost. The design recommendation should identify the recovery behavior before treating nominal flow as a solved problem.

## Check the feed-to-launcher interface

Wheel speed is not fuel exit speed. The entry condition, friction, compression, contact duration and interaction with a powered hood affect what leaves the robot. A four-wide drum can have uneven delivery across its width even if the drum itself is uniform. Shaft deflection, support placement, feeder geometry and occupied width all matter.

Measure trajectories from each portion of the effective width under realistic delivery. Include the first few fuel, a dense volley, a partly depleted hopper and worn fuel. Record misses and energy use along with release rate. A higher rate that increases misses can reduce score; a faster burst that leaves more residual fuel can increase the time before the next useful batch. The question is not whether the mechanism can eject quickly, but whether it can deliver controlled scoring quickly under its expected conditions.

The compact-turret alternative should be subjected to the same accounting. Continuous aiming can increase the useful shooting fraction, but the singulator, cable range and calibration can impose interruptions. Compare architectures with the same fuel distribution, battery condition and defense assumptions. A bench BPS comparison between one and four streams is not that experiment.

## Check the robot-to-field interface

Envelope, route graph and contact recovery are strategic properties. A taller hopper may gain capacity or a higher release point while losing a route and exposing another transit delay. A smaller chassis may escape more easily while reducing storage. A rounded or chamfered footprint can change how opponents apply rotational leverage, but it also changes available interior volume, bumper construction and service access.

Build a route model with states. For each route, specify the required configuration, expected travel time, likely queue and what happens if fuel is under the chassis. Include the transition time between states. If a hopper must retract before a passage, the robot needs somewhere for the fuel to go and a reliable way to recognize completion. “It fits in CAD” is insufficient without the loaded and interrupted cases.

## Check the robot-to-alliance interface

Two individually strong robots can fight over the same pile, occupy each other’s shooting region or collide during autonomous. A third supplier can improve output or increase congestion. A defender can help one scorer while forcing another to take a longer route. The architecture brief should state the intended alliance role and a plausible alternative when the expected partner is absent.

For a 2026 PCH rebuild, write several scenarios: a strong supplier, a weak supplier, contested midfield, denied return route and one disabled partner. Estimate useful output in each with uncertainty bounds. These estimates are model inputs, not source facts. Test the scenario that most threatens the architecture’s advantage. If a design only works when two exceptional suppliers maintain a perfect floor pattern, the team should know that before it builds the dependency into the machine.

## Use quantitative goals without false precision

A useful requirement has a metric, condition, target, confidence and deadline. “Score more than last year’s winner” lacks a role and condition. “Empty a useful full load at the chosen defended location before the active interval ends, with a known residual count and a recovery policy” can guide an experiment. Historical benchmarks can calibrate ambition, but the individual contribution still depends on partners and rules.

Use a simple model to identify the dominant term, then improve it with observations. If the robot is starved for half its active time, improving peak release rate is unlikely to be the first priority. If it has full hoppers but cannot empty before the window closes, the feed/launcher becomes more valuable. If transit failures dominate, loaded ground interaction and route access matter more. If it repeatedly misses after contact, distinguish aim recovery from inconsistent exit conditions.

## Make the recommendation reviewable

For each candidate architecture, include a short source map and a long causal explanation. State which principles are retained and which interfaces must be designed anew. Preserve the failed experiments that set the design boundaries. Give a minimum integrated prototype, the observations that would reject the candidate, the fallback architecture and a calendar gate that leaves real practice time.

The database supports that process; it does not replace engineering judgment or validation. A recommendation is strongest when it tells the team exactly what new evidence would change it. That is how historical robot knowledge becomes useful design reasoning instead of a collage of successful-looking mechanisms.

contextDocs.title: Evidence, versions and what “reviewed” means
contextDocs.body:
# Evidence, versions and what “reviewed” means

This edition adds long contextual notes, technical images, a RoboReplay review ledger and post-level research locators. These additions deliberately preserve the original coverage gaps. A longer account is not an exhaustive account, and a larger bibliography is not evidence that every item was read.

## Keep several timelines

A publication date, design revision date, competition use date and interview recording date can differ. An offseason release can describe an onseason part, a removed prototype or a new offseason modification. A CAD V-number can be a convenient export label rather than a competition configuration. Store those dates separately and leave them null when not established. Do not use a forum post date as the installation date of a mechanism.

A robot version should name the relevant assembly changes, the evidence supporting them and the interval where it is known to apply. If the interval is unknown, retain the change without inventing a date. Do not merge every described feature into a single ideal robot. The 1768, 1323 and 4414 deep notes include examples where doing so would create misleading architecture and performance claims.

## Distinguish the kinds of statements

- Official rules establish requirements for their dated version; they do not establish what a team built.
- A team release establishes what the publisher reports, with the conditions and uncertainty it provides.
- A reported measurement needs configuration, fuel/piece condition, metric definition and test setting.
- A commentator can identify a useful interpretation, but observed motion does not reveal private intent or prove a failure diagnosis.
- Analyst reasoning should expose its assumptions and the experiment that could reject it.
- A discovery locator points to something worth reading; it is not a summarized technical claim.

An agent should retrieve evidence at the level of the claim. A post supporting a transmission change does not establish the climber. A video discussing finals does not visually audit every match. An official phase-score table can locate where points differed without explaining why they differed.

## Caption review is a specific access method

All 33 downloaded RoboReplay transcripts were reviewed through their available text, including recovery of portions truncated in intermediate output. No claim is made to have visually watched their diagrams, replay frames or uncaptioned details. Automatic captions often substitute numbers, confuse “not” and “now,” or distort mechanism names. Exact scores and team identities should be cross-checked with the linked event record. The review notes therefore preserve uncertainty rather than copying questionable ASR numbers.

The ledger contains 44 discovered video IDs, sourced chiefly from the channel author’s announcements in two Chief Delphi discussions plus the season recap. Eleven discovered videos remain unreviewed after a transcript request was blocked. Direct channel enumeration was not completed, so 44 is a discovered lower bound, not the certified channel size. No access-control workaround was used. Future authorized access can update the ledger and this status without rewriting already reviewed notes.

The distributed package contains original summaries, analysis, metadata and timestamp navigation labels. It does not redistribute complete captions or entire forum discussions. This keeps the reference useful without turning it into a bulk copy of other creators’ work. Follow the original links for their complete explanations, diagrams and demonstrations.

## Image labels carry their own uncertainty

The first extraction produced 318 source-associated images. Curation removed non-mechanism covers, logos, screenshots, decorative material and several comparison images whose depicted team could not be established. Named team-published iteration images were added, and PDF figures were reconstructed with their transparency masks where available. The final manifest is authoritative for included counts.

A contact-sheet review establishes that an image is a useful technical figure or robot view; it does not certify every detail or dimension. A binder page’s keywords describe the surrounding discussion and may not label that particular figure. A named team asset is a stronger component label, but still does not prove competition use. Each asset therefore retains its original source, page or post, date when available, publisher label and review basis. Attribution is not a new license; consult the source before other reuse.

## When sources conflict

Retain both claims with their dates and evidence classes. Try to resolve whether they describe different versions, test conditions, definitions or simple errors. Do not average incompatible numbers. Do not prefer a newer commentary clip over a direct team explanation merely because it sounds confident. The unresolved 110-fuel claim and the disputed 2022 possession interpretation are deliberately visible examples.

For architecture recommendations, a conflict may not need immediate resolution if the decision is robust across the plausible values. State that explicitly. If it changes the selection—for example, whether capacity is sufficient for the planned active window—make it a required measurement before committing. This is more useful than hiding the uncertainty behind a single polished number.

The 125 robot-year sample, 227 technical notes, 27 publication-review robot-years and 98 focused studies remain unchanged. Complete mechanism/version histories, remaining binder discovery, CAD interpretation and exact event installations remain open.

All eleven pending exports from the prior 44-video inventory were recovered through normal YouTube access.
