contextDocs.body:
# 2025-254: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## UNDERTOW: short-cycle gearing and low mass placement

Version: UNDERTOW. [PDF p12](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=12)

**Published construction:** 29.5-inch square base; low 3×1 frame; X2i modules geared about 13.2 ft/s free speed.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Favor acceleration and grip over long-run top speed.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** For a short reef cycle, acceleration, braking and repeatable final alignment can matter more than a higher unloaded top speed. Lower gearing increases available wheel torque but does not guarantee traction; wheel compound, normal load and current limits still bound acceleration. A broad low base helps resist tipping while the elevator changes height, but occupies more traffic space. The useful comparison uses the actual route and raised mechanism state rather than a module specification on its own.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure complete reef-to-supply cycle time, stopping error and wheel unloading with the elevator at representative positions.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## UNDERTOW: floating continuous rollers and four-bar deployment

Version: UNDERTOW. [PDF p13](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=13)

**Published construction:** Foam/silicone continuous rollers, floating front plate, rubber-band dead-zone belts and four-bar deployment.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Admit longways coral and yield during collisions.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A continuous compliant surface can avoid the discrete kicks caused by spaced wheels, while a floating roller accommodates the changing cross-section presented by a tube approaching diagonally. Rubber bands bridge regions where neither main roller can maintain ownership. They also introduce wear, tracking and tension variables, so their role should be tested rather than treated as decorative assistance. The four-bar positions the deployed pickup without requiring its pivot at the very front of the chassis. Copy the contact geometry and trajectory together: substituting a single pivot can change both bumper clearance and handoff.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Approach coral at a grid of angles, measure uninterrupted contact, and repeat after a wall impact and belt replacement.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## UNDERTOW: flatten and index before handing off

Version: UNDERTOW. [PDF p14](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=14) · [PDF p15](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=15)

**Published construction:** Eight compliant/star wheels; guide wedges, flattening yoke and beam breaks; separate steep station funnel.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Create a repeatable handoff from either source.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Ground and station pickup arrive with different velocities and orientations. A common indexer lets the end effector see a smaller set of input states, but the funnel and pickup must not feed incompatible positions. Wedges and a flattening wheel create deliberate constraints; if they constrain too many dimensions at once, the tube can wedge rather than align. Sensors should identify the indexed state before the receiver moves. The station funnel adds redundancy and autonomous options, so its value depends on how much extra envelope and mass it costs alongside floor acquisition.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare handoff time and jam rate from both sources with skewed and bouncing arrivals; test the full state sequence after a missed detection.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## UNDERTOW: fast continuous elevator

Version: UNDERTOW. [PDF p16](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=16)

**Published construction:** Two-stage internal-belt lift; two X60s; welded support frame; team reports roughly 0.3-second full travel.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reach scoring heights rapidly and maintain stiffness.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A fast travel number does not include settling, alignment or release. Internal belts protect the drive path but make access, tensioning and inspection more important. The support frame must react lateral inertia from the raised wrist as well as the elevator’s own acceleration. If the system reaches height quickly but sways outside the coral-placement tolerance, the useful cycle has not improved. A matched recommendation needs carriage mass, output stiffness, profile constraints and a maintenance plan rather than only belt width and motor count.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure time until the coral tip enters and stays within scoring tolerance, not merely until the encoder reaches its height setpoint.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## UNDERTOW: Flying V compliance and an L1 pass-through

Version: UNDERTOW. [PDF p18](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=18) · [PDF p19](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=19)

**Published construction:** Wrist-mounted compliant coral roller, pipe-aligning Flying V, cam-controlled rear hoop and shared algae drive.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Fast branch placement with controlled piece handoff.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Mechanical alignment can absorb residual chassis error by guiding the end effector relative to the actual pipe. It must do so without pushing the tube into a trapped configuration or transmitting a large side load into the wrist. The movable hoop illustrates why the handoff and L1 scoring states differ: a stop that is necessary to receive coral can obstruct the intended exit. Sharing a motor between piece contacts reduces moving mass but couples their speed and torque requirements. The complete mechanism includes the cam state and sensing, not just the front roller.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Map tolerated lateral and angular pipe error, test handoff against L1 pass-through, and repeat with a worn wheel and occupied nearby branches.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## UNDERTOW: capture first, then winch the robot under the cage

Version: UNDERTOW. [PDF p17](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=17)

**Published construction:** Powered roller claw, passive latch, gas-spring deployment and low-mounted ratcheting winch.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Acquire a cage quickly and retain suspension after disable.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Separating capture from lifting allows the capture wheels to optimize entry while the winch carries the robot load. The latch and cage reaction surfaces must take over reliably before the wheels stop providing traction. Remoting the winch lowers mass but lengthens the tension path and adds rope-routing concerns. A deep-climb recommendation should identify acquisition tolerance, how the cage rotates, where the chain ends relative to the robot’s center of mass, and the load path after power is removed.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test swinging-cage acquisition, transition from powered rollers to latch, and power-off retention with the actual rope routing.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Intake | 3-in front; 2-in kicker; ~15-ft/s surface; reported ~0.15-s deploy | [Source p13](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=13) |
| Indexer | eight 4-in wheels; 8:48 gears; ~30-ft/s surface | [Source p14](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=14) |
| Lift | 11:50 gears; 36T pulleys; ~52-in travel; reported ~0.3 s | [Source p16](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=16) |
| Climb | 1:224 source notation; ratcheting rope winch | [Source p17](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=17) |
| Wrist | 210°; reported ~0.2 s; output CANcoder | [Source p18](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=18) |

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.

# 2025-2910: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## SPECTRE: base and module revision at Championship

Version: SPECTRE. [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=5)

**Published construction:** District Mk4i modules changed to prototype Mk5 at Worlds; ballast placement also changed.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Low center of gravity and short-cycle maneuverability.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A module swap is a robot version, even if the scoring architecture looks unchanged. Saving module weight can be reinvested as low ballast rather than removed from the robot, changing traction and stability differently from a simple weight reduction. A wide tread and different enclosure can alter friction, debris protection and maintenance. Retuning drive and autonomous behavior is part of the mechanical change: old acceleration and feedforward assumptions should not be carried over without measurements. The database should name the competition stage associated with each configuration.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare module slip, current and stopping repeatability before and after the change with the actual ballast and bumper package.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## SPECTRE: remote power at an integrated pivot

Version: SPECTRE. [PDF p6](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=6) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=9)

**Published construction:** Separate three-X60 shoulder and extension gearboxes; dead-axle pivot; two-stage cascade arm.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Fast motion with a low stowed center of gravity and serviceable arm.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Keeping heavy actuators near the base reduces distal inertia and lets the arm respond without carrying all its drive mass at the tip. The price is a more complicated transmission across the pivot and through the telescope. A coaxial extension drive must preserve tension and alignment over the shoulder’s range. A large shared pivot can support stiffness and removal, but its clamps and end plugs become critical load interfaces. Motor count alone does not explain speed: the arm’s inertia, reduction, current limits and acceleration profile determine whether it can move quickly without rocking the chassis.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure end-point settling after simultaneous pivot and extension; test removal/reinstallation repeatability and chain tension over the full range.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## SPECTRE: acquire, orient and score with one end mechanism

Version: SPECTRE. [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=8)

**Published construction:** Vertical and horizontal roller sets; four CANrange sensors; reversible front/back handoff and scoring.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Serve coral and algae tasks with the same manipulator.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Combining acquisition and scoring avoids a separate transfer interface, but makes the moving assembly larger and creates competing contact requirements. Coral has to be oriented differently for branches and L1; algae needs enough compliant pinch to stay captured during rapid motion. Multiple sensors can distinguish piece position and direction, provided their views remain reliable for both geometries. Front/back scoring reduces chassis rotation when the software chooses a sensible approach. The architecture should be assessed by complete cycle time and reach under defense, not by the number of available poses.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test front/back coral scoring, intentional horizontal L1 placement and algae capture with the same rollers after wear.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## SPECTRE: moving climb carriage manages the hanging center

Version: SPECTRE. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=7) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=9)

**Published construction:** Powered one-bar cage capture; carriage slides along arm; shoulder lifts; extension locks to bumper structure.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Balance under the chain while reusing the main arm.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The carriage is not just a convenient mount. Its translation changes where the cage pulls relative to the robot’s mass, allowing a controlled transition into suspension. The shoulder then supplies the lifting work and the arm lock supplies a post-match retention path. Those are separate functions and should be recorded separately. Reusing the arm reduces dedicated hardware but raises its required load and reliability. Any recommendation needs the actual cage contact, latch, shoulder and lock sequence rather than assuming that a strong scoring arm can safely substitute for a complete climber.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Capture at several swing angles, verify carriage travel under load, and test power-off retention through the intended bumper lock.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## SPECTRE: automate approach choice and L1 placement

Version: SPECTRE. [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=10)

**Published construction:** Automatic front/back reef choice; level/side selected by driver; distinct base/top L1 states.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Remove repeated alignment work from the driver.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Choosing the nearest face or easiest orientation can save time, but the shortest geometric route is not always the least congested or the most valuable remaining target. L1 stacking creates an occupancy problem as well as a pose problem: a fixed placement height is insufficient once previous coral changes the landing surface. The driver still needs strategic control over task and side, with software handling repeatable motion. A mechanism recommendation should include the sensors, pose references and operator choices required to realize its cycle advantage.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test automatic choices near boundaries between faces and with populated L1; verify deliberate driver override and recovery after a failed release.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Pivot/extension | 120.83:1 shoulder; 6.28:1 extension; three X60s each | [Source p6](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=6) |
| Intake | one X60 horizontal; two X44 vertical; four CANrange sensors | [Source p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=8) |
| Arm | two-stage cascade; #25 chains plus 3-mm UHMWPE rope | [Source p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=9) |

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.

contextDocs.title: 2025-341: technical construction and mechanism reasoning
contextDocs.body:
# 2025-341: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## MISS DAISY: orient on the floor and preserve collision compliance

Version: MISS DAISY XXIII. [PDF p19](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=19) · [PDF p20](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=20) · [PDF p21](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=21) · [PDF p22](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=22) · [PDF p23](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=23)

**Published construction:** Sprung OTB rollers with ramps; later stronger front tube and round shafts.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Broad-orientation acquisition and impact survival.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Orienting the tube before lifting reduces the number of uncontrolled handoff states. A wide compliant roller captures early while ramps and passive contacts bias the tube toward the desired orientation. That can fail if a ramp starts lifting one end too soon. Structural damage also changes the ball path: a bent mounting tube can turn a nominally symmetric intake into a one-sided jam. Preserve the sequence of revisions, because a successful final contact geometry may rely on the preceding stiffness fix.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Film diagonal approaches from both sides before and after impacts; measure ramp and roller alignment rather than judging symmetry by eye.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## MISS DAISY: diagnose jams from observed contact

Version: MISS DAISY XXIII. [PDF p24](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=24)

**Published construction:** Reduced compression, relocated support shaft, changed hard stops and redesigned ramp bends.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Slow-motion review identified different jams at successive events.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A jam is a geometric event, not merely insufficient motor power. A tube can press a belt into a support, climb at one end while the other end remains constrained, or stop a roller whose structure is bent. Each mode requires a different change. Moving the wheels forward changes both normal force and where the tube begins to rise. A useful agent should first ask which contacts stop moving and where the tube becomes over-constrained; recommending more torque without this observation can destroy the part that reveals the fault.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Create a repeatable failed orientation, isolate the first contact that arrests motion, change one dimension and compare the failure frequency.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## MISS DAISY: grip algae while allowing coral release

Version: MISS DAISY XXIII. [PDF p27](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=27) · [PDF p28](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=28) · [PDF p29](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=29) · [PDF p30](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=30)

**Published construction:** Coral compression reduced to 0.375 inch; drive ratio revised; harder wheels and algae shields added.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Improve coral release, pulley durability and algae retention.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The two pieces demand conflicting grip behavior. Increasing compression can improve retention but make a tube difficult to release without disturbing the target. A harder wheel can resist wear yet reduce conformity and change normal force. A larger drive pulley may reduce tooth loading and skipping while changing speed and torque. Shields can prevent a soft ball from folding around the side plates, addressing a failure that motor current alone cannot solve. These are linked empirical tradeoffs, so the record should preserve both piece types and the tested release geometry.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure coral release force and algae retention after representative wheel wear; inspect pulley teeth during repeated high-torque captures.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## MISS DAISY: rope geometry and structural stiffness evolved together

Version: MISS DAISY XXIII. [PDF p31](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=31) · [PDF p32](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=32) · [PDF p33](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=33) · [PDF p34](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=34) · [PDF p35](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=35) · [PDF p36](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=36) · [PDF p37](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=37)

**Published construction:** Horizontal Dyneema spool inspired by 1678; continuous lift; later U-crossplate and rigid side support.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Solve rope slip, poor tension and elevator lateral play.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A lift can have accurate motor position while its carriage moves laterally because the structure and rope system are different error sources. Rope routing should keep each run aligned as winding radius changes; overlapping wraps change effective motion per motor turn. A stiff top crosspiece limits upright splay, while a triangulated or rigid support reacts side loading without relying only on adjustable rods. These revisions show why copying the final spool alone is insufficient. The recommendation needs the complete routing, tension system and support geometry.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Track carriage height versus motor position and lateral tip error independently; inspect winding over repeated full strokes under load.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## MISS DAISY: shoulder and wrist serve different coordinates

Version: MISS DAISY XXIII. [PDF p38](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=38) · [PDF p39](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=39) · [PDF p40](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=40)

**Published construction:** 45:1 shoulder with lantern gear; 21.4:1 wrist with about ±100° motion.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Move between robot sides and reorient coral without collisions.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The shoulder changes the end effector’s position and reach, while the wrist changes the piece orientation. Those motions need not be performed serially, but simultaneous movement requires a collision-aware path. A lantern gear can place the reduction close to the output and control backlash; its performance still depends on bearing alignment and tooth/pin wear. A dead-axle wrist offers a clear reaction path, but the cantilevered mass and cable routing contribute torque and deflection. The useful model is the coral’s swept volume, not only each joint’s independent limit.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Generate and physically check the coral envelope during side swaps; measure output angle repeatability under reversing load.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## MISS DAISY: passive harpoon over a wheeled grabber

Version: MISS DAISY XXIII. [PDF p44](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=44) · [PDF p45](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=45) · [PDF p46](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=46) · [PDF p47](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=47)

**Published construction:** Levering climber; passive sprung harpoon; 675:1 reduction; steel gears replaced inadequate aluminum gears.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Similar capture performance with fewer vulnerable parts.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A high reduction can provide lifting torque, but it does not reduce the load carried by the final gear and support shaft. Material changes at that interface can therefore matter more than adding motor power. A passive hook can outperform powered acquisition when the robot’s approach already supplies sufficient engagement force and the cage geometry naturally directs the bar into the latch. That simplifies the controller while placing more importance on the approach envelope and retention geometry. Capture reliability should be assessed with swing and imperfect alignment, not only a stationary cage.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure engagement tolerance and inspect final-stage stress after repeated climbs; test retention with the cage rotated and the robot disabled.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## MISS DAISY: remove a dedicated algae intake that adds no useful capability

Version: MISS DAISY XXIII. [PDF p41](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=41) · [PDF p42](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=42)

**Published construction:** A separate floor-algae collector was removed after prototype comparisons.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** It did not outperform the end effector enough to justify complexity.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A subsystem can satisfy its own requirements and still be a poor robot-level choice. A dedicated collector may save a little positioning time while costing envelope, sensors, wiring, maintenance and driver decisions. If the primary end effector already serves the intended algae role, the marginal gain must exceed those costs. This is the right level for an architecture agent to reason: compare complete task contribution and reliability rather than rewarding more mechanisms. Keep the removed design in the history as an evaluated alternative, not as an installed feature of the final robot.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare complete algae cycles and failure recovery with and without the auxiliary system, including time spent switching modes.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Claw | 8.125:1 final listed; 0.375-in coral compression; 4.17-lb claw | [Source p28](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=28) |
| Wheel revision | 35A → 50A; drive pulley 14T → 16T | [Source p30](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=30) |
| Lift | two X60s; 3:1; 1.5-in spool; 52-in extension | [Source p36](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=36) |
| Shoulder | 45:1 | [Source p39](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=39) |
| Wrist | 21.4:1; ±100° | [Source p40](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=40) |
| Climber | 675:1; 6.8 lb; reported 3-s climb plus acquisition | [Source p47](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=47) |

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.

contextDocs.title: 2025-4946: technical construction and mechanism reasoning
contextDocs.body:
# 2025-4946: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## Alpha Dogs: retention, compliance and source fallback

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p7](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=7) · [PDF p8](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=8)

**Published construction:** Single roller became dual; long compliance linkage became compact sprung arm; first event used station funnel.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Solve escaping coral, collision vulnerability and packaging.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Capturing a tube is not the same as retaining it after the first contact. The second roller can close an escape path while increasing the need to control compression. An impact-yielding linkage can protect the pickup, but a long arm consumes chassis volume and increases bending moment. The report’s station-funnel fallback is evidence of a competition configuration, while its ground-intake drawings include developmental versions. Keep those distinct when recommending inspiration: a promising prototype is not automatically a demonstrated event mechanism.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test retention during braking and reverse motion; verify the exact event configuration before using a version as a performance example.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Alpha Dogs: conveyor and tray progressively consolidated

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p8](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=8) · [PDF p9](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=9)

**Published construction:** Opposed star-wheel conveyors evolved into a lighter polycarbonate assembly and integrated receiving cup.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Straighten coral and simplify the transfer structure.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A conveyor that both straightens and transports a tube can avoid a separate orientation stage, but its downstream tray must stop the tube without sending it back into the drive contacts. Removing redundant support material can improve access and mass while changing alignment under load. A receiving cup reduces uncertainty in the arm’s pickup position, provided it has no lip that prevents release into the gripper. The best architecture depends on the handoff’s repeatability and recovery after a partial acquisition, not only its nominal travel time.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test varied tube orientation and arrival speed, then interrupt the handoff to verify that the mechanism can recover without driver intervention.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Alpha Dogs: gripper envelope changed the architecture

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p10](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=10)

**Published construction:** Combined piece gripper revised after reach/envelope problems; elevator-mounted arrangement developed.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Keep the placing assembly within the intended geometry.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Adding a second piece function changes more than roller spacing: the swept volume, center of mass and necessary approach path may all grow. A gripper that works on a bench can violate the robot’s usable envelope when attached to an arm. Moving it onto an elevator changes the kinematic problem but does not by itself prove accurate release. The report leaves some final geometry and transmission details unresolved, so an agent should retrieve CAD or later event evidence rather than invent an elevator ratio or a final mechanism sequence.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Check the full loaded piece envelope and actual event revision; measure pickup, hold and release separately for each piece.

**Limits:** This engineering report documents development. It does not establish every final CAD dimension, elevator reduction or competition use of every pictured prototype.

## Alpha Dogs: reduce the cage mechanism to its useful load path

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p6](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=6)

**Published construction:** Complex capture concepts led to a simpler pivoting jack; chain endpoint targeted the robot’s mass center.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce weight and improve hanging geometry.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A cage mechanism must transfer the robot’s weight through a secure contact while allowing the robot to settle into a stable orientation. A design can capture well yet demand excessive torque because its chain line remains far from the center of mass. Simplifying to a lever reduces parts but can concentrate load at the main pivot and rope attachment. The analysis should identify the actual hanging geometry and load path, with an explicit boundary between proposed and competed revisions.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test off-center acquisition and load transition; confirm the final revision with dated match or pit evidence.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Alpha Dogs: camera view and reef occupancy are architecture inputs

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p12](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=12) · [PDF p17](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=17) · [PDF p18](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=18) · [PDF p19](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=19) · [PDF p20](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=20)

**Published construction:** Camera angle revised for close tags; field-region alignment and operator-entered reef occupancy are described.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce blind spots and repeated target-selection work.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A camera can see an AprilTag far away yet lose it at the exact distance where precision is needed. Mount angle and obstruction therefore belong in the early CAD review. Keeping reef occupancy in software changes the operator’s task from repeatedly aiming to maintaining a reliable shared state. Incorrect occupancy can send the robot toward a filled branch, so the system needs a quick correction and manual override. The mechanism recommendation should include what target information it assumes the controls will supply.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test tag visibility at every final scoring pose and recovery from deliberately incorrect occupancy entries.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.

# 2025-5940: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## BREAD 2025: floating intake plus dedicated L1 restraint

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_SqgJesNe7Tdq_ZP9_-2ZuEF4tBZFTFI/view#page=5)

**Published construction:** Floating front roller, centering wedges and deployable L1 bar with anti-bounce hooks.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Broad pickup and controlled L1 release.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A tube entering lengthwise needs space to rotate; a fixed narrow contact can eject it before alignment finishes. The floating front roller accommodates that transition. The L1 bar serves a different task: it changes the release boundary and prevents the intake from lifting or letting coral bounce away. This is a useful example for an agent because L1 capability is not merely “run the intake backward.” The intended orientation, release contact and state of the front roller determine whether coral stays where the alliance needs it.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test L1 placement at several existing pile heights and compare bounce-out with and without the restraint engaged.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## BREAD 2025: asymmetric star-wheel orientation

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p6](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_SqgJesNe7Tdq_ZP9_-2ZuEF4tBZFTFI/view#page=6)

**Published construction:** Asymmetric star-wheel indexer, beam-break extra-piece rejection and repeatable handoff tray.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce alignment jams and reject an unwanted second tube.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Symmetry can preserve a bad equilibrium: both ends of a skewed tube may be driven equally without ever rotating into the desired orientation. A deliberate asymmetry can break that state, but may also introduce a preferred direction and different behavior for mirror-image approaches. The extra-piece logic must distinguish a second tube from a long first tube passing multiple sensors. A tray then provides a controlled receiving state. Test these as one chain rather than optimizing the indexer’s standalone speed.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Feed mirror-image diagonal tubes and closely spaced pairs; record orientation time, rejection errors and handoff repeatability.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## BREAD 2025: cascade lift with counterbalance and chain control

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_SqgJesNe7Tdq_ZP9_-2ZuEF4tBZFTFI/view#page=7) · [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_SqgJesNe7Tdq_ZP9_-2ZuEF4tBZFTFI/view#page=8)

**Published construction:** Two-stage cascade; two X60s at 7:1; constant-force springs; cantilevered pivot and chain tensioner.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Rapid lift with lower current and controlled transmission.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Counterbalance reduces the gravitational load the motors must supply during part of the stroke, but its force and mounting geometry affect upward and downward behavior differently. A cascade lift magnifies travel and velocity while changing the force seen by each stage. A rolling chain tensioner can manage slack during acceleration, but does not cure a misaligned sprocket or insufficient tooth engagement. The cantilevered wrist support must react both bending and overturning moments. A fast reported stroke needs a settling and placement test to establish its useful cycle value.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Log lift current and tracking in both directions, inspect tension during reversals, and measure tip displacement under sideways load.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## BREAD 2025: shared drive for coral and algae contacts

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_SqgJesNe7Tdq_ZP9_-2ZuEF4tBZFTFI/view#page=9)

**Published construction:** One X60 drives distinct coral/algae contacts through different ratios and printed gear-pulley combinations.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Handle both pieces while reducing moving mass.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A shared motor saves wiring and mass but ties the contact speeds to fixed ratios. The design must provide enough algae holding torque without making coral release too abrupt. Combining a gear and pulley can shorten the assembly and remove redundant hubs, while concentrating loads into the printed part and its bearing interface. Material choice, print orientation and temperature therefore belong in the durability review. A successful borrowed geometry requires matching compression and piece position, not only duplicating the nominal ratio.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure algae retention and coral release after repeated cycles and heating; inspect printed tooth roots and bearing fits.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## BREAD 2025: centered single-tube cage support

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_SqgJesNe7Tdq_ZP9_-2ZuEF4tBZFTFI/view#page=10)

**Published construction:** Six-pound spear/flyswatter collector; spring deploy; string winch; reported 1.5-second lift.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Center the cage and use a compact lifting package.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A passive centering shape can simplify acquisition while making the load path highly dependent on where the cage settles. If retention relies partly on robot weight and friction, the transition into suspension needs careful testing before full load is applied. Spring deployment saves an actively driven extension but requires a reliable latch and stow sequence. The winch reduction determines available force, while rope radius and cage lever arm determine actual robot lift. A lift-time claim should remain distinct from total acquisition-plus-settling time.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test swinging-cage entry and interrupted lifts, including a case where only one contact is initially engaged.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## BREAD 2025: low chassis and direct reef ranging

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p4](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_SqgJesNe7Tdq_ZP9_-2ZuEF4tBZFTFI/view#page=4)

**Published construction:** Dropped X2 modules, low frame and CANrange reef-distance sensing.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Low center of gravity and repeatable approach.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Lowering the frame can improve stability while reducing ground clearance and access. A direct range measurement near the reef can refine the final approach, but only if the sensor sees the intended surface rather than a tube, branch or oblique panel. It should complement a known geometric model and a validated scoring tolerance. Treat a sensor as an observation with failure modes rather than proof of alignment.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Map distance error over reef approach angle, piece occupancy and elevator position; check collision and service clearances.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Intake | 65.33:1 deploy | [Source p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_SqgJesNe7Tdq_ZP9_-2ZuEF4tBZFTFI/view#page=5) |
| Indexer | 2:1 shaft reduction | [Source p6](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_SqgJesNe7Tdq_ZP9_-2ZuEF4tBZFTFI/view#page=6) |
| Lift | 7:1; two X60s; two 10-lbf constant-force springs | [Source p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_SqgJesNe7Tdq_ZP9_-2ZuEF4tBZFTFI/view#page=7) |
| Pivot | 52.08:1; 3.5-in-ID bearing | [Source p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_SqgJesNe7Tdq_ZP9_-2ZuEF4tBZFTFI/view#page=8) |
| End effector | 6.66:1 algae; 5.55:1 coral | [Source p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_SqgJesNe7Tdq_ZP9_-2ZuEF4tBZFTFI/view#page=9) |
| Climb | 25:1 winch; 6 lb; reported 1.5-s lift | [Source p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_SqgJesNe7Tdq_ZP9_-2ZuEF4tBZFTFI/view#page=10) |

# 2026-1987: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## CYCLONE: collector and frame share the impact path

Version: CYCLONE. [PDF p8](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=8) · [PDF p9](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=9)

**Published construction:** Full-width linear collector; 1.125-inch rollers; load-spreading hubs and washers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Acquire five columns and survive contact.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** An exposed roller’s compliance must be paired with a force path into the chassis. A small washer can concentrate force and start a crack even if the main plate is otherwise flexible. Distributing that load across a hub or a larger washer reduces local pressure, but the joint must still allow the intended movement. The collector width also has an autonomous geometry consequence: it changes which fuel columns can be reached without the chassis crossing a contested route. A width figure should be linked to the effective acquisition envelope rather than merely the distance between arms.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Map acquisition success across the entire mouth with off-center hits, then repeat after controlled impact loading.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## CYCLONE: DYE-inspired rotor with independent feed

Version: CYCLONE. [PDF p10](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=10)

**Published construction:** 22-inch rotor; eight-fuel ring; separate rotation/feed drives; reported 18-fuel/s feed.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Maintain bulk-to-single-stream flow in a compact package.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A rotor is not just a rotating bucket. Its moving boundary, internal feed contact and exit geometry jointly determine whether fuel circulates, enters the ring, or jams. Independent feed drive lets the team tune the launch supply without requiring the whole bulk pile to turn at that speed. A lower-profile center obstruction improves the area through which fuel can enter; reversing must not turn a hook or seam into a trap. A theoretical ring count multiplied by rotation rate is only an upper bound: pockets must actually fill and discharge.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure pocket occupancy and output variability at full, half and nearly empty loads; test reversing a deliberately bridged inlet.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## CYCLONE: floating hood, preload and turret support

Version: CYCLONE. [PDF p11](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=11)

**Published construction:** Compact turret; floating hood; constant-force spring; through-bore sensing; powered hood rollers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce backlash and preserve storage volume.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Spring preload can keep a reduction loaded against one tooth flank, reducing reversal uncertainty, but adds a torque that the motor must overcome in the opposite direction. Measuring the output rather than only the motor helps detect residual compliance between gearbox and hood. The feed path and turret bearing need common structural alignment; a compact height is valuable only if it does not permit the hood to deflect enough to change the exit angle. Powered hood rollers alter the spin/contact state, so their ratio belongs in the shot calibration rather than being treated as passive guidance.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure hood angle repeatability from both approach directions and at several turret headings; compare loaded and unloaded structure.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## CYCLONE: moving-shot compensation and variable feed

Version: CYCLONE. [PDF p13](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=13)

**Published construction:** Gyro latency compensation, empirical flight time and variable rotor speed are documented.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Maintain accurate mobile firing and stable throughput.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A turret can cancel chassis heading only if the controller uses the correct observation time and the actual release state. A latency error grows with angular velocity and can look like a mechanical aiming bias. Rotor speed also changes shot timing and inlet loading; a firing command is not the same as a ball leaving the hood. The mechanical and control record should include this delay and its variation. Slowing the feed may improve delivered score if it reduces wheel droop or keeps the exit state within tolerance.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Time-stamp vision, gyro, turret position, feeder transitions and ball release; compare miss direction against angular and translational velocity.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Intake | 1.5:1 rollers; 3.6:1 deploy | [Source p9](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=9) |
| Rotor | 22-in diameter; 20.67:1 rotation; 1:1 feed; reported 18 fuel/s | [Source p10](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=10) |
| Shooter | 4-in 60A main; two X60s at 1.25:1; 80.5:1 hood | [Source p11](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=11) |
| Turret | 25.6:1; 360° described range | [Source p11](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=11) |

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.

# 2026-2046: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## BEARRICADE: collector evolution and impact reinforcement

Version: BEARRICADE Mk.II. [PDF p22](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=22) · [PDF p23](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=23)

**Published construction:** Three rollers; dead-axle polycarbonate tubes; later metal stub-axle reinforcement.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Remove pickup dead zones and improve impact survival.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A compliant tube may survive bending while its end attachment fails. That makes the stub axle, bearing retention and local side-plate load path as important as the roller material. A lower transition roller closes the region where a single upper roller can push fuel rather than capture it. More contact points can improve acquisition, but they also add belt drag and opportunities for a ball to be over-compressed. The relevant question is whether the ball experiences a continuous forward velocity through the bumper transition, including when the robot is moving and the hopper is already full.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Film pickup from the side at maximum approach speed; inspect stub-axle displacement after repeated oblique hits.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## BEARRICADE: linked hopper and capacity states

Version: BEARRICADE Mk.II. [PDF p24](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=24) · [PDF p25](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=25)

**Published construction:** Collector-linked sliding walls; net; reported 60 fuel under trench and 75–80 over bump.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Increase useful storage without losing the travel state.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** These capacity figures describe different operating envelopes, not one universally available volume. A net can retain the top layer while allowing a changing envelope, but it adds elastic forces and can push fuel into the throat or against a wall. Sliding walls need enough overlap to remain guided under a side load without creating an inward shelf. Coupling deployment to the collector saves an actuator and synchronizes the opening, but also couples hopper faults to pickup. A good borrowed implementation preserves service access and allows the robot to recover when only one side deploys correctly.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure retained and feedable capacity after loaded bump travel, then test deployment with a damaged slide or displaced net.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## BEARRICADE: why the belt bed became rollers

Version: BEARRICADE Mk.II. [PDF p17](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=17) · [PDF p18](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=18) · [PDF p26](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=26) · [PDF p27](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=27)

**Published construction:** Belt bed abandoned; ten 1.25-inch rollers, successive 21:20 speed steps, two X44s.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Belt tension and ball motion were limiting the early design.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A belt bed pulls continuously on its support shafts; the tension required to transmit power can bend those shafts even before fuel loading is considered. A roller floor moves that challenge into shaft spacing, surface grip and transmission design. Incrementally faster rollers can stretch spacing between balls, but only if the fuel actually follows the surface and does not simply slip. Agitation is not automatically helpful: repeated upward kicks can keep a ball from settling into the receiving contact. This is why a rate test must observe the inlet to the superstructure, not only the speed of the floor.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure time to empty under several fill levels, compare stepped speeds against equal speeds, and count time balls spend recirculating at the inlet.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## BEARRICADE: integrated S-path and two-lane drum

Version: BEARRICADE Mk.II. [PDF p28](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=28) · [PDF p29](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=29) · [PDF p30](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=30) · [PDF p31](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=31)

**Published construction:** Four-inch drum; printed backing; hood range −10° to 60°; triple-lane prototype became dual.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Match launch capacity to indexing and preserve packaging.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Reducing lane count can improve the robot if the extra lane forces a worse feeder, more current or a larger structure. The S-shaped path is an integration choice, not a universal superiority claim over a J-shaped route. Negative launch angles create a specific close-to-hub shot envelope; they need geometric clearance and empirical tuning, especially where the robot is braced against a field element. Integrating shooter and tower plates can remove redundant material and align contact surfaces, while increasing the consequence of damage to that shared structure. The same binder also shows a turret concept; that image alone does not prove it competed.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test near-hub reverse shots and far shots at depleted battery; inspect integrated plate deflection while the feeder is fully loaded.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## BEARRICADE: delete the low-value climb

Version: BEARRICADE Mk.II. [PDF p6](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=6) · [PDF p32](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=32)

**Published construction:** The team rejected a six-pound, ten-point climbing package that occupied hopper space.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Fuel contribution outweighed the mechanism’s opportunity cost.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** This is direct team evidence for treating climb as a low-priority 2026 architecture choice. Its cost is larger than its actuator and hook: it can remove storage, require alignment practice, complicate wiring and consume testing that could improve fuel flow. A calculation that includes only seconds spent climbing misses those development and packaging costs. Conversely, a near-free existing device could have a different marginal cost. The agent should begin with the observed fuel-dominant game, then require a specific positive marginal case before adding climb. It should not recommend one merely because the manual awards points for it.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare scored-fuel loss from displaced volume and lost testing time against the expected climb contribution in the intended event role.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Base | 27×27-in; Mk5n L1 source label | [Source p20](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=20) |
| Capacity | 60 under trench; 75–80 over bump; team report | [Source p25](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=25) |
| Floor | ten 1.25-in rollers; 21:20 successive steps; 1410→2297 RPM | [Source p27](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=27) |
| Shooter | 4-in drum; listed 3000 RPM; −10°–60° hood | [Source p31](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=31) |
| Climb deletion | 6 lb; 10-point capability; occupied hopper volume | [Source p32](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=32) |

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.

# 2026-2056: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## DESPERATE MEASURES: linear collector as a controllable spring

Version: DESPERATE MEASURES rebuild. [PDF p8](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=8) · [PDF p9](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=9)

**Published construction:** Double-layer polycarbonate rack; two 2-inch rollers; low-stator-current deployment.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Large acquisition area with passive impact retraction.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A backdrivable, current-limited rack can yield during a collision rather than make the gearbox a rigid stop. That behavior depends on friction, reduction, acceleration limits and the controller remaining enabled; it is not supplied by polycarbonate alone. Stacking a structural plate beside the rack allows the designer to distribute load without relying only on gear teeth. A paired-roller collector should preserve positive contact as fuel crosses the bumper. The matching chassis and slide must react lateral hits, because a low-current motor primarily helps the axial direction.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure peak rack load during frontal and sideways impacts; check tooth engagement and deployment after the test.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DESPERATE MEASURES: active floor and inventory policy

Version: DESPERATE MEASURES rebuild. [PDF p10](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=10) · [PDF p20](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=20)

**Published construction:** 1.5-inch powered floor rollers; net; CANrange minimum-inventory control while passing.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Keep fuel available for the next scoring shift.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Inventory sensing changes the job of a passer. Passing every available ball can improve the alliance pile but leave this robot empty when the shift turns. A minimum reserve is a control policy tied to how quickly the robot can refill, return and shoot. A distance sensor sees a local surface, not a perfect total count; a sloped or bridged pile can produce the same reading at very different usable inventories. The threshold needs validation under different pile shapes and while accelerating. Reserve logic should have an operator override when alliance strategy intentionally assigns all fuel elsewhere.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare sensor reading with deliverable inventory for uneven fills and motion; measure reserve adequacy at the start of each shift.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DESPERATE MEASURES: constrained belts and collision sorting

Version: DESPERATE MEASURES rebuild. [PDF p12](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=12) · [PDF p13](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=13)

**Published construction:** Two rubber-coated conveyors, printed carryways, vertical kicker, quarter-pipe feed.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Turn bulk fuel into a reliable stream.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The carryway controls the support beneath the belt so compression does not change with belt sag. The vertical kicker addresses a different failure: two balls arriving at the quarter-pipe entrance can lock each other before either is captured. That distinction matters when diagnosing a singulator. Increasing belt speed does not necessarily release an arch; changing relative contact directions or reversing one element can. The quarter-pipe must preserve contact through the bend and deliver fuel at an appropriate velocity to the turret. A compact throat earns hopper space only if it remains serviceable and can clear a hard jam.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Feed deliberately paired balls and partially collapsed fuel; log current signatures before and after reversal and inspect carryway wear.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DESPERATE MEASURES: compact turret and continuous hood

Version: DESPERATE MEASURES rebuild. [PDF p14](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=14) · [PDF p15](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=15)

**Published construction:** Eight-inch bearing; ±185° turret; 4-inch Fairlane wheel; separate backspin kicker; variable hood.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Score and pass across a broad envelope.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The bearing and base plate must keep the launch contact aligned while the chassis accelerates and balls enter the shooter. Independent back contact permits spin tuning without changing the main wheel, but also introduces another speed and recovery condition. A range slightly greater than one turn reduces the frequency of an unwind; it does not create unlimited rotation. The cable chain must survive the worst combined hood and turret state. For a recommendation, the compact swept envelope and the singulator’s feed location are as important as the shooter’s wheel diameter.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Map accuracy over turret angle and hood angle, including near both cable limits and under representative chassis acceleration.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DESPERATE TIMES to DESPERATE MEASURES

Version: DESPERATE MEASURES rebuild. [PDF p2](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=2) · [PDF p24](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=24)

**Published construction:** Original hopperless four-to-two-to-one path replaced; turret reused; Orbit 1690 explicitly credited.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Original throughput did not justify minimal storage.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** This is a valuable negative result because it separates the concept from its execution. A narrowing conveyor can spread fuel longitudinally as it accelerates, yet still fail to maintain sufficient launch supply. Without a hopper, every interruption in acquisition becomes an interruption in scoring. Reusing the turret preserved calibrated software and known interfaces while the rest of the architecture changed. The proper historical record includes both machines and the transition; the later successful package should not be projected backward onto the initial competitions or treated as a season-long fixed architecture.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** For a rebuild, identify which calibrated interfaces can survive unchanged and which performance assumptions require new integrated testing.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Intake | 12:30 belt; 8:40 deploy gear; 12T 8DP rack pinion | [Source p8](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=8) |
| Singulator | 12:36 feed belts; 16:28 shooter-feed gears | [Source p12](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=12) |
| Turret | ±185°; 34° hood stroke; 73.5°–39.5° release | [Source p14](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=14) |
| Launch | 4-in Fairlane; 28:34 belt; independent backspin kicker | [Source p14](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=14) |

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.
