# 2026-6329: Roman I and Roman II solve different feed problems

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

Roman I uses a rotating floor/center drum and turret; first-party replies describe a roughly 20.75-inch outer drum and 6-inch center, with no fuel compression. Roman II replaces that path with a full-width roller floor and drum shooter. Its floor pivots about an intake dead shaft for electronics access; long four-bar arms fold under impact. The interview contrasts roughly 8 BPS before the rebuild with a reported 23 afterward.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team ties the rebuild to throughput limitations, the net to substantially greater retained inventory, and compact/flexible intake members to avoiding repeated bending. The release specifically credits 5687’s advice with setting Roman II in motion.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

The strategic change is not simply a faster wheel. Storage, feed width, shooting heading, electrical packaging and intake structure changed together. A comparison should include time spent aiming and avoiding defense, not only an unloaded discharge rate. The original no-compression spindexer and later low-compression drum entry must not be merged into an imaginary hybrid. Service access is especially useful after a rebuild because new routing and wiring require frequent inspection.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Compare complete-cycle output, residual inventory and defended aiming cost for both versions. Verify rate test conditions, and inspect shaft alignment after lifting the floor for service.

# 2026-5687: Capstan deployment and belt-floor lanes are dated fixes, not universal upgrades

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

First-party replies describe 2-inch upper rollers, a 1.25-inch lower roller and about half an inch of compression. The robot changed from roller floor to belt floor between URI and UVM, and from rack deployment to a rope capstan after tooth damage. A 6-inch, 1/8-inch-wall aluminum drum was urethane-coated, machined and balanced; its reported inertia is a little over 80 lb·in².

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team says lower collector compression reduced motor bogging. It reports lower current and faster feeding after the belt-floor change; belt spacing created lanes and reduced fuel spinning in place. Rope deployment addressed rack tooth failures, with rope tension becoming the continuing adjustment.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

This is a useful counterexample to choosing a floor from appearance alone. Belt spacing can organize deformable fuel and remove an unproductive rotating contact state, but that result depends on piece size, belt spacing, load and friction. A capstan cannot skip discrete gear teeth, yet it can slip, stretch, lose tension or suffer anchor damage. The team’s prior capstan experience also changes development risk: the decision was supported by an existing implementation history rather than an untested mechanism adopted casually midseason.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test lane stability, residual fuel, electrical demand and rope tension after repeated impacts. Preserve the report that auto shot timers shortened by over half a second without inventing exact before/after BPS.

## Limits

Selected first-party replies 14, 16, 21, 23, 38, 40 and 42 in topic 515683, plus code-release topic 524737. This is a discussion/code-release review, not a reviewed technical binder.

# 2026-9483: Small turret throughput cannot be inferred from exterior geometry

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

First-party replies describe separate X44s for indexer and spindexer, a spinning floor/cone with no deliberate wall compression, and multiple feeder-wheel and ratio trials. The third intake version adds a kicker and movable secondary kicker. The shooter lacks an upper roller; its moving-shot solution combines tuned lookup data and a physics calculation that compensates for spin.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team says the movable kicker resolves earlier collector difficulty and clarifies that the feeder delivers fuel without spin. It does not provide a definitive causal explanation for all of the achieved spindexer throughput. The added flood light helps close-range tag reliability rather than substantially increasing long-range detection.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

The absence of a counter-roller makes spin an explicit aiming input rather than something to assume away. A compact turret may leave more free hopper area, but the detailed explanation of dead zones and geometry offered by another commenter is expressly an outsider’s hypothesis. Keep that hypothesis separate from the team’s replies. Successful self-unjamming also does not mean jams never occur; the source explicitly acknowledges occasional jams.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Measure entrance spin and moving-shot error across turret angles, record jam/recovery frequency and time, and inspect exact CAD before copying clearances or interpreting an image-based diameter estimate.

## Limits

Selected first-party replies 26, 30, 33, 35 and 47 in topic 515383. Reply 44 is outside analysis, not team intent or a CAD inspection.

# 2025-111: Floor supply changes the mechanism without replacing the scoring arm

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A floor collector was added after Northern Lights while the elevator/arm architecture remained. The retained account identifies roughly 16 pounds of added collector mass, offset by lighter carriage/effector parts. Internal rollers retain coral while the mechanism holds it inverted during algae acquisition. Coral and algae contact regions are offset by about six inches.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team explicitly identifies difficult station alignment under defense and successful floor pickups on 1778/2046 as motivations. The offset is described as allowing algae removal and coral placement in one fluid transition.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A floor collector should be evaluated as a new cycle source, not an isolated pickup demo. The existing arm must keep coral controlled through the algae motion, and mass must be recovered elsewhere without creating excessive compliance. The six-inch separation is an interface dimension for that combined motion; it is not a universal clearance between any two manipulators.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Compare defended station cycles with complete floor-to-score cycles, including failed pickups and inverted retention. Check whether the mass-saving parts preserve L4 accuracy and fatigue life.

## Limits

# 2025-180: Self-deploying acquisition still requires indexed possession

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A compliant four-bar floor collector feeds a funnel and rotating effector on a two-stage continuous elevator. The retained interview describes reverse roller action deploying the collector. One collector sensor and three arm sensors manage entry, indexing and retention; camera-based acquisition chooses a robot pose relative to the pickup.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team connects floor pickup to shorter coral cycles and describes automatic reef-facing behavior as a way to streamline the driver’s next scoring action. It sought both task-related and climb ranking points.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

Passive or roller-driven deployment reduces a dedicated actuator but makes friction, game-piece contact and the initial mechanism state part of the deployment logic. Multiple sensors provide intermediate possession states instead of equating “something entered” with “ready to score.” A combined coral/algae mechanism must also preserve the retained object through rotation, not just when stationary.

# 2025-190: Funnel closure and adaptive grip are separate control problems

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A retroreflective beam across the station funnel detects entry and triggers closure before coral rolls to the end effector. An extending roller acquires ground algae. The retained scoring assembly uses an elevator and arm; the climb deploys with a gas shock and captures the cage while the robot advances.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The interview describes varying algae-holding voltage using current-related feedback, with more effort when the piece is farther out and less after it is seated. Exact thresholds are not supplied.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

An entry beam establishes interruption, not orientation or secure final possession. The handoff therefore needs additional state and a recovery path. Adaptive grip can reduce unnecessary loading after capture, but current also changes with friction, compression and voltage; it cannot be treated as a direct position measurement without calibration. The gas-shock climb similarly depends on a defined hard stop and a controlled chassis approach.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Induce partial entry and bounced coral, measure algae retention at different compression and current, and verify cage capture over realistic lateral offsets.

## Limits

# 2025-359: A telescoping arm avoids a handoff but moves a large work envelope

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The interview describes four shoulder motors with a stated 111:1 reduction, a chain-driven dead-axis pivot, and a two-motor telescoping arm. Its wide collector uses front/back roller groups and aluminum centering guides to acquire differently oriented coral; rigid guide plates reflect coral’s low compressibility. The retained record describes extending stage length for L4/net reach.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team links the multi-motor shoulder to power demand. Its acquisition geometry is intended to bring floor coral into the same mechanism that scores it, avoiding a separate transfer.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

Eliminating a handoff trades transfer risk for arm inertia, sweep clearance and control burden. Extension changes both shoulder torque and the position of the robot’s loaded center of mass. A floor hard stop can define a repeatable pickup plane, but should not be confused with clearance throughout the rest of the motion. Thin coral tolerates less forced compression than foam fuel, so roller selection must be paired with a controlled guide gap.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Map shoulder current and deflection through extension, test pickup against a wall, and verify coral control during acceleration and sudden chassis braking.

## Limits

Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

# 2025-604: Precision depends on stiffness, backlash and feeding order

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A single-stage elevator is driven by chains on both sides to reduce twist; the arm/wrist and shimmed transmissions aim to minimize backlash. The large corrugated-plastic station funnel damps entry. Independently stopped feed rollers can hold coral while the gripper handles algae, and a compact climber fits beneath the funnel.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team explicitly treats accuracy as a mechanical and software requirement, identifies dual-sided elevator drive with resisting twist, and explains pausing coral feed during algae possession.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A vision system can command the correct pose yet miss a branch if the scoring frame deflects or the transmission reverses through backlash. Hybrid cycles add a scheduling constraint: the incoming coral must not collide with a manipulator that is still gripping algae. The funnel and climber also compete for the same physical space, so a copied climber cannot be assumed to fit behind another team’s station system.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Measure effector displacement under lateral load and direction reversal; test queued coral while holding algae. Compare repeatability after repeated elevator cycles and drivetrain impacts.

## Limits

# 2025-694: A dedicated low-task arm adds work without monopolizing the elevator

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The station funnel uses powered surfaces and an IR entry sensor. The separate Froggy mechanism acquires coral/algae from the floor and scores L1/processor; its source gives a 48:1 X60 pivot and 2:1 X60 roller drive. A linked shaft/chain keeps the side plates synchronized, while added angle reinforcement stiffens their weak direction.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team describes reinforcement after structural analysis and a software interlock that delays retracting Froggy until the chassis backs away from the reef. The main arm’s motor placement is also used for counterbalance.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

Low-level work can justify a dedicated mechanism when it shortens cycles and releases the primary scorer for another role. That benefit is conditional on interference: two mechanisms must be able to store, acquire and move without colliding. A geometric safety interlock should therefore be part of the architecture reference. “Button released” is not sufficient evidence that an external mechanism can retract safely.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test concurrent main-arm/Froggy poses, compare complete L1/algae cycles, and verify retreat detection before retraction under localization error.

## Limits

# 2025-1678: Wide pickup, light elevator and faster cage capture solve different delays

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A wide four-bar collector feeds the lightweight coral/algae effector on a string-driven continuous elevator. The interview describes thicker carbon after a week-five collector member bent and cracked; the caption does not safely establish the thickness. Later cage guides and capture wheels replace a slower alignment approach.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team links width to driver tolerance, elevator construction to speed/weight/CG, and the revised cage capture to reducing an approximately twenty-second climb process toward roughly ten seconds.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

The motorized scoring cycle is only one part of match throughput. Wide acquisition can reduce driver correction, while a faster endgame can recover entire scoring cycles. Those gains can justify mass in guides or reinforcement even when they increase subsystem weight. The original and revised climb should not be averaged into one time, and the gain should not be applied to a team whose approach geometry differs.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Measure failed-pickup rate, full extension deflection and complete cage-approach-to-secured time. Repeat impact tests on the reinforced collector instead of assuming more carbon fixes every load direction.

## Limits

contextDocs.body:
# 2025-1690: Differential arm/elevator motion keeps motors low but couples control

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The source describes an efficient floor collector, V-shaped powered centering path and a differential elevator/arm transmission. Equal coordinated belt motion translates the carriage; differential motion changes arm angle while the motors stay low. The retained technical record also describes a custom-sealed suction effector and piston/scotch-yoke vacuum source.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team’s explicit objective is short, fast coral cycles and resistance to defense without excessive sacrifice of algae capability. Keeping arm/elevator drive motors at the base serves low moving mass.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A differential does not eliminate shoulder or elevator effort; it redistributes that demand across shared actuators. Motion limits, current and saturation must be considered in joint space and motor space. The vacuum end effector can reduce exposed gripping hardware, but seal geometry and surface condition become critical. A short-cycle strategy also needs coordinated human-player supply and a path that avoids interference with partners.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test simultaneous lift/rotation near motor limits, vacuum retention on damaged or wet pieces, and recovery after a partially seated coral. Preserve emergency climb acceleration as a high-load exception, not the normal durability baseline.

## Limits

Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

# 2025-1706: Cable control and a later algae arm are essential version details

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The robot retains an elevator-based station-fed scorer and later adds a compact curved-rack algae intake. A constant-force spring pulls the elevator cable carrier inward after it repeatedly broke, flopped outward or entered the funnel. The climber uses the funnel’s rear region and was revised to grab one cage bar.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team describes the algae arm as lightweight and quick to deploy, and identifies the spring as the response to cable-carrier failures. The updated climb seeks easier capture rather than a larger nominal grasp.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A cable carrier is a moving structural interface, not an afterthought in the electrical system. Its force, bend radius and free envelope affect elevator current and what can enter the station funnel. An added algae collector also changes the safe pose space of an already working scorer. The architecture should retain the dated add-on history rather than imply the final robot existed at the first event.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Run full-stroke cable fatigue tests and check the spring at maximum extension. Test coral loading with the algae mechanism deployed and verify cage capture under angular misalignment.

contextDocs.body:
# 2025-1771: Wrist freedom creates L1 value and a collision-planning obligation

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The team explicitly credits 4414’s 2023 continuous elevator. Its carriage combines a pivot, wrist and compliant coral/algae end effector; range sensors and a transverse wheel actively center coral. The software models tested safe poses and allows only transitions connected in a graph.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The interview ties the wrist to effective L1 cycles and the pivot to serving both ground and station acquisition. The restricted transition graph is intended to prevent destructive arm/elevator interactions and overshoot.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

The wrist should not be justified only by branch reach. It also changes how coral can be presented to the trough, so its value can rise in a low-task alliance role. The price is a larger configuration space: correct endpoint poses do not prove that the path between them is safe. A tested edge graph is a concrete way to carry mechanical clearance assumptions into software.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test every allowed transition under lag, sensor error and simultaneous chassis motion. Measure L1 throughput as well as L4 reach, and verify active centering before the final placement motion.

# 2025-1778: Game simulation preceded the ground-intake commitment

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A narrow initial ground concept became a wide collector, feeding an internally belted elevator and arm that can score toward either side. The team reports offseason experience with similar mechanisms. Each software state specifies the collector, elevator, arm and roller setpoints together, with explicit transition conditions.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team describes running match simulations on day two after kickoff to test the significance of unprotected station defense. It connects the floor collector to that strategic result and the monolithic state structure to predictable safe motion.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

This is a process reference as much as a hardware reference. The team tested a game constraint before committing to a cycle architecture, then used known mechanism families to reduce development risk. Wide acquisition helps only when the handoff can keep up and the arm can safely retract past both field and robot structure. A multi-subsystem state should retain possession information so a timing variation does not silently drop coral.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Repeat the strategic simulation with plausible opposing and partner robots. Test interrupted transfers and safe recovery from each intermediate state, rather than validating only the nominal score sequence.

# 2025-2481: Floor orientation and a moving scorer share the alignment workload

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The collector uses one motor, a passive guide wall and wheel/roller contact to orient floor coral without a separate vertical-roller stage. A chain-driven lateral slide on Igus guides corrects scorer position. A cascade elevator and custom drivetrain complete the retained architecture.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team explicitly connects floor pickup to human players rolling coral near the reef. Its custom-module discussion emphasizes traction and useful gearing rather than adopting an unmodified commercial package.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A passive orienter exchanges actuator count for sensitivity to incoming pose, wall friction and driving direction. A lateral scorer can remove some last-meter chassis correction, but it must be stiff enough that the camera’s intended offset corresponds to the actual end-effector position. Ground-source supply and local correction should therefore be assessed as one cycle, including the human player’s delivery error.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Sample many coral approach orientations and supply distances. Measure lateral-slide backlash/deflection under acceleration, and compare whole-cycle time against a fixed scorer with chassis-only alignment.

contextDocs.body:
# 2025-3005: A serializer rebuild must eliminate stable wrong orientations

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

Before Worlds, passive polycarbonate funneling and one lower belt were replaced by molded powered flaps that contact awkward coral orientations. The retained ladder-style placement mechanism also received a cam after early L4 tipping/alignment difficulties. The interview separately describes a ratcheting climb that can retain partial progress after disable.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The serializer change is explicitly tied to coral settling into specific trapped orientations. Retaining a climb after power-off is described as an important requirement, not an incidental effect of gearing.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A funnel that succeeds in the common orientation can still create a stable mechanical equilibrium in an uncommon one. Powered flaps need to disturb that equilibrium without ejecting or crushing the piece. Likewise, an L4 scorer should be judged by placement stability and alignment delay, not only reaching the nominal height. These are distinct revisions and should not be attributed to one unchanging opening-week robot.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Deliberately place coral in every previously trapped pose, measure recovery time, and test L4 placement after abrupt chassis stops. Verify retention with the actual disabled climb configuration.

## Limits

# 2025-3663: A sideways elevator makes pass-through feasible with different interference

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

# 2025-3683: Station retention, orientation recovery and fast lift must work together

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A post-Niagara ramp/retention change reduces coral bounce-out and permits longer-distance station delivery. Two sensors support orientation detection and unjamming, while the ramp can queue coral during algae possession. The internally belted three-stage elevator has two low motors and tie-rod stiffening; the team reports slightly over half a second to full extension.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The source ties the ramp revision directly to entry bounce and the tie rods to rigidity. The retained record describes using an upper roller to redirect coral for L1 as well as higher-level scoring.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A fast unloaded lift is valuable only if the queued piece remains controlled and the effector settles accurately. Keeping the next coral on the ramp while holding algae can remove travel from the next cycle, but requires distinct possession states and a deliberate handoff. The reported lift time should remain a mechanism claim rather than a full-cycle time.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Measure loaded settle time, queued-piece retention during lift motion, and unjamming success for sideways coral. Check cable retention over repeated rapid extensions.

The historical lineage should be specific: the team mentions 254’s 2022 hollow-roller construction, while the 2025 task requires orienting rigid coral rather than simply transporting foam cargo. Copying fabrication technique is different from copying an entire intake path. A shared pinch claw can reduce moving mechanisms but its force and retained orientation must remain acceptable for two very different pieces.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test pickup orientation tolerance, failed handoff recovery, and claw retention through rapid arm motion. Keep the original and rebuild capabilities separate in recommendations and comparisons.

# 2025-5990: Protected power and adjustable rigging support a ground-source cycle

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The two-stage floor intake keeps its motor inside the chassis, then uses a belt and centering wheel to orient coral. A fixture/beam-break locates the handoff. The continuous elevator has two motors and wrench-adjustable ratchet tensioners for its ropes; a rack positions the shared gripper.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team explicitly connects internal motor placement to preventing collision damage and the ratchet arrangement to maintaining rope tension. The interview also demonstrates vision-based coral acquisition.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A protected motor still transmits impact through shafts and belts, so the whole load path needs inspection. Adjustable rigging is useful when it makes a repeatable service procedure possible; excessive or unequal tension can add friction and rack a carriage. Vision-directed pickup should be evaluated with the mechanical centering tolerance rather than as an independent AI success.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Document a reproducible rope-tension procedure, check left/right travel under load, and test handoff after impacts. Measure acquisition success with occlusion and adjacent pieces.

## Limits

Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

# 2024-359: A shorter telescoping arm preserves direct note handling

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The arm retains an A-frame/shoulder architecture and reduces the telescope to one moving stage. A guided arm-end collector sends notes directly into the top/bottom-wheel launcher; extension is used for amp and trap. Multiple pose cameras and a note-detection camera support acquisition and scoring.

Reducing extension stages can remove mass, cable length, backlash and maintenance points while retaining the needed task envelope. The comparison must use actual amp/trap geometry and the stage clearance rules, not maximum theoretical arm reach. Direct note handling avoids transfer errors but carries the launcher’s mass and flexible note through the arm’s motion.

# 2024-604: Controlled centering preserves deliberately asymmetric shooting contact

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

Centering is therefore part of generating the intended spin, not merely getting the note somewhere inside the robot. The driver-feedback example also shows how a small state signal can reduce wasted acquisition motion without changing motor power.

# 2024-1323: A low pivot and controlled note tunnel protect shot repeatability

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

A low tunnel can limit note bending and moving mass, but a protective cover also needs to avoid becoming a new trapping surface. Separately powered funneling allows transport behavior to be tuned without forcing the ground pickup to the same speed. The useful reference is a consistent note state at release; a compact exterior alone does not establish that consistency.

# 2024-1678: Staging before selecting a scorer preserves tactical optionality

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The collector changed from relatively rigid plates to more flexible material after early bending, with replaceable side assemblies. Two beam breaks track staging before the robot chooses the main shooter or elevated amp/trap path. The team describes an early simple robot, a problematic multi-arm beta and the final architecture.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team connects flexible plates to surviving contact and says the intermediate architecture did not work well. Retaining a staged note before selecting its destination is an explicit feature of the final flow.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

The branch point in a transfer path is a strategic decision. Delaying the destination choice lets the alliance respond to amplification, traffic or a blocked route without reacquiring the piece. The cost is an extra controlled state that must keep the note centered and releasable. Historical version labels should not collapse the failed beta into the final competition mechanism.

Test repeated stage-and-wait cycles, destination changes after acquisition and jam recovery at the branch. Evaluate repair time for a damaged collector side as well as pickup speed.

# 2024-1690: A small robot still needs protection against rare disabling note poses

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A compact custom-swerve robot feeds its launcher through pivot-concentric transmission elements. The retained launcher uses four horizontal contacts and a rack-based angle mechanism. A note deflector was added before championships after notes lodged beneath the shooter in two losses; the climb controller corrects roll and coordinates trap release with swing.

The team explicitly contrasts the season’s small/simple objective with the prior year’s complexity. The deflector is a response to two specific disabling events, not a decorative cover.

Rare jams can dominate an otherwise excellent scoring architecture because they remove the whole robot’s contribution. Preventing entry to a bad configuration can be more reliable than detecting and reversing it later. Concentric feeding preserves operation across launcher angles, but actual clearances and moving power transmission still need review. Trap timing based on swing is a separate dynamic-control problem, not proof of static shot accuracy.

# 2024-1756: Omni centering and reoriented transfer need defined staging states

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

Omni wheels and printed wedges center the note while allowing lateral motion. The rotating shooter aligns with the intake to receive it; paired sensors detect travel and possession. The same moving assembly uses gentle roller release for amp/trap rather than a high-speed shot.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team identifies lateral freedom as the reason for the omni contact choice. Sensor feedback reduces the driver’s need to see the note and helps avoid acquiring a second piece.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A roller can create useful forward traction while resisting necessary lateral centering. Omni contact addresses that conflict, but the wedges still establish the note’s final alignment. A moving transfer interface adds a temporal constraint: feeding must wait for receiving geometry, then stop at a verified state before reorientation. Gentler release for a confined goal is a separate control mode from speaker firing.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test diagonal entries and sensor disagreement; measure capture/transfer tolerances at the rotating interface and retention during the following motion.

# 2024-1771: Low moving mass and rapid prototyping support a multi-task pivot

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A protected under-bumper collector and polycord conveyor feed a central pivoted scoring assembly. Motors sit near the pivot and long belt runs carry power outward. Independent shooting sides provide note spin; the same mechanism serves ground pickup, speaker and amp poses.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

Moving motors toward the pivot can reduce rotational inertia, but long belts introduce compliance, tension and replacement considerations. A shared pivot simplifies the number of mechanisms while making each pose and connecting motion more important. Rapid printed iterations are a development capability that another team must budget for, rather than assume it receives by copying the final CAD.

# 2024-1778: Minimal intake rollers and redundant climb capacity have different justifications

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The over-bumper collector uses four rollers after early prototyping. An indexer retains the note and serves amp delivery through a virtual linkage. The top/bottom launcher uses asymmetric wheel contact. Each climber has two motors, and the team describes continuing after one side was removed following a failure.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team ties the reduced collector to sufficient pickup performance with lower mass, and the unusual climb power to single-side operation and imperfect chain alignment. Asymmetric contact is reported to improve spin/stability and range.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

Simplicity should be evaluated per task rather than imposed uniformly. Removing an unnecessary roller can improve collector dynamics, while adding climb reserve can preserve a match outcome after damage. Those are compatible engineering decisions. Single-side climbing also changes structural loads and roll, so redundancy is only real if the frame and scoring mechanisms tolerate the alternate load case.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test the minimum collector with worn notes and wall contact. Validate disabled-side climb loading and harmony clearance, rather than extrapolating from two-side nominal lifts.

## Limits

# 2024-2910: Any-heading note loading is the prerequisite for a useful turret

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

Under-bumper acquisition feeds four vertical rollers that move the note around the turret’s receiving cage. A light amp guide directs an upward release. The source describes a late, simple worm-drive climb and software superstates that coordinate turret, feeder and launcher rather than binding unrelated commands independently.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team explicitly emphasizes feeding at different turret headings. Climb packaging was constrained by its late addition, motivating simplicity and low mass.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A turret adds little directional independence if it must return to one heading to acquire every note. The receiving cage and its contact sequence are therefore as important as aiming range. A superstate helps express the common readiness condition, but needs fault handling when only some mechanisms reach their setpoints. A worm transmission should not be assumed to hold every load without checking its actual efficiency and disabled behavior.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Measure transfer success versus heading, note wear and acceleration. Test partial readiness, cable limits and power-off climb retention. The viewer-disabled binder remains unreviewed; do not substitute a guessed download.

contextDocs.body:
# 2024-2974: Pivot-settle delay and belt skipping require dated evidence

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The build thread records replacing a slower, note-damaging conveyor with a more direct curved feed, carbon-roller shooter changes, replaceable intake assemblies and pivot stiffening. Later posts describe a friction damper, changing pivot belts, a ratio change from 125:1 to 100:1, and Worlds logs exposing belt skipping when the arm extended.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team explicitly ties the direct feed to speed/note preservation, the damper to waiting several seconds for the angle to settle, and the revised ratio to faster rotation. Log comparison between motor and external encoder exposed a mechanical slip rather than merely a software aiming error.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

This history explains why commanded angle, measured motor angle and true launcher angle are different quantities. Increasing control gains cannot reliably fix a slipping transmission. The fastest pivot also is not the one with the shortest complete aim-to-shot time if it oscillates afterward. The early proposal to climb using the shooter must remain a proposal unless later installation evidence supports it.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Compare motor and external encoder trajectories under arm extension, measure request-to-exit latency, and inspect intake damage after contact.

## Limits

First-party build posts in topic 452466, especially 2, 5, 21, 27 and 32. The previously linked w0AFxJFMOqg video is match/driver audio, not a technical interview; it is rejected as construction evidence here.

contextDocs.body:
# 2024-4613: Different contact stiffness enables amp delivery without a pivot

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The under-bumper collector and guides feed two independently driven launcher rollers. The interview describes a lower-durometer lower contact relative to the upper contact, combined with speed control, to curve the amp delivery without moving the whole launcher. A deflector protects the climber from dropped notes.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team explicitly chose the contact/speed arrangement to perform both speaker and amp tasks without a pivot, with robustness as a stated benefit. The climber guard responds to the possibility of a falling note disabling it.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

Eliminating an angle actuator shifts trajectory control into contact deformation, spin and launch speed. That reduces joints and moving wiring, but may increase sensitivity to note wear, temperature and compression. The guard illustrates that a rare dropped piece can create a structural failure state even when the main transport path works.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Map amp accuracy with used notes, varying voltage and repeated shooting. Test the dropped-note guard from several directions and verify that it does not obstruct normal climbing.

# 2024-6328: Routing the note and routing the chain are both architecture interfaces

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A full-width collector uses leading rollers, wedges and slippery passive centering surfaces. The indexer selects the main shooter or rack-driven amp/trap backpack. Double-sided belts package opposite roller directions. Climb-side fangs guide the chain over areas where it could catch the shooter/backpack; four pose cameras use deliberately different views/lenses.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The source explicitly connects the fangs to avoiding chain entrapment and the camera arrangement to useful tag visibility on approach to scoring locations. It treats camera placement as a deliberate strategy choice rather than simply adding identical cameras.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A compact scorer and climber can each work separately but fail when a flexible chain sweeps through their shared space. Passive routing surfaces are therefore a mechanism interface, not cosmetic guards. Similarly, extra cameras help only when their sight lines and uncertainty provide information the existing views lack.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test chain capture with lateral error and robot roll, inspect every backpack handoff, and measure pose availability along the intended routes rather than only at a parked test position.

# 2023-111: Symmetric acquisition and sufficient release clearance are different requirements

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A vertically symmetric gripper acquires cubes and upright/tipped cones from either robot face. A continuous lift uses synchronized sides, guides and adjustable structural stays. The interview reports redesigning the claw to open farther because cubes remained trapped after the release command.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team explicitly ties gripper symmetry to the arm working on both sides. The larger opening responds to failed cube release rather than poor initial acquisition.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A mechanism that holds both pieces well can still release one poorly. Compliant foam and tapered cones create different contact/retention conditions, so acquisition success is not a substitute for a release test. Through-robot arm travel also makes lift parallelism and cable clearance part of both scoring directions.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Measure release delay and remaining contact for worn cubes, test cone orientation extremes, and check lift binding after frame contact.

# 2023-125: Split rack collectors preserve a central arm corridor

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

Two cantilevered rack-and-pinion collector halves leave space for a telescoping arm, synchronized by a cross-shaft with service couplers. The shoulder transmission is nested below the arm; a compact wrist and roller claw complete direct scoring.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team identifies robust, controllable deployment and avoiding pneumatics as reasons for the rack choice. Shoulder placement is tied to maximizing useful stowed arm length.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

The center gap is not wasted intake width: it is clearance purchased for another mechanism. Synchronization must keep both collector halves from racking while still permitting fast replacement. As the arm extends, gravity torque rises with lever arm, so tuning only the retracted shoulder does not establish controllability at high reach.

Test one-sided collector impacts, service-coupler realignment and shoulder tracking at maximum extension with each game piece.

# 2023-1325: Remote wrist actuation and practiced direct pickup avoid a second collector

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

A small square chassis carries a shoulder/elbow/wrist arm with low-mounted transmissions and a remote aircraft-cable wrist drive. Fixed gripper spacing handles both pieces. A separate Rapid React-style collector was prototyped but not adopted; arm motion uses waypoint/path-following ideas related to the drivetrain tools.

Remote cable drive reduces distal motor mass but makes tension, stretch and backlash important. Safe endpoint waypoints also do not certify the swept volume between them.

# 2023-1577: A compliant collector must hand off at the actual revised arm geometry

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A low-pivot collector uses mecanum/omni contact to center a tipped cone, then rotates it toward a narrow gripper. The extending scoring arm keeps its transmission low and measures actual arm angle beyond gearbox backlash. Shoulder-style bearing support helps retain bearings in flexible plates.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A wide pickup can improve acquisition while increasing the range of states presented to a narrow receiver. Compliance helps survive contact but must not erase the repeatable pose needed for transfer. Measuring the joint after transmission backlash improves observability; it does not mechanically remove the backlash.

Test handoff after collector impacts, compare actual and motor-side angle under reversals, and verify bearing retention after repeated plate flex.

# 2023-1678: Simple continuous rigging still requires deliberate line management

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

# 2023-1756: Deployable bash guards protect a collector but can obstruct scoring

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

# 2023-2075: Backlash and compliant handoff tolerance must be separated

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A floor beater/roller collector hands pieces to a shoulder/elbow arm and claw. The source describes high shoulder loads and early slop problems. The wider claw accommodates variable lateral arrival and can also acquire at the shelf.

The team ties a rigid shoulder transmission to consistent placement and the wide/compliant receiver to successful handoff from a broad collector.

Useful compliance at the receiver is different from uncontrolled angular lost motion at the shoulder. One enlarges acquisition tolerance; the other shifts the end-effector position unpredictably at the node. A good transfer should center or otherwise define the retained piece before the arm uses precision scoring poses.

## Published / retained construction account

A curved roller gripper directly acquires both pieces on a virtual-four-bar/extension architecture. Linkage/sprocket geometry serves floor, station and scoring positions; holding rollers idle at lower speed in the last useful direction.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team identifies fast cycles and a wide acquisition aperture as priorities, and describes testing drivetrain/contact choices for charge-station traction.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A virtual linkage can coordinate joints mechanically, but its coupled path still needs field/robot clearance. Idle roller direction must match possession state or it can eject the wrong piece.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test every acquisition/release pose, interrupted transitions and low-speed holding under chassis acceleration.

## Limits

Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

contextDocs.body:
# 2025 full season recap with a 2022 retrospective

Authored expansion from selected timestamped passages, with the retained prior full-caption review. This is not a new full visual audit or a claim that the enrichment covers every spoken point.

[Original video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1UsbJD-zRjU)

## Retained full-caption account

The recap follows kickoff incentives, floor-supplied coral, 1323’s preplaced autonomous and L1 specialization, 2910’s backside auto and algae security, then Einstein. The author disclaims knowing who invented several techniques first. Its 2022 three-second-possession interpretation is disputed and must not become rule guidance.

## 1. Kickoff: rank incentives differ from point value

[Navigation 150–395 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1UsbJD-zRjU&t=150)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The commentator compares match points with the ease of earning different ranking points. In his retrospective, leave-plus-one-coral and a deep climb plus park appear relatively accessible, making coral-level completion an important qualifier differentiator.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** This is a prediction framework tied to a field of teams, not an immutable task ranking. If a bonus becomes routine, its marginal ranking value falls even though its point value is unchanged. Evaluate the expected event population and rule revision before allocating mechanism effort.

## 2. Why algae looked unattractive early

[Navigation 600–665 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1UsbJD-zRjU&t=600)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The recap explains why some teams initially discounted processor play: scoring could also deliver algae to the opponent, whose human player might convert it. It contrasts that with the apparent availability and speed of coral cycles.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** Expected net value depends on the receiving human player and the opponent’s recovery opportunity. Treating all processor actions as a fixed two-point gain, or all algae as poor value, erases those conditions. A kickoff judgment can be reasonable and still become obsolete as skills and congestion change.

## 3. Rule-aware starting geometry

[Navigation 860–925 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1UsbJD-zRjU&t=860)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The author highlights 5614 exploiting the permitted starting relationship to the robot line, rather than conservatively placing the whole robot behind it.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** A legal starting pose can shorten autonomous travel without a mechanism change. The exact legality belongs to the applicable manual and inspection interpretation; the video is a source of a question to verify, not the governing rule.

## 4. Floor supply changes cycle geography

[Navigation 1120–1185 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1UsbJD-zRjU&t=1120)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The source contrasts an early defensive third robot with another scorer sharing limited space. It then identifies 1690’s human-player floor supply as reducing travel toward the reef.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** The architecture must accept a supply distribution, not a guaranteed piece at a fixed point. The third robot’s best role depends on marginal scoring, interference and defense opportunity; a robot with low standalone output may be useful without occupying another scorer’s lane.

## 5. 1323 spends surplus coral to save time

[Navigation 1370–1435 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1UsbJD-zRjU&t=1370)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The commentator describes a more aggressive field-supply approach: many coral pieces are delivered, collisions help move them forward, and some leftovers are accepted because the alliance does not need to score every available piece.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** Unused inventory is not necessarily waste if it buys shorter cycles. This changes the pickup objective from perfect recovery to fast acquisition of any convenient piece. It also creates traffic, visibility and finite-supply questions that should be tested before copying the method at a different skill level.

## 6. Backside autonomous protects partner access

[Navigation 1620–1685 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1UsbJD-zRjU&t=1620)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The recap credits 2910 as the example the author remembers, while expressly declining to establish who invented the route. A fast backside route lets partners retain straightforward station access.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** An autonomous routine should be valued by alliance output and route compatibility, not only its own piece count. Ground pickup of predictably positioned pieces can make a longer-looking route more reliable. Keep observed example, claimed priority and invention credit separate.

## 7. Finite algae produces a score swing

[Navigation 1850–1915 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1UsbJD-zRjU&t=1850)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The source explains that when branch output is similar, a missed algae can deprive one alliance of a net score and give the opponent the corresponding opportunity.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** The eight-point potential swing is conditional: both sides must otherwise have converted the contested piece. Do not double-count denial and a scored piece as two independent guaranteed gains. The important generalization is that a finite contested resource can determine the match after another scoring channel becomes similar.

## 8. Einstein: parallel roles and accumulated cycle advantage

[Navigation 2070–2325 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1UsbJD-zRjU&t=2070)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The recap contrasts backside autonomous and algae security with inconsistent supplied pickups, then explains how small cycle differences and algae access force the trailing alliance into late risks. Its broad arc places L1 work within the elite alliance plan.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** Do not infer that L1 begins only after all branches are full. Preserve the separate 1323 L1/algae role account and 2910/4272 branch allocation. A close displayed score can conceal a remaining-resource disadvantage, but exact per-match assignments and counterfactual outcomes still require direct match review.

## 9. 2022 comparison: supply denial and unreliable rule commentary

[Navigation 2420–2675 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1UsbJD-zRjU&t=2420)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The retrospective uses Rapid React to discuss redistributing opposing cargo and denying convenient supply. It also asserts a three-second possession interpretation that the retained research flags as disputed.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** Transfer the supply/denial reasoning only after verifying game-specific legality. Do not convert the narrator’s disputed possession explanation into a legal design constraint. Climb scoring in 2022 also cannot be projected onto the low-value 2026 tower context.

## Quiz prompts

- Why can unused coral improve an alliance’s score?
- When is one stolen algae an eight-point potential swing rather than four?
- How can an autonomous route help partners without maximizing its own count?
- Which rule claim in the 2022 retrospective needs independent verification?

## Remaining uncertainties

- Selected passages span the recap but do not constitute a sentence-by-sentence new annotation.
- Inventor priority is expressly uncertain.
- Exact Einstein role timing and all rules need separate primary verification.

No new visual match audit. Timestamp spans are navigation aids; the selected-passages manifest distinguishes the new recheck from the inherited full-caption review.

# 2023 retrospective: failure response and defensive leverage

Authored expansion from selected timestamped passages, with the retained prior full-caption review. This is not a new full visual audit or a claim that the enrichment covers every spoken point.

[Original video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=umznfQq_ACI)

## Retained full-caption account

The commentator follows 1678 after an intake failure: test remaining acquisition, then switch to defense on major scorers. Flat bumper contact, wall leverage and release timing matter. Late denial depends on whether the opponent still has time for another cycle and balance. A suspected module failure is commentary, not a verified diagnosis.

## 1. Diagnose quickly, then change role

[Navigation 110–175 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=umznfQq_ACI&t=110)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The source describes 1678 testing cube and cone acquisition after a collector failure, then promptly becoming a defender when neither works.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** The decision variable is remaining useful capability. A short diagnostic sequence can prevent spending the rest of teleop attempting an impossible task. The value of defense rises when it replaces zero scoring rather than a productive cycle.

## 2. Maintain a useful bumper relationship

[Navigation 329–394 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=umznfQq_ACI&t=329)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The commentator praises rotating with 3005 while leaving enough separation to avoid being flung out of position by mismatched rotation. He suspects a module problem later.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** “Stay in contact” is too crude a defensive instruction. Relative angle, wall position, escape routes and the timing of recontact matter. The module diagnosis is a commentator hypothesis, not verified mechanical causation.

## 3. Block the acquisition face and evaluate time remaining

[Navigation 548–613 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=umznfQq_ACI&t=548)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The account describes parallel blocking of 1114’s pickup face, forcing a longer approach near the end of the match.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** A defender need not stop a robot forever. It may need only to make one remaining cycle infeasible before balancing. Exact effectiveness requires checking the match clock, remaining tasks and penalties, not merely counting contact seconds.

## Quiz prompts

- What should a drive team test immediately after losing acquisition?
- Why can a small defensive gap improve control?
- How does remaining balance time change the value of denying one pickup?

## Remaining uncertainties

- No visual verification of the suspected module failure.
- Contacts and timing are reported commentary, not independently annotated frames.

# 2024 retrospective: hybrid poaching against double passing

Authored expansion from selected timestamped passages, with the retained prior full-caption review. This is not a new full visual audit or a claim that the enrichment covers every spoken point.

[Original video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IGlyCDDcFlE)

## Retained full-caption account

The analysis contrasts 1678 with two passers against a single passer, cleaner and hybrid defender/poacher. 1729 pressures routes and changes targets rather than chasing one robot indefinitely. Source protection and long detours constrain the defender. The late amplification burst narrows the score gap; penalties remain decisive.

## 1. Choose the pass disruption target

[Navigation 149–214 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IGlyCDDcFlE&t=149)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The source describes 1729 switching among passers and using wall leverage, while 4613 escapes by backing up and rotating.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** A fixed assignment to the strongest opponent is not always best. The defender should consider escape skill, replacement supply and how much disruption can actually be sustained.

## 2. Poaching can combine scoring with denial

[Navigation 448–513 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IGlyCDDcFlE&t=448)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The commentator contrasts costly source-zone contact with stealing a note that would otherwise have been passed. He describes that theft as a two-note opportunity swing.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** The swing is conditional on both alliances’ ability to use the piece. Penalties can erase the gain. A hybrid defender/poacher needs a low-detour acquisition route, not only a strong chassis.

## 3. Release a losing contest for a timed amplification opportunity

[Navigation 746–811 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IGlyCDDcFlE&t=746)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** Late in the analysis, the defender leaves a risky contest to collect a dropped note while the alliance has an amplification opportunity.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** Defensive persistence can be strategically wrong when the next offensive contribution has higher marginal value. The passage connects remaining clock, penalty risk, inventory and amplifier readiness; it is not a general instruction to abandon passing defense late.

## Quiz prompts

- When is switching defensive targets better than following one passer?
- What conditions make a poached note a two-note opportunity swing?
- Why might a defender leave contact with only seconds remaining?

## Remaining uncertainties

- Reported counts and foul interpretation need official match/rule confirmation.
- No frame-by-frame timing audit.

[Original video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c5rvL_wVdXc)

## Retained full-caption account

The narrator connects 6672’s defense on 1577 to supply and cleanup demands elsewhere, then discusses 4099 pressuring 254. Late shot disruption, climb contact and the decision to keep shooting are interpreted in the context of a close match. Counts and intent remain commentator observations.

## 1. Two scoring zones and the third robot’s job

[Navigation 146–211 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c5rvL_wVdXc&t=146)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The commentator models each alliance’s main scorers dividing convenient cargo regions, with the third robot often defending rather than splitting supply into three smaller regions.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** Random hub redistribution makes a rigid circular route less useful than opportunistic local collection. A third scorer must add more than the supply and space it removes from stronger partners.

## 2. Defense imposes route and decision costs

[Navigation 437–502 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c5rvL_wVdXc&t=437)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The account follows 1577 abandoning contested cargo for a longer arc, and 254 accepting a pin situation while escaping pressure near a hangar.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** The value of contact includes detours, lost favorable shot positions and delayed decisions. A missed steal opportunity may be rational if it would make the next defensive interaction late; counterfactual advice needs the full route and clock.

## 3. A late scoring cycle competes with climb margin

[Navigation 728–793 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c5rvL_wVdXc&t=728)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The narrator describes a late 1577 climb attempt and a hook remaining on the lower rung, contrasting that with an earlier undefended traversal attempt elsewhere.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** The strategic cost is not just a nominal five-point rung difference. Reduced approach and retry time changes completion probability. The exact awarded rung depends on official support/contact rules, so keep the commentator’s causal account separate from the official score.

## Quiz prompts

- Why can a third scorer reduce alliance output in Rapid React?
- Which defensive costs are missed by contact-time statistics?
- How should a late shot be compared with climb reliability?

# Scouting analysis with Tableau

Authored expansion from selected timestamped passages, with the retained prior full-caption review. This is not a new full visual audit or a claim that the enrichment covers every spoken point.

[Original video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R11PUq_m8Fk)

## Retained full-caption account

This tutorial builds averages, phase breakdowns, scatterplots, box plots and shared selection filters. It emphasizes match-level context: the same average autonomous score can represent different capability and reliability distributions, and an outlier deserves match review. This is a 2024 tutorial using historical example data, not current Tableau documentation.

## 1. Identifiers are dimensions, not quantities

[Navigation 225–290 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R11PUq_m8Fk&t=225)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The tutorial distinguishes team and match labels from values to aggregate, and notes that Boolean observations can be represented separately.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** A data model that averages team numbers or counts rows when it intends to average performance can look polished while answering the wrong question. Define the unit of observation—robot-match, alliance-match or event—before building plots.

## 2. Show phase context without hiding units

[Navigation 675–740 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R11PUq_m8Fk&t=675)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The source organizes tooltips to separate auto, teleop, endgame and overall output, reducing clutter in a bubble/scatter view.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** A clean display should retain metric definitions. Dock points are not a count of docks; alliance points are not individual contributions. Cross-game phase labels can conceal different scoring actions, especially 2026 endgame fuel versus tower points.

## 3. Outliers are match-review leads

[Navigation 1125–1190 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R11PUq_m8Fk&t=1125)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The commentator recommends inspecting the match behind a peak or failure, asking whether the performance is repeatable and fits the intended alliance.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** A peak is useful evidence of capability only after identifying the enabling conditions. A mean depressed by a breakdown may hide upside, but removing failures without judging repairability overstates expected output. Evaluate reliability and ceiling separately.

## Quiz prompts

- What is the unit of observation in this plot?
- When should a high outlier affect alliance selection?
- How could averaging disguise a breakdown or autonomous incompatibility?

## Remaining uncertainties

- Historical Tableau tutorial, not current software documentation.
- No causal validation of example outliers.

# 2025 kickoff predictions

Authored expansion from selected timestamped passages, with the retained prior full-caption review. This is not a new full visual audit or a claim that the enrichment covers every spoken point.

[Original video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_lSTGCRcbdM)

## Retained full-caption account

At kickoff the author considers rapid L1 specialists, high-level coral scorers, algae and deep climbs. The video anticipates reef saturation and collection defense, and warns that two coral stations constrain three autonomous robots. These are January hypotheses rather than observed season outcomes.

## 1. Early L1 specialization hypothesis

[Navigation 68–133 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_lSTGCRcbdM&t=68)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** At kickoff the narrator imagines an L1 specialist winning through substantially faster cycles, possibly combined with easy ground algae work.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** The hypothesis compares total points per complete cycle, not points per placed coral. Later elite L1/algae roles should be compared with this prediction without pretending the kickoff author already knew the final alliance allocation.

## 2. Finite branches and station contention

[Navigation 203–268 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_lSTGCRcbdM&t=203)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The source predicts branch saturation at strong events and identifies two coral stations serving three autonomous robots as an emerging coordination problem.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** Mechanical reach alone does not solve alliance throughput. A third robot can obstruct station access or force a longer route. Consistent floor supply and backside routes later address this particular bottleneck.

## 3. Collection denial rather than constant scoring interference

[Navigation 339–404 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_lSTGCRcbdM&t=339)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The prediction focuses defense on intercepting station access and forcing long routes rather than repeatedly bumping a loaded scorer near the reef.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** This remains a hypothesis tied to January rules and expected driver skill. A ground-source robot changes the supply graph and can make station camping irrelevant. Pin timing and protected geometry must be read in the applicable manual.

## Quiz prompts

- What cycle-time advantage must justify L1 specialization?
- Why is autonomous a three-robot routing problem?
- How does floor supply change collection defense?

## Remaining uncertainties

- Predictions, not observed final-season outcomes.
- Do not reuse kickoff RP thresholds or pin explanations as current legal guidance.

No new visual match audit. Timestamp spans are navigation aids; the selected-passages manifest distinguishes the new recheck from the inherited full-caption review.

# 2025 week zero finals: collection defense

Authored expansion from selected timestamped passages, with the retained prior full-caption review. This is not a new full visual audit or a claim that the enrichment covers every spoken point.

[Original video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sekPy0RgPig)

## Retained full-caption account

The author analyzes 190/2877/5422 against 166/4909/1073, discussing early failures, coral-station interception and excessive chasing. The algae-specialist/defender idea is a forecast. The video anticipates denial becoming more valuable near saturation; it does not establish that prediction as the season’s eventual universal meta. ASR frequently truncates 4909 to 499.

## 1. Early failure changes what the match can demonstrate

[Navigation 153–218 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sekPy0RgPig&t=153)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The source identifies the two finals alliances and describes autonomous and mobility failures that alter the opening balance.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** Week-zero evidence is valuable but censored by incomplete robots. A defense tactic succeeding against a malfunctioning acquisition system does not establish its effectiveness against a mature robot.

## 2. Win station position, then exploit the queue

[Navigation 458–523 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sekPy0RgPig&t=458)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The account praises moving between an opponent and the station, forcing a longer route and creating contention with its partner.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** The cost of denial includes the partner waiting for supply, not only the defended robot’s delay. A defender that merely chases the back of a departing robot may surrender the position that made the tactic valuable.

## 3. Pinning and blocking create different escape opportunities

[Navigation 764–829 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sekPy0RgPig&t=764)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The narrator contrasts a short pin followed by required separation with maintaining a useful approach-denial position.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** Treat this as a geometry and timing lesson, with exact pin rules independently verified. The trailing scorer also needs a prepared station-switch plan; assuming it can always change human-player source ignores mechanism and driver-practice constraints.

## Quiz prompts

- Why are week-zero results weak evidence for mature-system effectiveness?
- How does one blocked station affect two scorers?
- Why might a legal non-pin block be more valuable than a pin?

## Remaining uncertainties

- ASR often truncates 4909 to 499.
- Algae-specialist and saturation claims are early forecasts, not universal conclusions.

# 2025 first Israel event: 1690 floor supply and defensive counters

Authored expansion from selected timestamped passages, with the retained prior full-caption review. This is not a new full visual audit or a claim that the enrichment covers every spoken point.

[Original video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pDr6u-53fC8)

## Retained full-caption account

The narrator connects 1690’s ground-fed autonomous with reduced travel, then follows coral-station defense and offensive switches. Algae scoring provides another useful task when coral access is contested. Bumper dimensions and simultaneous climb access are discussed. The author’s early reservations about floor pickup should be retained alongside later evidence of its success.

## 1. Dominance does not settle the final scoring order

[Navigation 153–218 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pDr6u-53fC8&t=153)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The source describes early 1690 floor-fed cycles and a high-to-low branch priority, while explicitly leaving room for future rapid trough strategies.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** Preserve that uncertainty. A priority order rational at the first event can change when branches saturate, floor supply improves or an alliance assigns dedicated low-level work.

## 2. Distributed floor supply defeats a fixed station block

[Navigation 459–524 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pDr6u-53fC8&t=459)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The commentator describes 1690 selecting available floor coral instead of entering a defended station approach, leaving the defender without useful work.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** The defender’s control problem is the set of useful acquisition locations. A broad supply field requires denial, piece displacement or target switching, rather than assuming one station remains the bottleneck.

## 3. An escape move works until the defender adapts

[Navigation 764–829 s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pDr6u-53fC8&t=764)

**Source account / attributed commentary:** The account analyzes a bait-and-switch that gains a bumper corner and station access, then notes a later central defensive position that removes that opening.

**Conditional interpretation — analyst reasoning:** Do not turn one successful driver move into a deterministic playbook. Record the counter-adaptation and the cost of choosing another station or algae role. The field state and opponent reaction are part of the tactic.

## Quiz prompts

- Why can floor supply make station defense worthless?
- What changed between the successful escape and its counter?
- Why should early reservations about floor pickup remain in the history?

## Remaining uncertainties

- Narrator’s early floor-pickup reservations are retained alongside later success.
- Reported match counts and robot identities need checking where captions truncate numbers.
