technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Map acquisition success across the entire mouth with off-center hits, then repeat after controlled impact loading.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: CYCLONE: DYE-inspired rotor with independent feed
technicalNotes.construction: 22-inch rotor; eight-fuel ring; separate rotation/feed drives; reported 18-fuel/s feed.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Maintain bulk-to-single-stream flow in a compact package.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A rotor is not just a rotating bucket. Its moving boundary, internal feed contact and exit geometry jointly determine whether fuel circulates, enters the ring, or jams. Independent feed drive lets the team tune the launch supply without requiring the whole bulk pile to turn at that speed. A lower-profile center obstruction improves the area through which fuel can enter; reversing must not turn a hook or seam into a trap. A theoretical ring count multiplied by rotation rate is only an upper bound: pockets must actually fill and discharge.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure pocket occupancy and output variability at full, half and nearly empty loads; test reversing a deliberately bridged inlet.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: CYCLONE: floating hood, preload and turret support
technicalNotes.construction: Compact turret; floating hood; constant-force spring; through-bore sensing; powered hood rollers.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Reduce backlash and preserve storage volume.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Spring preload can keep a reduction loaded against one tooth flank, reducing reversal uncertainty, but adds a torque that the motor must overcome in the opposite direction. Measuring the output rather than only the motor helps detect residual compliance between gearbox and hood. The feed path and turret bearing need common structural alignment; a compact height is valuable only if it does not permit the hood to deflect enough to change the exit angle. Powered hood rollers alter the spin/contact state, so their ratio belongs in the shot calibration rather than being treated as passive guidance.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure hood angle repeatability from both approach directions and at several turret headings; compare loaded and unloaded structure.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: CYCLONE: moving-shot compensation and variable feed
technicalNotes.construction: Gyro latency compensation, empirical flight time and variable rotor speed are documented.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Maintain accurate mobile firing and stable throughput.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A turret can cancel chassis heading only if the controller uses the correct observation time and the actual release state. A latency error grows with angular velocity and can look like a mechanical aiming bias. Rotor speed also changes shot timing and inlet loading; a firing command is not the same as a ball leaving the hood. The mechanical and control record should include this delay and its variation. Slowing the feed may improve delivered score if it reduces wheel droop or keeps the exit state within tolerance.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Time-stamp vision, gyro, turret position, feeder transitions and ball release; compare miss direction against angular and translational velocity.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: 3467: redundant rack support and expanding walls
technicalNotes.construction: Double polycarbonate rack plates; powered and idler pinions; walls move with intake.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Impact tolerance, tooth engagement and more storage.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Supporting a rack at more than one point reduces its tendency to peel away from the drive pinion under load. Two rack plates can distribute stress, but only if their tooth timing and guidance are aligned; otherwise they can fight each other. Moving the walls with the collector creates agitation as well as extra volume. Agitation may improve flow near the floor but can also throw a top layer out unless the lid and wall overlap control it. A side load remains a separate case from a frontal collapse.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test rack deflection, skipping and skew with a side hit; observe fuel near moving wall seams during repeated deploy/retract cycles.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: 3467: active centering into two launch streams
technicalNotes.construction: Ten floor rollers; powered stacked-belt side wedges; central divider; live-axle tower roller.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Center fuel while limiting tower oscillation.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Active side contact can rotate or translate fuel away from a bottleneck rather than relying on gravity against a fixed wall. Its surface direction has to agree with the desired stream; excessive inward force can create an arch at the divider. The live-axle tower roller is a structural answer to rapidly changing multi-ball loads, reducing a source of compression variation. The useful comparison is not simply belts versus rollers: it is whether the particular contact geometry establishes two repeatable, supplied paths through the entire range of hopper fill.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Feed off-center piles, log each stream separately, and compare tower deflection under single-ball and paired-ball arrivals.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: 3467: two independent launchers and stored energy
technicalNotes.construction: Two launchers; four 3-inch 45A wheels per launcher with inertia kits; adjustable hood.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: High rate with controllable exit conditions.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Independent launch drives can compensate for asymmetric supply, but increase the number of conditions that must be measured. Added inertia can reduce transient speed droop while consuming mass and spin-up time. A soft wheel increases compliance and contact duration, but changes compression as it wears or heats. Hood range should be translated into a validated scoring and passing envelope, rather than assuming every geometric angle produces a useful trajectory. The desired test is a full stream of representative fuel, not a single ideal ball launched repeatedly.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Compare both streams’ exit speed distributions and accuracy through a long volley, at fresh and worn surface conditions.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: 3467: camera structure and predictive trench ducking
technicalNotes.construction: Braced camera towers; measured shot gates; future-pose hood retraction for trench entry.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Preserve localization and avoid hood collisions.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Camera vibration produces an apparent pose error even if the vision algorithm is otherwise correct. Bracing the mount to the shooter can stiffen it, but also transmits shooter vibration; the net effect should be measured. Trench protection is a dynamic clearance problem: retracting at the boundary is too late when the mechanism takes time to move. The lookahead should include speed, control delay, deceleration and an uncertainty margin, with a safe fallback if localization becomes invalid. This is a control requirement created by the mechanism’s envelope.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Run approach tests at several speeds and headings with degraded pose data; verify the hood clears before the physical entry plane.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: DOWNPOUR original: linear collection and linked hopper
technicalNotes.construction: Rack deployment, multiple powered rollers, pin-slot hopper extension.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Compact stow and broad acquisition.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The intake and expanding wall are physically linked, so their travel, friction and alignment cannot be optimized independently. A pin-slot joint can accommodate different trajectories but may create a high local pressure at the end of travel. A multirotor pickup needs enough overlap to avoid an uncontrolled interval as fuel crosses the bumper. If the linkage binds, commanding more motor torque can damage the rack before solving the wall alignment. The architecture should retain a way to inspect and replace the joint without disassembling the whole fuel path.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Cycle the linkage under hopper side loading and inspect slot wear; test an interrupted deployment and recovery.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: DOWNPOUR original: serpentine and turret feed
technicalNotes.construction: Belt serpentine; curved backing replaces interfering upper wheels; 400° turret.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Compact routing with controlled feed and independent aim.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Removing a wheel can improve a mechanism when the wheel occupies the same space needed by another moving assembly. Curved backing trades active contact for sliding contact and must keep fuel captured through the bend. The turret’s rotation range is a cable-management specification as much as an aiming specification. The original design and its later replacement are separate records: a successful collection system does not prove the single-stream scorer met the team’s later competitive needs. Prototype targets must remain labeled targets even when the surrounding prose sounds confident.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Sweep the full turret range while feeding deliberately varied fuel, and compare useful output with the original target under realistic voltage.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: DOWNPOUR DCMP: repair the collision path
technicalNotes.construction: Single-pivot intake; higher round bash bar; extra motor-plate bracing; passive lower bar.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Stop bar deflection from stalling rollers; save power and weight.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A bash bar can become the failure if it bends into the very roller it protects. Moving the reaction member above the rotating contact changes that failure geometry. Reverting a powered element to a passive surface is an important counterexample to the rule that more powered contacts always help: the added drive may cost current without improving capture in the tested geometry. This result should not be transferred blindly to another bumper gap or approach speed. It supports testing the actual bottleneck and force path before adding a motor.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure bar-to-roller clearance after impact; compare capture probability and current with powered and passive lower contact.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: DOWNPOUR DCMP: net, trench access and electrical relocation
technicalNotes.construction: Net-topped storage; bumper-mounted panels; electrical panel flipped upward.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Retain fuel, use trench routes and protect electronics.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A bumper-mounted wall can simplify robot mass allocation but introduces a service interface: removing or shifting the bumper can change hopper alignment and expose a gap. The net adds a travel envelope that depends on fuel loading and deformation. Flipping the electrical panel exchanges one exposure for another, so the skid plate, drainage and access plan must be considered with the new layout. The correct capacity test measures fuel retained after the actual route and then delivered to the shooter, rather than the empty CAD volume.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Remove and reinstall bumpers repeatedly, inspect wall alignment, then run full-load trench and bump routes followed by complete discharge.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: DOWNPOUR DCMP: single-stream turret to four-wide drum
technicalNotes.construction: Four-wide transfer; mixed-diameter rollers; three X60 shooter drives and two feeder drives.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Original single stream was too slow for the intended competition level.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The rebuild changes both the launcher and the supply path. Wider discharge without wider feeding would preserve the original restriction. Gradually accelerating fuel can reduce crowding before launch, but it must preserve contact and avoid forcing balls against a stationary roof. The strategic claim is specific to this team’s execution and operating conditions; it does not invalidate compact turrets that achieve a different combination of capacity, sustained firing and maneuverability. Preserve the original development and the district-to-DCMP transition so a recommendation can learn from the pivot rather than only its final appearance.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Compare complete cycle score against the original under the same fuel supply, defense and active-window timing.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: DOWNPOUR: proposed telescope and later compact hooks
technicalNotes.construction: Original telescope did not compete at districts; later pivoting hooks replaced it.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Weight, space and scoring priorities displaced the initial climb.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The presence of a climber CAD image in an early binder is not proof it was installed or used. The later brief supplies a useful version boundary by explicitly saying the earlier mechanism did not compete. The new hook package should be recorded as a compact capability, not evidence that climbing became strategically central. In a fuel-dominant game, retain the opportunity cost in storage, mechanism power, alignment and testing. A low-mass hook can still be a poor choice if it blocks a valuable fuel route.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Audit actual installation and match use separately from prototype drawings; calculate lost usable fuel volume before selecting a climbing package.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: 971 2022: a deliberate West Coast drive simplicity choice
technicalNotes.construction: Six Colson-wheel West Coast drive; two dual-Falcon gearboxes; 8:70 gearbox tooth ratio.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Robustness, low maintenance and short-distance acceleration.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A differential drive sacrifices direct sideways motion while reducing the number of independent drive and steering mechanisms. That trade can fit a robot whose turret provides aiming independence and whose collectors support acquisition from opposite sides. Wheel choice affects maintenance and turning losses as well as traction. The team’s post-COVID experience constraint is part of this architecture decision: the most sophisticated available module is not automatically the strongest choice when integration and practice capacity differ. Preserve the resource assumption rather than presenting a universal drivetrain ranking.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure short-cycle path time, turning current and defended maneuverability using the actual collector and turret operating policy.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: 971 2022: center and guide cargo rather than only gripping harder
technicalNotes.construction: Flex-wheel prototype became mecanum-centered pickup with compliant chain/arm geometry and extra upper guides.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Use known intake behavior and improve transfer support.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The pickup must establish both ownership and a useful lateral position for the catapult transfer. Mecanum contact supplies centering while the compliant arm accommodates shape and pressure variation. Additional upper rollers address the transition after the initial capture, where a ball can lose support or arrive at the receiver at an uncontrolled height. The lesson is to diagnose the entire handoff path: improving the first roller’s grip cannot solve a downstream gap that lets cargo escape.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Track the ball center through acquisition and transfer with several inflation states; test off-center pickup at realistic driving speed.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: 971 2022: flippy arms combine retention and release
technicalNotes.construction: Spring-loaded paired transfer arms; one-way-bearing action opens them when rollers reverse.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Hold cargo in the catapult, then release it for firing.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The transfer mechanism serves as a timed constraint on the projectile. It must hold the cargo through turret alignment but stop exerting an unwanted force at release. Coupling reversal to opening reduces an actuator but creates a mechanical timing relationship that software must understand. Spring force and ball compression affect both retention and release delay. If the catapult controller assumes the ball is free before the arms actually clear, a perfectly tracked motor trajectory can still produce a poor shot.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure arm clearance and ball release timing relative to motor command, over cargo pressure and spring-wear variation.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: 971 2022: a controlled catapult instead of a flywheel
technicalNotes.construction: Light carbon catapult, two Falcons, 7:99 tooth ratio and model-predictive launch control.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Team prototypes favored tolerance to cargo pressure and surface-friction variation.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A motor-driven catapult sets the projectile’s velocity through the motion of a supporting arm rather than relying primarily on slip against a high-speed wheel. That can reduce one source of friction sensitivity while introducing trajectory tracking, release timing and structural stiffness requirements. A lighter arm spends less energy accelerating itself and leaves more actuator authority for the cargo. The controller needs the correct state at release, not merely a final position, because angle and velocity together determine the shot. This is a specific tested alternative, not a claim that catapults universally beat flywheels.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure release angle and velocity across inflation and surface variation, compare with the flywheel prototype under equal conditions, and test mis-timed retention release.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: 971 2022: turret structure must also react climbing loads
technicalNotes.construction: Turret carries catapult and climber; paired bearing support; climber revisions progress toward a spring-extended high-bar package.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Support firing and hanging loads with compact packaging.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A bearing sized only for smooth aiming may be inadequate once the suspended robot applies an overturning moment through the turret. Two support locations can define a load path for that moment while maintaining axis alignment. Shared structure saves space but couples the climber’s strength requirements to the shooter’s pointing stiffness. The documented objective changed from a mid-rung solution toward higher reach, so do not infer traversal capability from a general “climber” label. Each pictured prototype also needs its own competition-use evidence.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Check bearing and mount loads through firing and hanging, verify output-axis alignment afterward, and establish the dated competed climb configuration.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: AURELIA: package the base around two different clearances
technicalNotes.construction: 28-inch square chassis; X2i elevator-side modules and X2t intake-side modules; custom lowering spacers.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Motor protection, low chassis and intake gearbox clearance.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Choosing different module orientations within one drivebase is a packaging solution rather than a reason to recommend mixed modules universally. A motor placed inside can protect the elevator-side envelope while an outward placement can free an intake drive path. The lowering hardware must preserve module stiffness and ground clearance under a loaded, accelerating robot. Low mass is helpful, but the more relevant quantity for fast reef approach is the loaded center of mass and its motion as the shoulder and elevator change state. Include bumper and battery interfaces in the same model.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Sweep the complete intake/elevator envelope against each module; measure clearance and wheel unloading through aggressive scoring transitions.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: AURELIA: separate coral and algae contacts on a shared axis
technicalNotes.construction: Coaxial intake pivots; separate deployment reductions; shared roller drive; bilateral transfer tubes.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The team explicitly ties this intake choice to horizontal L1 placement, alongside concerns about a separate centering/indexing system.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Sharing an axis does not make these one generic intake. Each piece needs a different contact geometry, and the dedicated L1 action depends on their relative positions. Driving both sides helps prevent an arm from twisting out of phase during asymmetric contact. A common roller drive saves a motor and packaging but couples the desired surface speeds of the two pickup functions. The useful retrieval target is the entire relative geometry and state sequence: which surface acquires, which guides, and which constrains the coral during release. A lone roller photo cannot explain the L1 performance.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Film the complete L1 cycle from first floor contact through release; vary coral orientation, reef occupancy and approach angle.
technicalNotes.limitations: Team reply reports difficult horizontal approaches beyond about 45 degrees, extensive practice and late-season durability work. Successful match execution is not proof of effortless any-orientation pickup.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: AURELIA: center coral before a direct handoff
technicalNotes.construction: Flex upper rollers, grippy lower rollers, about 0.125-inch coral compression and proximity detection.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Center coral and hand directly into the end effector.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A low-compression pickup can reduce the force required to accept an awkwardly oriented tube, but it leaves less traction margin when the surfaces are dirty or the coral is wedged against another piece. Centering before transfer reduces the number of states the end effector must solve. A direct handoff avoids an intermediate tray, while demanding that the receiving geometry arrive at the right position before the piece loses its previous constraint. Sensor placement should identify the handoff state, rather than simply report that some portion of a long tube is nearby.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test slow, diagonal and multi-piece approaches; observe whether detection occurs before, during or after reliable ownership transfers.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: AURELIA: four-stage lift on a rotating shoulder
technicalNotes.construction: Shoulder-supported four-stage continuous elevator; internal HTD belts; interlocking extended-stage stops.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Compact packaging with stiffness at scoring height.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The shoulder changes both the lift’s direction and its center-of-mass path. A multi-stage lift can reach high while stowing short, but introduces more interfaces that can deflect or develop play. Hard stops that engage at extension can add stiffness where the mechanism otherwise has the least overlap; they must not produce damaging impacts at operating speed. The carriage’s integrated gearbox reduces redundant structure while making belt access and service sequencing important. In the alliance role described by the user, much of the robot’s value comes from low scoring and algae, yet its high reach still supplies capability and tactical flexibility.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure tip error and settling after shoulder/elevator transitions, including side acceleration and partial rather than only full extension.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: AURELIA: differential wrist and independently driven rollers
technicalNotes.construction: Printed bevel differential; paired 61.6:1 drives; independent coral rollers; front algae pinch wheels.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Reorient coral while keeping the moving end effector compact.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A differential combines two motor coordinates into two output motions. That can package orientation control densely, but means a joint motion may require both motors and leave less authority for the other axis at the same instant. Printed bevel gears need controlled bearing alignment and a stiffness model; backlash at a small output stage becomes placement error at the coral tip. Independent roller contacts can change tube orientation before release, which is particularly valuable for intentional L1 placement and stacking. The same hardware can support very different alliance jobs, so high-level capability must be separated from the task actually assigned in a match.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Command combined wrist motions under realistic piece load; measure output backlash and horizontal-coral placement consistency across L1 pile heights.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: AURELIA: reuse the shoulder and reposition the cage
technicalNotes.construction: Powered cage capture, passive latches, sliding support and shoulder-driven lifting; algae intake supplies support.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Reuse primary joints while controlling the hanging geometry.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A shared-joint climb saves dedicated structure only if the primary system can react the new loads. Capturing one cage tube is different from supporting the robot after the cage rotates; the lower reaction point and position of the chain relative to the robot’s center of mass determine the motion. The sliding support permits that geometry to change rather than requiring a single fixed pivot to solve every phase. Reuse also couples faults: a damaged shoulder, end effector or intake latch can affect climb. Record the support contact explicitly instead of reducing the design to “uses its arm to climb.”
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test cage swing and off-center capture, inspect every reaction contact, and verify retention after power is removed.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: SPECTRE: base and module revision at Championship
technicalNotes.construction: District Mk4i modules changed to prototype Mk5 at Worlds; ballast placement also changed.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Low center of gravity and short-cycle maneuverability.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A module swap is a robot version, even if the scoring architecture looks unchanged. Saving module weight can be reinvested as low ballast rather than removed from the robot, changing traction and stability differently from a simple weight reduction. A wide tread and different enclosure can alter friction, debris protection and maintenance. Retuning drive and autonomous behavior is part of the mechanical change: old acceleration and feedforward assumptions should not be carried over without measurements. The database should name the competition stage associated with each configuration.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Compare module slip, current and stopping repeatability before and after the change with the actual ballast and bumper package.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: SPECTRE: remote power at an integrated pivot
technicalNotes.construction: Separate three-X60 shoulder and extension gearboxes; dead-axle pivot; two-stage cascade arm.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Fast motion with a low stowed center of gravity and serviceable arm.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Keeping heavy actuators near the base reduces distal inertia and lets the arm respond without carrying all its drive mass at the tip. The price is a more complicated transmission across the pivot and through the telescope. A coaxial extension drive must preserve tension and alignment over the shoulder’s range. A large shared pivot can support stiffness and removal, but its clamps and end plugs become critical load interfaces. Motor count alone does not explain speed: the arm’s inertia, reduction, current limits and acceleration profile determine whether it can move quickly without rocking the chassis.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure end-point settling after simultaneous pivot and extension; test removal/reinstallation repeatability and chain tension over the full range.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: SPECTRE: acquire, orient and score with one end mechanism
technicalNotes.construction: Vertical and horizontal roller sets; four CANrange sensors; reversible front/back handoff and scoring.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Serve coral and algae tasks with the same manipulator.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Combining acquisition and scoring avoids a separate transfer interface, but makes the moving assembly larger and creates competing contact requirements. Coral has to be oriented differently for branches and L1; algae needs enough compliant pinch to stay captured during rapid motion. Multiple sensors can distinguish piece position and direction, provided their views remain reliable for both geometries. Front/back scoring reduces chassis rotation when the software chooses a sensible approach. The architecture should be assessed by complete cycle time and reach under defense, not by the number of available poses.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test front/back coral scoring, intentional horizontal L1 placement and algae capture with the same rollers after wear.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: SPECTRE: moving climb carriage manages the hanging center
technicalNotes.construction: Powered one-bar cage capture; carriage slides along arm; shoulder lifts; extension locks to bumper structure.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Balance under the chain while reusing the main arm.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The carriage is not just a convenient mount. Its translation changes where the cage pulls relative to the robot’s mass, allowing a controlled transition into suspension. The shoulder then supplies the lifting work and the arm lock supplies a post-match retention path. Those are separate functions and should be recorded separately. Reusing the arm reduces dedicated hardware but raises its required load and reliability. Any recommendation needs the actual cage contact, latch, shoulder and lock sequence rather than assuming that a strong scoring arm can safely substitute for a complete climber.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Capture at several swing angles, verify carriage travel under load, and test power-off retention through the intended bumper lock.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: SPECTRE: automate approach choice and L1 placement
technicalNotes.construction: Automatic front/back reef choice; level/side selected by driver; distinct base/top L1 states.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Remove repeated alignment work from the driver.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Choosing the nearest face or easiest orientation can save time, but the shortest geometric route is not always the least congested or the most valuable remaining target. L1 stacking creates an occupancy problem as well as a pose problem: a fixed placement height is insufficient once previous coral changes the landing surface. The driver still needs strategic control over task and side, with software handling repeatable motion. A mechanism recommendation should include the sensors, pose references and operator choices required to realize its cycle advantage.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test automatic choices near boundaries between faces and with populated L1; verify deliberate driver override and recovery after a failed release.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: UNDERTOW: short-cycle gearing and low mass placement
technicalNotes.construction: 29.5-inch square base; low 3×1 frame; X2i modules geared about 13.2 ft/s free speed.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Favor acceleration and grip over long-run top speed.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: For a short reef cycle, acceleration, braking and repeatable final alignment can matter more than a higher unloaded top speed. Lower gearing increases available wheel torque but does not guarantee traction; wheel compound, normal load and current limits still bound acceleration. A broad low base helps resist tipping while the elevator changes height, but occupies more traffic space. The useful comparison uses the actual route and raised mechanism state rather than a module specification on its own.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure complete reef-to-supply cycle time, stopping error and wheel unloading with the elevator at representative positions.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: UNDERTOW: floating continuous rollers and four-bar deployment
technicalNotes.construction: Foam/silicone continuous rollers, floating front plate, rubber-band dead-zone belts and four-bar deployment.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Admit longways coral and yield during collisions.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A continuous compliant surface can avoid the discrete kicks caused by spaced wheels, while a floating roller accommodates the changing cross-section presented by a tube approaching diagonally. Rubber bands bridge regions where neither main roller can maintain ownership. They also introduce wear, tracking and tension variables, so their role should be tested rather than treated as decorative assistance. The four-bar positions the deployed pickup without requiring its pivot at the very front of the chassis. Copy the contact geometry and trajectory together: substituting a single pivot can change both bumper clearance and handoff.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Approach coral at a grid of angles, measure uninterrupted contact, and repeat after a wall impact and belt replacement.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: UNDERTOW: flatten and index before handing off
technicalNotes.construction: Eight compliant/star wheels; guide wedges, flattening yoke and beam breaks; separate steep station funnel.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Create a repeatable handoff from either source.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Ground and station pickup arrive with different velocities and orientations. A common indexer lets the end effector see a smaller set of input states, but the funnel and pickup must not feed incompatible positions. Wedges and a flattening wheel create deliberate constraints; if they constrain too many dimensions at once, the tube can wedge rather than align. Sensors should identify the indexed state before the receiver moves. The station funnel adds redundancy and autonomous options, so its value depends on how much extra envelope and mass it costs alongside floor acquisition.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Compare handoff time and jam rate from both sources with skewed and bouncing arrivals; test the full state sequence after a missed detection.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: UNDERTOW: fast continuous elevator
technicalNotes.construction: Two-stage internal-belt lift; two X60s; welded support frame; team reports roughly 0.3-second full travel.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Reach scoring heights rapidly and maintain stiffness.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A fast travel number does not include settling, alignment or release. Internal belts protect the drive path but make access, tensioning and inspection more important. The support frame must react lateral inertia from the raised wrist as well as the elevator’s own acceleration. If the system reaches height quickly but sways outside the coral-placement tolerance, the useful cycle has not improved. A matched recommendation needs carriage mass, output stiffness, profile constraints and a maintenance plan rather than only belt width and motor count.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure time until the coral tip enters and stays within scoring tolerance, not merely until the encoder reaches its height setpoint.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: UNDERTOW: Flying V compliance and an L1 pass-through
technicalNotes.construction: Wrist-mounted compliant coral roller, pipe-aligning Flying V, cam-controlled rear hoop and shared algae drive.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Fast branch placement with controlled piece handoff.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Mechanical alignment can absorb residual chassis error by guiding the end effector relative to the actual pipe. It must do so without pushing the tube into a trapped configuration or transmitting a large side load into the wrist. The movable hoop illustrates why the handoff and L1 scoring states differ: a stop that is necessary to receive coral can obstruct the intended exit. Sharing a motor between piece contacts reduces moving mass but couples their speed and torque requirements. The complete mechanism includes the cam state and sensing, not just the front roller.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Map tolerated lateral and angular pipe error, test handoff against L1 pass-through, and repeat with a worn wheel and occupied nearby branches.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: UNDERTOW: capture first, then winch the robot under the cage
technicalNotes.construction: Powered roller claw, passive latch, gas-spring deployment and low-mounted ratcheting winch.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Acquire a cage quickly and retain suspension after disable.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Separating capture from lifting allows the capture wheels to optimize entry while the winch carries the robot load. The latch and cage reaction surfaces must take over reliably before the wheels stop providing traction. Remoting the winch lowers mass but lengthens the tension path and adds rope-routing concerns. A deep-climb recommendation should identify acquisition tolerance, how the cage rotates, where the chain ends relative to the robot’s center of mass, and the load path after power is removed.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test swinging-cage acquisition, transition from powered rollers to latch, and power-off retention with the actual rope routing.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: MISS DAISY: orient on the floor and preserve collision compliance
technicalNotes.construction: Sprung OTB rollers with ramps; later stronger front tube and round shafts.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Broad-orientation acquisition and impact survival.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Orienting the tube before lifting reduces the number of uncontrolled handoff states. A wide compliant roller captures early while ramps and passive contacts bias the tube toward the desired orientation. That can fail if a ramp starts lifting one end too soon. Structural damage also changes the ball path: a bent mounting tube can turn a nominally symmetric intake into a one-sided jam. Preserve the sequence of revisions, because a successful final contact geometry may rely on the preceding stiffness fix.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Film diagonal approaches from both sides before and after impacts; measure ramp and roller alignment rather than judging symmetry by eye.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: MISS DAISY: diagnose jams from observed contact
technicalNotes.construction: Reduced compression, relocated support shaft, changed hard stops and redesigned ramp bends.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Slow-motion review identified different jams at successive events.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A jam is a geometric event, not merely insufficient motor power. A tube can press a belt into a support, climb at one end while the other end remains constrained, or stop a roller whose structure is bent. Each mode requires a different change. Moving the wheels forward changes both normal force and where the tube begins to rise. A useful agent should first ask which contacts stop moving and where the tube becomes over-constrained; recommending more torque without this observation can destroy the part that reveals the fault.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Create a repeatable failed orientation, isolate the first contact that arrests motion, change one dimension and compare the failure frequency.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: MISS DAISY: grip algae while allowing coral release
technicalNotes.construction: Coral compression reduced to 0.375 inch; drive ratio revised; harder wheels and algae shields added.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Improve coral release, pulley durability and algae retention.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The two pieces demand conflicting grip behavior. Increasing compression can improve retention but make a tube difficult to release without disturbing the target. A harder wheel can resist wear yet reduce conformity and change normal force. A larger drive pulley may reduce tooth loading and skipping while changing speed and torque. Shields can prevent a soft ball from folding around the side plates, addressing a failure that motor current alone cannot solve. These are linked empirical tradeoffs, so the record should preserve both piece types and the tested release geometry.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure coral release force and algae retention after representative wheel wear; inspect pulley teeth during repeated high-torque captures.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: MISS DAISY: rope geometry and structural stiffness evolved together
technicalNotes.construction: Horizontal Dyneema spool inspired by 1678; continuous lift; later U-crossplate and rigid side support.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Solve rope slip, poor tension and elevator lateral play.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A lift can have accurate motor position while its carriage moves laterally because the structure and rope system are different error sources. Rope routing should keep each run aligned as winding radius changes; overlapping wraps change effective motion per motor turn. A stiff top crosspiece limits upright splay, while a triangulated or rigid support reacts side loading without relying only on adjustable rods. These revisions show why copying the final spool alone is insufficient. The recommendation needs the complete routing, tension system and support geometry.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Track carriage height versus motor position and lateral tip error independently; inspect winding over repeated full strokes under load.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: MISS DAISY: shoulder and wrist serve different coordinates
technicalNotes.construction: 45:1 shoulder with lantern gear; 21.4:1 wrist with about ±100° motion.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Move between robot sides and reorient coral without collisions.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The shoulder changes the end effector’s position and reach, while the wrist changes the piece orientation. Those motions need not be performed serially, but simultaneous movement requires a collision-aware path. A lantern gear can place the reduction close to the output and control backlash; its performance still depends on bearing alignment and tooth/pin wear. A dead-axle wrist offers a clear reaction path, but the cantilevered mass and cable routing contribute torque and deflection. The useful model is the coral’s swept volume, not only each joint’s independent limit.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Generate and physically check the coral envelope during side swaps; measure output angle repeatability under reversing load.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: MISS DAISY: passive harpoon over a wheeled grabber
technicalNotes.construction: Levering climber; passive sprung harpoon; 675:1 reduction; steel gears replaced inadequate aluminum gears.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Similar capture performance with fewer vulnerable parts.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A high reduction can provide lifting torque, but it does not reduce the load carried by the final gear and support shaft. Material changes at that interface can therefore matter more than adding motor power. A passive hook can outperform powered acquisition when the robot’s approach already supplies sufficient engagement force and the cage geometry naturally directs the bar into the latch. That simplifies the controller while placing more importance on the approach envelope and retention geometry. Capture reliability should be assessed with swing and imperfect alignment, not only a stationary cage.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure engagement tolerance and inspect final-stage stress after repeated climbs; test retention with the cage rotated and the robot disabled.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: MISS DAISY: remove a dedicated algae intake that adds no useful capability
technicalNotes.construction: A separate floor-algae collector was removed after prototype comparisons.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: It did not outperform the end effector enough to justify complexity.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A subsystem can satisfy its own requirements and still be a poor robot-level choice. A dedicated collector may save a little positioning time while costing envelope, sensors, wiring, maintenance and driver decisions. If the primary end effector already serves the intended algae role, the marginal gain must exceed those costs. This is the right level for an architecture agent to reason: compare complete task contribution and reliability rather than rewarding more mechanisms. Keep the removed design in the history as an evaluated alternative, not as an installed feature of the final robot.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Compare complete algae cycles and failure recovery with and without the auxiliary system, including time spent switching modes.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: OPR 2025: floating capture and protected pivot drive
technicalNotes.construction: 20-inch OTB intake; coaxial roller drive; synchronized pivot sides; floating upper roller.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Tolerant coral pickup with motors protected in the frame.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Coaxial power transmission lets a roller remain driven as the intake pivots without a long changing-center belt run. The floating contact accommodates an awkward tube orientation while the lower contact keeps it moving into the robot. Synchronizing both sides resists twist, but an impact can still concentrate load at the polycarbonate-to-aluminum joint. Large clamps distribute this force and retain the bearing as the plate flexes. Automatic retraction protects the collector only after the sensor has confirmed that the tube is safely inside.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test diagonal pickup, asymmetric loading and capture-triggered retraction; inspect bearing retention following a side impact.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: OPR 2025: independent straightening drives and staged cradle sensing
technicalNotes.construction: Independently driven straightener sides; current-triggered reversal; two-sensor cradle with anti-bounce step.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Align coral and recover jams before handoff.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Independent sides permit relative slip or reversal instead of forcing both ends of a tube forward at the same speed. Current sensing can identify resistance, but must distinguish a normal capture transient from a persistent jam. The cradle then changes the problem from continuous alignment to a discrete known handoff position. A stop lip and anti-bounce feature control longitudinal motion, while cutouts provide room for the receiving gripper. Excessively constraining the tube at the same time as the gripper closes can create a new jam, so the handoff sequence matters as much as the tray shape.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Feed tubes at skewed angles, tune jam detection against false triggers, and test receiver clearance during an interrupted handoff.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: OPR 2025: reduce moving inertia without losing algae grip
technicalNotes.construction: Formed-sheet arm replaced tubing; lighter geared gripper drive; remoted motor; velocity-matched coral ejection.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Reduce mass and pivot moment while keeping functional grip.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Removing mass far from the pivot reduces inertia more effectively than removing the same mass near the axis. A remoted motor achieves that while adding a transmission whose backlash and compliance must be controlled. Formed sheet can provide a stiff section with low mass if the flanges and joints react the actual loads. Matching ejection to chassis motion can reduce unwanted relative velocity at release, but requires consistent roller surface speed and piece position. It is a coordinated robot motion, not a passive property of the gripper.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure tip settling and grip under acceleration; test scoring while approaching and backing away at several speeds.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: OPR 2025: stiff internally belted elevator
technicalNotes.construction: Two-stage continuous lift, internal 18-mm HTD belt, two X60s; reported about 0.6-second travel.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Fast motion with lateral stiffness and camera visibility.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The upright supports, top bridge and bearing guidance determine how much commanded height becomes actual end-effector position. Internal belts protect the tension path but demand a practical inspection and replacement route. Integrating a wrist gearbox into the carriage removes interfaces while increasing the consequences of a carriage service problem. Cameras on both uprights can preserve tag visibility as the robot approaches different branch sides, but their structural reference must remain stable as the lift moves.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure tip error at full and intermediate height during chassis braking; verify camera visibility and calibration on both scoring sides.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: OPR 2025: lightweight winch and guided cage capture
technicalNotes.construction: 4.5-pound climbing package; rope winch, ratchet, sprung deployment and printed cage guides.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Easy alignment, legal cage clearance and power-off retention.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A guide can enlarge the capture envelope without adding an actuator, but its shape must not let the cage rotate into the elevator or chain contact an illegal surface. Rope lifting places high local loads at the spool, attachment and pivot; these should be checked independently of motor torque. A ratchet provides a mechanical holding path after disable, while the magnet and collars manage capture and slippage. The architecture record should identify which elements guide, which retain and which actually carry the robot.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test rotating and swinging cages, inspect the rope at attachment bends, and verify chain clearance through the full lift.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: BREAD 2025: floating intake plus dedicated L1 restraint
technicalNotes.construction: Floating front roller, centering wedges and deployable L1 bar with anti-bounce hooks.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Broad pickup and controlled L1 release.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A tube entering lengthwise needs space to rotate; a fixed narrow contact can eject it before alignment finishes. The floating front roller accommodates that transition. The L1 bar serves a different task: it changes the release boundary and prevents the intake from lifting or letting coral bounce away. This is a useful example for an agent because L1 capability is not merely “run the intake backward.” The intended orientation, release contact and state of the front roller determine whether coral stays where the alliance needs it.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test L1 placement at several existing pile heights and compare bounce-out with and without the restraint engaged.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: BREAD 2025: asymmetric star-wheel orientation
technicalNotes.construction: Asymmetric star-wheel indexer, beam-break extra-piece rejection and repeatable handoff tray.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Reduce alignment jams and reject an unwanted second tube.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Symmetry can preserve a bad equilibrium: both ends of a skewed tube may be driven equally without ever rotating into the desired orientation. A deliberate asymmetry can break that state, but may also introduce a preferred direction and different behavior for mirror-image approaches. The extra-piece logic must distinguish a second tube from a long first tube passing multiple sensors. A tray then provides a controlled receiving state. Test these as one chain rather than optimizing the indexer’s standalone speed.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Feed mirror-image diagonal tubes and closely spaced pairs; record orientation time, rejection errors and handoff repeatability.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: BREAD 2025: cascade lift with counterbalance and chain control
technicalNotes.construction: Two-stage cascade; two X60s at 7:1; constant-force springs; cantilevered pivot and chain tensioner.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Rapid lift with lower current and controlled transmission.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Counterbalance reduces the gravitational load the motors must supply during part of the stroke, but its force and mounting geometry affect upward and downward behavior differently. A cascade lift magnifies travel and velocity while changing the force seen by each stage. A rolling chain tensioner can manage slack during acceleration, but does not cure a misaligned sprocket or insufficient tooth engagement. The cantilevered wrist support must react both bending and overturning moments. A fast reported stroke needs a settling and placement test to establish its useful cycle value.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Log lift current and tracking in both directions, inspect tension during reversals, and measure tip displacement under sideways load.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: BREAD 2025: shared drive for coral and algae contacts
technicalNotes.construction: One X60 drives distinct coral/algae contacts through different ratios and printed gear-pulley combinations.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Handle both pieces while reducing moving mass.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A shared motor saves wiring and mass but ties the contact speeds to fixed ratios. The design must provide enough algae holding torque without making coral release too abrupt. Combining a gear and pulley can shorten the assembly and remove redundant hubs, while concentrating loads into the printed part and its bearing interface. Material choice, print orientation and temperature therefore belong in the durability review. A successful borrowed geometry requires matching compression and piece position, not only duplicating the nominal ratio.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure algae retention and coral release after repeated cycles and heating; inspect printed tooth roots and bearing fits.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: BREAD 2025: centered single-tube cage support
technicalNotes.construction: Six-pound spear/flyswatter collector; spring deploy; string winch; reported 1.5-second lift.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Center the cage and use a compact lifting package.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A passive centering shape can simplify acquisition while making the load path highly dependent on where the cage settles. If retention relies partly on robot weight and friction, the transition into suspension needs careful testing before full load is applied. Spring deployment saves an actively driven extension but requires a reliable latch and stow sequence. The winch reduction determines available force, while rope radius and cage lever arm determine actual robot lift. A lift-time claim should remain distinct from total acquisition-plus-settling time.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test swinging-cage entry and interrupted lifts, including a case where only one contact is initially engaged.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: BREAD 2025: low chassis and direct reef ranging
technicalNotes.construction: Dropped X2 modules, low frame and CANrange reef-distance sensing.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Low center of gravity and repeatable approach.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Lowering the frame can improve stability while reducing ground clearance and access. A direct range measurement near the reef can refine the final approach, but only if the sensor sees the intended surface rather than a tube, branch or oblique panel. It should complement a known geometric model and a validated scoring tolerance. Treat a sensor as an observation with failure modes rather than proof of alignment.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Map distance error over reef approach angle, piece occupancy and elevator position; check collision and service clearances.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: Alpha Dogs: retention, compliance and source fallback
technicalNotes.construction: Single roller became dual; long compliance linkage became compact sprung arm; first event used station funnel.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Solve escaping coral, collision vulnerability and packaging.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Capturing a tube is not the same as retaining it after the first contact. The second roller can close an escape path while increasing the need to control compression. An impact-yielding linkage can protect the pickup, but a long arm consumes chassis volume and increases bending moment. The report’s station-funnel fallback is evidence of a competition configuration, while its ground-intake drawings include developmental versions. Keep those distinct when recommending inspiration: a promising prototype is not automatically a demonstrated event mechanism.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test retention during braking and reverse motion; verify the exact event configuration before using a version as a performance example.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: Alpha Dogs: conveyor and tray progressively consolidated
technicalNotes.construction: Opposed star-wheel conveyors evolved into a lighter polycarbonate assembly and integrated receiving cup.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Straighten coral and simplify the transfer structure.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A conveyor that both straightens and transports a tube can avoid a separate orientation stage, but its downstream tray must stop the tube without sending it back into the drive contacts. Removing redundant support material can improve access and mass while changing alignment under load. A receiving cup reduces uncertainty in the arm’s pickup position, provided it has no lip that prevents release into the gripper. The best architecture depends on the handoff’s repeatability and recovery after a partial acquisition, not only its nominal travel time.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test varied tube orientation and arrival speed, then interrupt the handoff to verify that the mechanism can recover without driver intervention.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: Alpha Dogs: gripper envelope changed the architecture
technicalNotes.construction: Combined piece gripper revised after reach/envelope problems; elevator-mounted arrangement developed.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Keep the placing assembly within the intended geometry.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Adding a second piece function changes more than roller spacing: the swept volume, center of mass and necessary approach path may all grow. A gripper that works on a bench can violate the robot’s usable envelope when attached to an arm. Moving it onto an elevator changes the kinematic problem but does not by itself prove accurate release. The report leaves some final geometry and transmission details unresolved, so an agent should retrieve CAD or later event evidence rather than invent an elevator ratio or a final mechanism sequence.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Check the full loaded piece envelope and actual event revision; measure pickup, hold and release separately for each piece.
technicalNotes.limitations: This engineering report documents development. It does not establish every final CAD dimension, elevator reduction or competition use of every pictured prototype.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: Alpha Dogs: reduce the cage mechanism to its useful load path
technicalNotes.construction: Complex capture concepts led to a simpler pivoting jack; chain endpoint targeted the robot’s mass center.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Reduce weight and improve hanging geometry.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A cage mechanism must transfer the robot’s weight through a secure contact while allowing the robot to settle into a stable orientation. A design can capture well yet demand excessive torque because its chain line remains far from the center of mass. Simplifying to a lever reduces parts but can concentrate load at the main pivot and rope attachment. The analysis should identify the actual hanging geometry and load path, with an explicit boundary between proposed and competed revisions.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test off-center acquisition and load transition; confirm the final revision with dated match or pit evidence.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: Alpha Dogs: camera view and reef occupancy are architecture inputs
technicalNotes.construction: Camera angle revised for close tags; field-region alignment and operator-entered reef occupancy are described.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Reduce blind spots and repeated target-selection work.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A camera can see an AprilTag far away yet lose it at the exact distance where precision is needed. Mount angle and obstruction therefore belong in the early CAD review. Keeping reef occupancy in software changes the operator’s task from repeatedly aiming to maintaining a reliable shared state. Incorrect occupancy can send the robot toward a filled branch, so the system needs a quick correction and manual override. The mechanism recommendation should include what target information it assumes the controls will supply.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test tag visibility at every final scoring pose and recovery from deliberately incorrect occupancy entries.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: SIDEWAYS: compliant dual four-bar collection
technicalNotes.construction: Dual pneumatic four-bars; quarter-inch polycarbonate arms; large front and smaller transfer rollers.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Acquire from either side and yield in collisions.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Two intake directions reduce the turn needed to collect the next cargo while keeping the shooter in a useful field orientation. The four-bar defines the roller’s approach and stowed position; the arm material supplies lateral compliance that the linkage alone cannot. Different roller diameters and reductions establish surface velocities through the transition. An apparent increase in grip is unhelpful if it arrests the ball between contacts. This architecture should be understood as two collectors feeding one shared storage and shooter system, not as two independent scoring paths.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure acquisition at speed and across approach angles, then verify both directions still transfer correctly after impact.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: SIDEWAYS: serialize two wide inputs and reject wrong-color cargo
technicalNotes.construction: Centering wheels and rollers; beam-break position tracking; color sensing; deliberate opponent-cargo ejection.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Maintain two-cargo ownership and consistent shooter feeding.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The serializer converts a broad acquisition front into an ordered narrow output under a possession limit.
