Storing the first accepted ball away from the active intake leaves room for the second; that is a spatial control policy, not merely a conveyor. Color rejection adds an adversarial constraint: an unwanted ball must leave without corrupting the state estimate or helping the opponent more than necessary. A sensor detects contact or color at one location, so software must preserve identity as balls move and occasionally slip. A jam can be a state-estimation failure even when all rollers turn.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Run correct/wrong-color pairs from both sides, interrupt the feed, and verify the estimated inventory against video.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: SIDEWAYS: wrap, surface matching and a moving target
technicalNotes.construction: Nine-inch main wheel, driven back rollers, adjustable hood and ±120° turret.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Long contact and controlled spin for accurate mobile shots.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A long wrap increases the time available to accelerate the cargo and can reduce the impulse required at any single contact. Driving the backing rollers changes both friction loss and the ball’s angular velocity. Surface-speed matching is a kinematic idea; the actual ball may slip or deform, so launch spin must be measured. The turret reduces chassis-heading dependence, while the hood and speed map determine range. None of these removes the need to account for robot velocity and shot timing. The relevant comparison is the repeatability of the exit state under a sequence of shots.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure ball translation and spin with high-speed video, compare first and second shots, and test motion compensation across turret headings.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: SIDEWAYS: react against the truss before reaching traversal
technicalNotes.construction: Chain elevator, reaction arm, passive telescoping stinger and retention latches.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Reorient the robot to reach traversal within the envelope.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: This climb is a sequence of changing load paths. The elevator first loads a rung; the reaction arm then changes the robot angle by pushing against the truss; the stinger finally reaches a farther rung. Large internal forces can occur while the robot barely moves because opposing contacts create a short lever arm. A tensile strap can carry a known directional load efficiently, but cannot resist compression or uncontrolled reverse motion. The passive stinger can be light because it need not retract under robot load. Copying only its telescoping tubes would omit the reaction geometry that makes the reach possible.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Instrument reaction loads and verify every intermediate retention state; test misalignment and incomplete hook engagement before increasing speed.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: SIDEWAYS: first swerve and deliberately low mass placement
technicalNotes.construction: Mk4i L3 modules, added motor-shaft support bearings, low solid bellypan and central battery.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Maneuver around defense and maintain stability.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The drive choice supports the collector and turret by allowing travel direction to change without the chassis continuously pointing toward the next ball. Lowering mass helps resist wheel unloading during fast transitions, while the chosen ground clearance still has to survive real field debris and cargo. Extra bearing support changes how module loads reach the motor shaft. A reusable design record should retain these integration details because a module family name alone cannot explain collision survival or handling.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Compare stopping and lateral acceleration with representative cargo and bumper loads; inspect motor-shaft support alignment after impacts.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: BREAKDOWN: independent vertical and lateral extension
technicalNotes.construction: Vertical elevator plus 15° inclined three-stage carbon-fiber laterator; PEEK guidance rollers.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Fast reach with low moving mass.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Separating vertical and outward motion turns scoring poses into two mostly independent coordinates. That can simplify the end-effector geometry and let the chassis remain farther from the grid, but adds another flexible stage and a collision envelope between stages. Low-mass carbon structures reduce inertia; guidance roller preload and tube alignment determine whether they move freely without excessive play. The laterator’s angle contributes vertical motion as it extends, so the control system still needs a coupled pose model. A reported travel time describes one axis, not a complete pickup-to-placement transition.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure coral-equivalent tool-tip error under simultaneous axis motion and chassis acceleration; inspect guidance play and cable drag across the entire stroke.
technicalNotes.limitations: The PDF required OCR. Page 12 elevator construction was checked visually; other numerical OCR details should be checked in the original before fabrication.

technicalNotes.title: BREAKDOWN: articulate contacts for cones and cubes
technicalNotes.construction: Articulating roller claw with distinct cube and cone contacts; over-center cone grip.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Serve upright cones and cubes without pursuing every floor orientation.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A cone and a cube present different contact and centering problems. An articulated claw can open enough for a cube while using a different smaller contact to constrain a cone. Over-center geometry can supply retention without continuous high motor force, provided the piece is located in the intended three-point contact. Choosing not to solve sideways floor cones is an explicit scope decision linked to expected high-level supply; it must not become a universal claim that such pickup has no value. A local event or a disrupted supply plan can change that assumption.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test each intended piece orientation and define a safe fallback for excluded orientations; measure grip after approach collisions.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: BREAKDOWN: rack-deployed cube floor pickup
technicalNotes.construction: Rack-and-pinion polycarbonate extension and a small grippy roller feed the main claw.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Lightweight, robust access to floor cubes.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Linear extension preserves roller height while changing its distance from the chassis, which is useful when a simple pivot would change the pickup geometry too much. A rack cut directly into the side plate reduces part count but concentrates wear and impact load in that plate. The floor mechanism does not solve every piece task; it supplies a known cube path to the articulating claw. That specialization can be efficient when the human-player and game-piece plan makes it sufficient.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test cube acquisition near walls and with oblique contact; inspect rack alignment and tooth wear after repeated forced retractions.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: BREAKDOWN: forks change the robot’s balance interface
technicalNotes.construction: Carbon-fiber forks and a sliding carriage react against bumper structure; rope lift.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Lift alongside partners and balance quickly.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The forks are an alliance interaction mechanism. Their usefulness depends on the partner’s underside, bumper placement and where the combined load settles on the platform. Reacting through bumper wood can counter sag but creates a load path that needs appropriate mounting and repeatability. A mechanism that works under one partner may interfere with another, so compatibility belongs in the selection criteria. This differs fundamentally from a cage or rung climb despite sharing motors, rope and lifting motion.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test with representative partner geometries, unequal loading and platform tilt; verify the load path through the bumper attachment.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: BREAKDOWN: collision avoidance and compliant station intake
technicalNotes.construction: Intermediate superstructure states, reduced-precision transitions and a compliant laterator intake mode.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Move quickly while avoiding collisions and station impact loads.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A Cartesian-looking mechanism still needs a safe sequence through its intermediate states. Requiring every joint to settle precisely at every waypoint wastes time, while removing all intermediate conditions can create a collision. A compliant acquisition mode trades position stiffness for reduced impact, so its transition back to scoring control must be deliberate. Vision and odometry should supply a confidence-aware pose; the mechanical compliance is a complement to that estimate rather than evidence that accurate sensing is unnecessary.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Start transitions from unexpected interrupted states, test a station impact, and verify that the mechanism returns to a known scoring reference.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: OPR 2023: low-backlash articulated arm
technicalNotes.construction: Two driven joints, dead axles, bronze bushings and gas-shock shoulder counterbalance.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Fast repeatable motion with motor-side position sensing.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: An articulated arm can reach floor, station and grid positions without a tall lift, but the endpoint error combines both joint errors. A small shoulder angle error becomes a larger tip error as the arm extends. Reducing backlash at shafts, gears and chains supports motor-side sensing only if elastic deformation remains acceptable. Gas shocks reduce gravitational torque over part of the motion but produce a changing torque with angle. A bronze bushing can be appropriate for high load and limited rotation, while friction and wear must be included in control tuning.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure tip repeatability approaching the same pose from both directions, under load and after chain wear.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: OPR 2023: piece-specific active contacts
technicalNotes.construction: Pneumatic top roller for cubes, synchronized side rollers for cones and piece-specific sensors.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Center and hold both pieces while limiting damage.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The top roller and side pinch solve different shapes rather than forcing both through one fixed gap. Timing the side mechanism prevents one arm closing first and pushing the cone away. A sensor that reliably detects a cube may not see a cone in the same position, which explains why sensing belongs in the physical design. The control should stop or change the roller command after capture to avoid damaging the soft piece. Compliance reduces impact severity but must not let the frame spread enough to lose the intended contact geometry.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test skewed cone entry, cube retention during traversal and sensor-triggered transitions with worn or deformed pieces.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: OPR 2023: base mass supports arm motion
technicalNotes.construction: Low Mk4i base; rear steel ballast and solid bellypan; rigid tower and dead-axle shoulder support.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Stable traversal and a stiff arm reference.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A lightweight arm does not eliminate its overturning moment. Low ballast and a broad support polygon can permit more aggressive joint motion, while adding driving load and stopping energy. Tower deflection appears as arm error even when both joint encoders are exact. The base, tower and arm should therefore be tested as one structure. The appropriate ballast location depends on the arm’s range and battery placement rather than a generic preference for more robot weight.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure wheel unloading and tool-tip motion during combined driving and arm transitions over cable track and platform edges.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: ECHO: compliant vector pickup and cone centering
technicalNotes.construction: Sponge/noodle roller, dustpan, powered centering flappers and bent-polycarbonate structure.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The binder lists construction; detailed comparative selection reasoning is not supplied.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A broad soft contact can accommodate variation in approach and distribute pressure on a deformable piece. The dustpan supplies support underneath, while the flappers create a separate centering action. That is a different mechanism from merely adding compliant wheels to an arm. The soft material’s wear and compression set can alter intake behavior over an event; the structure must remain aligned while yielding to impacts. Because the binder does not give a complete rejected-alternatives account, these are engineering implications rather than a claim about the team’s exact selection process.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure centering success across cone orientations and roller wear, and inspect whether the dustpan or flappers create an escape path.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: ECHO: lightweight telescoping arm and roller end effector
technicalNotes.construction: Sheet-metal pivot structure, carbon telescope, shimmed hex interfaces and light dead-axle end rollers.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Weight and backlash reduction are explicitly documented.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Reducing distal mass improves both arm acceleration and the chassis stability needed to exploit it. A light telescoping tube still needs sufficient overlap and guidance to resist bending and torsion at full extension. Shimmed interfaces target lost motion, while structure and belt elasticity remain separate error sources. Dead-axle rollers can remove rotating shaft mass and simplify the wheel assembly, but their supports must retain alignment. A recommendation should compare endpoint settling and piece ownership under load rather than claiming a material alone makes the arm fast.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure endpoint deflection at full reach and after reversing both axes; inspect telescoping guidance and roller support wear.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: ECHO: nonparallel balance-fork linkage
technicalNotes.construction: Carbon-rod forks, nonparallel four-bar lift and over-center deployment with ratchet release.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Lift and tilt relative to a partner and the floor.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A nonparallel four-bar controls orientation as well as translation. That can lift a robot while changing its attitude without another actuator, but the force and mechanical advantage vary through the stroke. Over-center deployment can hold a state mechanically, while the ratchet provides a separate release/retention function. Partner geometry and platform angle determine the contact loads. The design should be retrieved as an alliance-specific balance solution rather than grouped indiscriminately with climbers from other seasons.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Model linkage force through the entire stroke and test with multiple partner undersides and off-axis loading.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: ECHO: preload catapult and vacuum swiper are distinct tactical tools
technicalNotes.construction: Spring-released one-shot cube catapult; dual vacuum cups added in a three-day development period.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Preload launch and opponent loading-zone cube acquisition.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A one-shot mechanism can be mechanically simpler than forcing the main manipulator to execute the same autonomous action, but it spends mass on a narrow use. Its value depends on repeatability and the time it frees for the rest of the routine. Vacuum acquisition relies on seal area, surface condition and resistance to peeling; it is poorly described by a generic grip-force number. The swiper is a dated tactical addition, not proof every earlier robot revision carried it. Keep the development date and task boundary attached to the feature.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test preload release over the allowed setup variation and vacuum retention under peeling loads and imperfect cube surfaces.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: VORTEX: centered under-bumper acquisition
technicalNotes.construction: Mecanum front contact, kicker rollers and angled powered funneling wheels.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Accept side approaches and center notes without jamming.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A note arriving sideways or off-center should be translated toward the feeder before the shooter demands a repeatable entry state. Mecanum and angled contacts can supply that transverse velocity, but excess lateral force can fold or wedge the note. A stiff bumper and intake mount preserve the intended compression under defense. The correct performance measure includes successful ownership from the edge of the mouth, not only straight-on pickup at the center.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Map pickup across the mouth with deformed notes, oblique approaches and bumper impacts; observe the first region where motion stops.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: VORTEX: annular feed removes the intake-indexing heading constraint
technicalNotes.construction: Two-direction annular feeder supplies a turret without returning it to the intake; 720° cable system.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Maintain goal tracking during acquisition and feeding.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The architectural benefit is not merely a large turret angle. Many turreted designs must rotate to an intake alignment before receiving a note, losing continuous tracking. An annular feed trades that delay for a larger guided path whose friction, seams and direction switching must be managed. Choosing the shorter route can reduce feed time, while a reversal must preserve piece state. The cable system makes the aiming envelope physically usable; without reliable wire guidance, the extra angular range is only a CAD possibility.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Feed at multiple turret headings including through a direction change; test note wear, guide friction and cable-chain operation near both limits.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: VORTEX: revised shooter separates feed and launch contacts
technicalNotes.construction: Second-revision quad-wheel shooter; staged feed rollers; asymmetrical wheels; sector-gear hood.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Controlled note entry and spin for a flatter useful trajectory.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The note’s flexible ring makes its entry orientation and deformation important to launch repeatability. A dedicated first stage can establish the approach before the high-speed wheels impart the final velocity and spin. Asymmetric contact can bias spin, but the resulting flight still needs empirical validation over wear and range. Hood backlash is an angular error that becomes more consequential at some distances than others. The revision label matters: a final shooter image must not silently stand in for an earlier competition version.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure entry deformation and shot dispersion with several note conditions; compare hood approaches from both directions and both feed routes.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: VORTEX: amplifier is a second routing destination
technicalNotes.construction: Roller carriage on an elevator routes notes to amp/trap and accepts human-player feed.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Support multiple scoring and shuttling roles.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The amplifier is not just a final scoring roller. It adds a branch to the note-routing state machine and a distinct human-player acquisition path. Shared use can justify the mechanism’s mass if those roles are valuable in the alliance plan, but creates more transitions and collision states. Passive trap-reaction wheels supply a structural contact during climbing, tying its geometry to the endgame sequence. The agent should explain those dependencies before recommending the package to a team that only needs one of its functions.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test every routing transition and interrupted sequence; verify that the trap reaction contact does not dislodge the stored note.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: VORTEX: rapid rope climb establishes trap height
technicalNotes.construction: Sprung hook arms and a low-mounted rope winch pull the robot to trap height.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Lift quickly while enabling the amplifier to reach the trap.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The climb’s lift distance is determined by the scorer’s required geometry, not just the minimum suspension score. Gas springs can deploy the hooks while the winch retracts them under load. A rope path needs secure anchors, consistent winding and sufficient clearance as the robot swings. If retention relies on drivetrain or motor braking behavior, that exact power-off state should be validated rather than assumed. The trap sequence must preserve the reaction contact and note orientation throughout the lift.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test acquisition, lift, trap alignment and disable as one sequence with several chain heights and swing angles.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: OPR 2024: chassis and module geometry create the intake path
technicalNotes.construction: Modified front module clearance; under-bumper conveyor; post-Newmarket aluminum side plates and added bracing.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Wide pickup, consistent centering and impact rigidity.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: An under-bumper path consumes the same volume as frame rails and module motors, so module orientation and mounting plates are part of the intake design. Increasing plate rigidity preserves compression but can transmit more collision load elsewhere. The documented event boundary should be retained: the stronger side plates and bracing were a precautionary update rather than necessarily the initial robot. Intake width is useful only if the full path can move off-center notes without trapping them at a module or frame corner.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test side pickup and corner impacts, then compare roller alignment and chassis squareness before and after the update.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: OPR 2024: pre-compression, differential spin and revised release angle
technicalNotes.construction: Pre-compression contacts, independent left/right drives, low-backlash pivot; flywheels later tipped down 6°.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Consistent feed and greater useful shot range.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A flexible note can enter the same nominal wheel gap in different shapes. Pre-compression aims to control that shape before final acceleration. Independent side speeds then create spin, while mechanically linked upper/lower contacts preserve another aspect of consistency. A six-degree structural change alters the reachable trajectory envelope even if the control software is unchanged. Distinguish output speed, compression and release geometry when diagnosing misses: increasing RPM cannot necessarily compensate for a deformed or inconsistently presented note.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Compare shot distributions before and after the geometric revision with the same notes, recording entry deformation and wheel recovery.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
technicalNotes.performance_status: Reported values retain source conditions; validation recommendations are proposed tests, not completed tests

technicalNotes.title: OPR 2024: pneumatic lift and an explicitly different disable behavior
technicalNotes.construction: Dual pneumatic cylinders and revised double hook; single-acting valve retracts on loss of power.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Fast hanging and compatibility with a partner-loaded chain.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A pneumatic climber stores energy before the lift, reducing the need for a large electric winch during the final action. Available force depends on regulated pressure, piston area and the retracting-side rod area, while repeated actions consume finite stored air. The hook geometry must accommodate a chain already displaced by a partner. The described valve behavior is specific to this plumbing and control configuration; it should not become a generic assumption about all solenoids or an instruction to rely on an untested after-buzzer action.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test force and timing at the lowest expected pressure, including partner chain displacement and the actual disabled valve state.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: OPR 2024: adapt autonomous to whether a note is actually present
technicalNotes.construction: Game-piece camera, drive-to-point correction, missing-note diversion and velocity-compensated aiming.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Avoid wasting autonomous time on absent or displaced notes.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: An intake with a large acquisition envelope becomes more useful when the path can correct toward the observed note. The controller must decide early enough that a failed attempt does not consume the rest of autonomous. A missing-note branch is a strategy choice tied to contested supply and partner routes, not simply a vision feature. The shot system also depends on current robot velocity and a stable angle reference. Database recommendations should include these feedback assumptions alongside the mechanical pickup.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Displace or remove expected notes and test diversion timing, partner-route safety and the resulting end pose.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: ROTI: under-bumper pickup feeds a movable shooter
technicalNotes.construction: Full-width intake with pickup rollers and centering wheels.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Center notes before they enter the shooter.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The collector has to supply a consistent location and shape to a scorer whose height and angle can change. Centering at the floor reduces the uncertainty the moving receiver must handle. A shallow pickup can preserve chassis protection but needs clearance around module and frame structure. Surface speed should capture a note without throwing it past the receiving contact. The effective system includes the handoff state that determines when the elevator may move away.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test off-center acquisition and interrupted handoff while varying the receiver’s initial height and angle.

technicalNotes.title: ROTI: one lift creates scoring height and endgame capability
technicalNotes.construction: Continuous rope lift with overextending carriage; passive lower hooks retain the chain after initial lift.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Use one shooter for speaker, amp and trap.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Moving the shooter upward changes its release geometry and can improve defended shot access, while stowing preserves travel routes under the stage. That broad capability costs raised mass and a multi-state handoff. The passive lower hooks are central to the climb: they take over the suspension load so the elevator can extend again for trap scoring. Without that load transfer, the same actuator cannot independently hold the robot and reposition the scorer. This is an architectural sequence rather than an elevator plus an unrelated climber.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Verify passive-hook engagement before re-extension; test full-height stability and stowed route clearance with the actual scorer mass.

technicalNotes.title: ROTI: counterbalanced pivot and shaped note feed
technicalNotes.construction: Gas-spring counterbalance; output-angle sensing; asymmetric launch speeds; conical/mecanum feeder contacts.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: One shooter serves several release geometries.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A counterbalance reduces gravitational torque but changes the motor’s required effort across the angular range. Sensing the output helps distinguish gearbox motion from actual scorer angle. Conical and mecanum feed contacts can shape and spread the note before launch; their useful effect depends on how the flexible ring deforms. The front roller angle also affects trap delivery, so optimizing only speaker shots may degrade another required mode. A recommendation needs the complete scoring envelope and mode transition tests.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure output-angle hysteresis and shot dispersion in every scoring mode, with both new and damaged notes.

technicalNotes.title: Team Kika Mana: technical sheet supports construction, not a complete design history
technicalNotes.construction: Asymmetric 3-inch Colson shooter; side-compression feed; rack hood; elevator-mounted scoring package.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The sheet attributes spin to shot accuracy; broader selection reasoning is not documented.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: This source is useful for geometry and component identification but should not be promoted to a full engineering binder. Different wheel count or speed across the note can create spin; compression controls the contact state and must remain consistent through the feed. A moving scorer adds position and angle errors that require joint calibration. The exact tolerance, rejected alternatives and event-by-event revision history are not established by one illustrated sheet. The agent should use it to locate a mechanism family and then seek CAD, interviews or team replies before claiming why every dimension was selected.

technicalNotes.limitations: One-page technical sheet only. Complete trade studies, final reductions and season revision history remain unverified.

technicalNotes.title: 9470: triple-channel scorer to an open drum path
technicalNotes.construction: Triple shooter at early events; DCMP drum uses a full-width roller, pivoting hood rollers and three feeder rollers.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Higher ceiling without a channel-settling step.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The significant change is the removal of restrictive channel interfaces, not simply a larger launch wheel. Dividers can stabilize a piece path while creating an arch or an extra alignment delay; an open drum path can accept a broader front but needs consistent compression across its width. The early triple shooter remains an intentional schedule choice rather than a failed idea in every context. A team with an early event can rationally choose a lower ceiling that preserves practice time, then rebuild once the feed and current demands are understood.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Compare first-shot delay, sustained output and nearly-empty-hopper output across both configurations under the same supply conditions.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: 9470: reinforce the proven failure while preserving geometry
technicalNotes.construction: Worlds intake uses stacked quarter-inch SRP side plates with leaf-spring mounting and reinforced motor plates.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: DCMP damage made intake survival the next priority.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Changing material without changing the mounting boundary may fail to create the intended compliance. A leaf-spring arrangement needs room to bend, a predictable load path and fasteners that do not clamp the compliant region into an unintended rigid joint. Reinforcing the motor plate addresses a concentrated load while preserving the pickup geometry that the drivers already know. This is a useful rebuild principle: once the collection and shot behavior work, the largest improvement may be a structural interface that prevents losing the entire match rather than another nominal-rate optimization.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure deflection and residual alignment after repeatable corner hits, and time a side-plate replacement without disturbing the roller assembly.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: 9470: floor redesign follows the scorer and service needs
technicalNotes.construction: Final floor has eight mixed-compliance rollers, one X60 and a two-screw pivot for access.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Simpler feeding and fast electronics service.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A floor that works for one shooter architecture may create unnecessary volume and transfer stages for another. Mixing hard tubes and compliant contacts can maintain support while encouraging fuel through a problematic region. The service pivot adds a deliberate state outside gameplay: technicians must be able to open the floor, reach electronics and restore alignment quickly. That can improve event reliability more than reducing a small amount of mass. Include cable routing, fastener retention and the post-service check in the architecture record.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Time an actual electrical repair through the pivot, then verify floor alignment and feeding after repeated open/close cycles.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: 9470: empirical calibration and practice deadline
technicalNotes.construction: Interpolated shot map, measured first-shot correction and time-of-flight lookahead; fixed pre-event ship deadline.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Preserve practice and tuning time.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: An empirical map can be a technically rigorous choice when it captures the dominant real-world exit behavior within the available build window. It still needs enough sampling, a stable mechanical reference and a policy for replacing worn surfaces or changing fuel. The deadline is part of the architecture’s feasibility: every additional mechanism competes with the time needed to calibrate and drive it. A borrowed model should include its data-collection procedure and failure fallback rather than promising accuracy from a published algorithm name.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Repeat calibration after surface replacement and at low battery, then validate moving shots outside the original tuning trajectories.
technicalNotes.limitations: The process page is a team account. Dynamic homepage counters rendered as zero in static retrieval and were not imported as historical records; one L1 valuation on the page is not accepted as a rules authority.

technicalNotes.title: RIPCURRENT: shape the chassis and bumpers around the feed system
technicalNotes.construction: Chamfered 25×32-inch base; offset battery rail; structural bumper/hopper walls and low electronics.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Preserve low rotor diameter and storage area within the perimeter.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A singulator occupies a swept area, not just a rectangular bounding box. Changing chassis corners can preserve the parts of that area that most improve ring diameter while removing less useful perimeter. Moving the battery to an edge creates a new structural problem because the rail still has to carry drive and impact loads. Using the bumper backing as a hopper boundary can reclaim interior width, while tying scorer alignment to a removable impact structure. The package needs a repeatable bumper interface, and the stored-fuel center of mass must be evaluated alongside the empty robot.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Reinstall bumpers and measure scorer alignment; test loaded lateral acceleration and rotor clearance after representative impacts.

technicalNotes.title: RIPCURRENT: independently driven rotor, packing relief and passive contact
technicalNotes.construction: Separate rotor/feed drives; shaped fin and wrap guides; passive rollers and omni contacts.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Reduce packing pressure, friction and belt slip.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A bulk pile can load the singulator even when the exit path is clear. Agitating the pile and supplying the launch stream are different motions, so separating drives gives useful tuning freedom. A shaped fin can alter where that pile pressure is released; passive rollers reduce sliding resistance where balls push against each other. These details explain why a DYE-inspired design cannot be generalized as a generic circular indexer. The critical behavior is the changing network of contacts at full, partial and nearly empty loads, including a controlled reverse to clear a bridge.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure stream continuity and current at several load states; observe whether agitation increases entry occupancy or merely recirculates fuel.

technicalNotes.title: RIPCURRENT: compliant racks and a separately latched lower contact
technicalNotes.construction: Stacked polycarbonate racks; primary and lower powered rollers; strengthened hubs and shear interfaces.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Impact compliance and reliable pickup with retained storage.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Stacking plates can create controlled flex only if the plates and fasteners permit the intended relative motion. A low roller that remains deployed adds another ownership contact near the bumper, while its latch removes continuous holding load from an actuator. Stronger hubs and distributed shear interfaces address local failure modes that a thicker arm alone may not fix. The collector also moves storage boundaries, so its success must be measured while the hopper is loaded and the side walls are being pushed by fuel.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test diagonal wall contact, rack synchronization and lower-latch retention; inspect roller-end alignment and capacity after impact.

technicalNotes.title: RIPCURRENT: compact shooter swept volume and stored energy
technicalNotes.construction: Four-X44 3-inch flywheel; added dense inertia; powered hood roller; vertically stacked motor package.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Reduce protrusions while preserving the desired launch contact.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A compact turret can improve the whole robot by leaving more feed and storage volume around its swept envelope. That benefit must be weighed against launch-contact repeatability, motor cooling, wire access and flywheel recovery. Dense inertia stores energy in limited space, but increases spin-up energy and bearing loads. A powered hood contact changes the spin state and must remain geometrically consistent as the hood moves. The key comparison with a drum is delivered scored fuel during usable windows, including time moving and acquiring, rather than a single instantaneous output rate.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Map exit velocity and spin versus hood angle, turret heading and volley length; inspect belt tracking under acceleration.
technicalNotes.limitations: The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

technicalNotes.title: RIPCURRENT: calibration and uncertainty remain empirical
technicalNotes.construction: Team reply describes robust-shot selection followed by measured angle and velocity calibration.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Choose trajectories tolerant of exit-state errors.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A nominal ballistic solution is not enough when fuel compression, wear and launch contact change the actual exit velocity. Searching for a region of successful trajectories can improve tolerance, but the model must be anchored to measurements of the real mechanism. Separate localization, hood-reference and exit-speed errors before retuning: otherwise one correction can conceal another. This is a transferable technical procedure, not evidence that every team should adopt the same equation set or that the robot can score under every motion and defense condition.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Use stationary known-pose tests to isolate launch error, then add translation, rotation and tilt one at a time.

technicalNotes.title: FIREFLY: wheel stiffness is part of end-effector accuracy
technicalNotes.construction: Custom Grip Lock hubs, lowered Mk4-C base and later lower drive gearing.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Reduce tire flex and preserve a stiff floor-to-tool reference.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Wheel compliance permits the chassis to rotate relative to the carpet even when the frame and elevator are stiff. The resulting angular error becomes a larger displacement at an elevated tool, so a tire-hub change can improve L4 placement without changing the wrist. A low frame and ballast distribution address another component of the same stability problem. The gearing revision also changes acceleration and braking behavior; it needs drive retuning with the real mechanism load. Do not treat a module model or a free speed as a complete explanation of placement repeatability.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure tool-tip displacement under known lateral load and during stopping, separating tire deflection from lift deflection.

technicalNotes.title: FIREFLY: short lift and low-mounted carriage actuators
technicalNotes.construction: Single-stage counterbalanced lift; thin-wall tube; algae, coral and arm drives mounted low on carriage.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Low moving center of gravity and direct piece delivery.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Remoting the roller drives removes mass from the far end of the arm while keeping it on the lift carriage. That reduces one component of arm inertia without eliminating the carriage mass that the lift must accelerate. A single-stage lift can simplify guidance but requires the arm to supply the remaining reach and orientation. Counterbalance reduces gravity demand, while belt tension and routing still determine tracking and friction. The integration goal is a useful task sequence with no wait for piece delivery, rather than a collection of independently fast axes.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure lift current and tool settling during combined motion; verify belt tension and direct-handoff clearance at every relevant pose.

technicalNotes.title: FIREFLY: sideways orientation while maintaining coral ownership
technicalNotes.construction: Sideways reorienting belt, compliant tube rollers, independent roller drives and twisted-belt transmission.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Direct handoff or controlled L1 without staging the coral.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A sideways belt gives the tube a deliberate transverse velocity rather than relying only on passive wedges. The remaining contacts must keep ownership while that reorientation happens; an unconstrained gap can erase the advantage. Separate roller drives permit holding a tube for L1 or continuing into the end effector, but create more state choices and sensor requirements. Twisted and bent belts solve an off-axis power-routing problem, while adding tracking, wear and alignment concerns. Their tension cannot be chosen solely for torque transmission if the belt also participates in piece contact.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Film diagonal and lengthwise entries through both L1 and handoff branches, then repeat after belt wear and an intake impact.

technicalNotes.title: FIREFLY: dedicated floor-algae route integrates with climb
technicalNotes.construction: Counter-rotating floor-algae rollers; reinforced printed bevel gears; three-piece jackshaft around climb packaging.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Acquire algae and deliver it to the arm without subsystem interference.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A dedicated floor pickup lets the main end effector specialize in retention and scoring rather than reaching a difficult carpet pose. That value must exceed the added mass and handoff complexity. Segmenting the jackshaft can make assembly possible around another subsystem, but every joint adds an alignment and torque-transfer interface. Printed bevel gears need stable bearing support and an appropriate tooth load; a successful material in another mechanism does not certify this one. The pathway should remain useful if the climb is damaged, consistent with the robot’s stated degraded-operation objective.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test floor acquisition and handoff while climb is stowed, partially deployed and disabled; inspect bevel alignment under peak capture load.

technicalNotes.title: FIREFLY: internal coral grip and algae torque selected by test
technicalNotes.construction: Internal coral gripping; compliant placement geometry; shared tool also acquires and scores algae.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Control both pieces while keeping moving structure light.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Gripping inside a tube changes the reference surface and can leave the outside clearer for placement. It still needs a controlled release and enough compliance to tolerate the branch without wedging the tool. Algae retention is a different torque problem: the wheel must deform and hold a soft sphere rather than simply spin at the desired acquisition speed. A practical way to choose the ratio is to measure the required final-shaft torque, then check speed and motor current under that load. This is more informative than selecting a reduction from a famous robot without matching its compression and geometry.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure algae pull-in torque and holding current, then test coral release with intentional branch misalignment and the same worn contacts.

technicalNotes.title: FIREFLY: powered magnetic cage acquisition and sensed latching
technicalNotes.construction: Magnetic TPU intake wheels pull cage into two one-way latches; winch/rotation share a drive.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Capture before automatically lifting.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Magnetic attraction can improve the first contact with a steel cage, but the final robot load should pass through the designed latch and structure. Two capture switches give the controller a stronger condition than assuming engagement after a fixed time. Shared winch and rotation power saves hardware while tying the phase sequence to transmission geometry. The dated timeline records later additions to the cage collector and automation, so the final system should not be projected back to the robot’s first event. Total climb time includes acquisition and settling, not just the powered lift.

technicalNotes.title: FIREFLY: custom cycloidal reduction is an iterative capability
technicalNotes.construction: 23:1 dual-disc cycloidal; hardened steel discs; rolling pins; team reports about 0.3° backlash.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Compact, lightweight low-backlash joint drive.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A cycloidal gearbox trades ordinary spur stages for a shaped eccentric load path with multiple contacts. Opposed discs can reduce dynamic imbalance, but machining accuracy, pin support and eccentric bearings still control vibration, efficiency and backlash. The reported backlash is a team result for its design and measurement conditions. It should not be assumed for a copied outline made with a different process. This is a mature, revised manufacturing capability, so its adoption cost includes inspection, heat treatment and assembly knowledge rather than just CAD availability.

technicalNotes.title: NOCTURNE: passive centering trades motor count for geometry
technicalNotes.construction: Fast under-bumper rollers with passive wedges replacing an active-centering beta design.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Reduce current while retaining useful acquisition.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A passive wedge can convert forward motion into centering without another motor, but requires the right approach velocity, contact friction and space for the note to move laterally. If a note is pinched against the wedge before it is captured, a faster roller can make the jam worse. The source represents the Granite State configuration, and a later team account describes impact failures and difficult repairs. The observed update is therefore part of the technical recommendation: a pickup can satisfy its contact objective while losing event value through poor service access.

technicalNotes.title: NOCTURNE: reuse a familiar joint and simplify the architecture
technicalNotes.construction: Single-joint arm, paired planetary drives, chain final reduction and output-angle sensing.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Reuse 2023 experience and preserve time before week 1.

It still needs a force-path and backlash review for its new payload. Multiple chain runs can distribute load but require matched tension so one does not carry nearly everything. A hard-stop shot gives a mechanically referenced fallback when vision or arm control fails, but repeated impact into the stop can change alignment. Schedule feasibility is a legitimate architecture criterion alongside reach and nominal speed.

technicalNotes.title: NOCTURNE: stage the note before launch while minimizing distal mass
technicalNotes.construction: Eight launch wheels; lightweight staging rollers and low-friction guides integrated with the scorer.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Hold and preaccelerate without another storage mechanism.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A staging section can establish a repeatable note entry and prevent an uncontrolled piece from touching the flywheels prematurely. Using a smaller motor reduces moving mass only if it still supplies enough capture and feed force. The structure must resist both wheel vibration and arm acceleration; a flexible mount changes the launch angle even with correct encoder readings. A grippy stage and low-friction guides serve different purposes: one supplies drive while the other avoids wasting that effort. Test the full transfer at operating speed rather than assuming more grip everywhere is better.

technicalNotes.title: NOCTURNE: the real field exposed calibration and fallback needs
technicalNotes.construction: Pose-based shot map, motion lookahead and automatic intake stop after note detection.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Aim through brief vision loss and avoid accidental extra possession.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A consistent pose estimate can still be systematically wrong if the practice target or camera geometry is wrong. Calibrating a lookup table against an inaccurate practice field can make reliable local shots fail at an event. A safe fallback should use a mechanically repeatable pose with a validated close shot, rather than trusting the same mistaken distance model. The fixed under-bumper intake also creates a possession-control requirement because it cannot simply retract away from a second piece. Mechanical geometry and sensor timing must be verified together.

technicalNotes.title: OVERLOAD: floor versions change what should be copied
technicalNotes.construction: Alpha floor, SVDE split-axle floor, CVDE continuous axle and Worlds captured fixed-center floor are distinguished.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Eliminate binding, belt escape, shaft failure and fuel trapped beneath the floor.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: An adjustable joint can make prototyping easier while becoming a weak structural interface under a full hopper. A split axle is especially sensitive because bending, thread retention and tension adjustment meet at the same small connection. Capturing a cam follower must account for lateral deflection as well as the nominal two-dimensional motion; otherwise the follower can escape around a track that looks constrained in a sketch. Fixed centers can improve reliability once the correct tension is known, but require accurate geometry and assembly. The correct inspiration for a rebuild is a dated floor version with its failure history, not simply “254 belts.”
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Load the floor unevenly, push the intake backward, test lateral racking and inspect whether fuel can get underneath before copying the travel geometry.

technicalNotes.title: OVERLOAD: shared feeder power is a different optimization from floor tilt
technicalNotes.construction: Team says final floor tilt helped modestly; compares its output with 2910’s mechanically shared feeder/floor drives.

Mechanically sharing motors can let the available power serve those changing demands instead of leaving some motors lightly loaded while another stage struggles. That benefit trades away independent control and can transmit a jam farther through the system. Extra floor tilt is a separate variable: it may improve the entry geometry without justifying a complicated cam and narrow packaging. Compare the complete energy and service cost rather than assuming every feature of the reference robot is worth retaining.

technicalNotes.title: Preacceleration, passive restraint and retrofit compression
technicalNotes.construction: The interview describes a two-X44 intake at 2.5:1, passive carbon upper roller, roller-floor transmission described as 17:19, and a 3-inch steel drum driven by four X60s with powered hood rollers. A previously powered upper feed roller was made passive after jamming. Drum-region compression is reported as 3/8 inch and final roller compression as 1/2 inch.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The team explicitly connects the stepped compression to fitting a replacement shooter in the existing robot, and the passive roller change to avoiding fuel being driven downward into jams. Collector repair access is deliberate because it receives impacts.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The important reference is the sequence of contacts, not simply four launcher motors. Upstream acceleration reduces the velocity increment demanded of the drum, while the passive restraint prevents one contact from injecting fuel into an already occupied region. More powered surfaces can therefore lower useful flow. A retrofit also fixes the available path length and elevation; its compression distribution cannot safely be transplanted without the same incoming velocity and support geometry. Separately, the agitation priority hierarchy means collector deployment and automatic shooting agitation are competing commands rather than independent subsystems.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure hopper-to-exit rate and current with the upper restraint passive versus driven, at several fill levels. Check worn fuel and simultaneous agitation. Preserve the source ratio order until driver/driven orientation is verified.

technicalNotes.title: Dish packaging and shooting independence require a coordinated robot
technicalNotes.construction: The interview describes an eleven-position dish, front and rear vertical roller sets to clear its center, approximately 425 degrees of turret freedom, a 3-inch main shooter wheel, a 1-inch upper roller and additional feed wheels. A third X44 was added for difficult passes and corner shots. Intake and drivetrain packaging are shaped around the large dish.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The team identifies moving shots, shooting under defense and simultaneous acquisition as reasons to retain the turret architecture. The doubled vertical rollers address fuel left in the dish center; the extra shooter motor addresses range/power demand.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A centrally packaged turret is a whole-robot commitment. The dish determines where modules, structure and storage can sit, and its useful capacity depends on clearing the central dead region rather than nominal perimeter volume. Turret range is only useful if localization, target selection, hood travel and cable management support it. The FMS-aware timing offset is a flight-time decision: fuel released before activation must arrive while scoring is valid. That offset is not a transferable constant without checking release-to-arrival time and the applicable game timing.

technicalNotes.title: A rising fuel path makes agitation and service mass consequential
technicalNotes.construction: The collector kicker changed from a hanging deployed bar to a member that folds with the hopper. Side agitation, passive dead-zone rollers, added gripping rollers and a belt-linked roller elevator feed the drum. The retained dated source account records the climber being installed March 1 and removed March 19 before the first event.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The folding kicker is explained as improving bump clearance. Added contact surfaces respond to trapped fuel and insufficient feed. The retained team account attributes removing the climber to weight, with later mass devoted to reliable feeding.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: This design transports fuel upward before release, so every additional elevation change has a traction and packing cost. An apparently small passive roller may be important because it removes a place where the moving stream can unload into a dead pocket. The coupled hopper/kicker motion is also a route-clearance feature, not merely storage expansion. Removing a climber should be understood as reallocating mass and development effort to the bottleneck; it does not imply that tower scoring was mechanically impossible or that endgame fuel should be counted as climb value.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Log current and residual inventory along the entire rising path, test folding while fully loaded, and compare bump clearance before and after the kicker folds. Do not derive undisclosed gear ratios from the interview wording.

technicalNotes.title: Protected carbon intake and continuous J-path launcher feed
technicalNotes.construction: A 2×1 aluminum crash member protects a carbon intake roller. Later wrist plates use half-inch stock with raised hard-stop contact regions and pocketing. The shooter uses a J-shaped accelerating tunnel, a separate feeder, a four-X60 steel drum and powered hood rollers; its hood pivot is supported independently of the drum. Two side cameras were added to the original front Limelight.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The team links the crash member to allowing a light but impact-sensitive roller, larger hard-stop contact to reduced wear, low electronics/wiring to a lower floor, and additional cameras to midfield vision gaps found at Half Moon Bay. The source also describes replacing an earlier S-shaped path after direction reversal hurt consistency.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The useful package combines structural load routing with flow continuity. The crash member must intercept contact before the carbon roller does; copying only the carbon tube removes the condition that made it practical. A lower floor reduces the climb imposed on loose fuel, while a J-path avoids reversing the velocity component that was just created upstream. Independent hood support can reduce parasitic coupling, but hood and drum still need controlled compression over their complete angle range. The camera change is evidence that good scoring performance near the hub did not guarantee adequate pose observability in midfield.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure path velocity and compression through hood travel, inspect crash loads with the collector extended, and compare localization availability in midfield before and after adding side views. Retain a separate shooter-ready gate before enabling the floor.

technicalNotes.title: Precondition fuel before a compact turret, then manage defended stability
technicalNotes.construction: The interview describes eleven active carbon/silicone floor rollers powered by an X60 through a stated 2:1 reduction, with 3-mm-pitch GT2 inter-roller belts. A later acceleration stage is described as delivering approximately 8 m/s with near-zero incoming spin. Compact turret packaging shares shafts and places hood-drive hardware to limit diameter. A defended shooting mode cancels shooting on the move.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The team explicitly cites efficiency at small pulley radii for its belt choice and compactness for the turret transmission layout. Its defended mode is explained as planting the robot to resist being pushed and emptying more accurately.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Preconditioning is a useful way to separate high-volume transport from precision release. A turret receiving fuel with controlled velocity and spin needs to add less correction, but it inherits errors in every upstream roller and transfer gap. The reported 8 m/s is an internal-stage claim, not a measured final trajectory specification or match-average rate. A planted mode also shows why turret capability does not require moving continuously: the best control mode depends on contact conditions. A future implementation must budget traction and battery demand for both upstream acceleration and chassis resistance.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure entrance velocity/spin distribution, current at each stage, and accuracy under controlled lateral contact. Compare planted and moving modes with the same fuel condition and load rather than ranking them from an undefended demo.

technicalNotes.title: Twin spindexers trade packaging freedom for multiple coupled interfaces
technicalNotes.construction: The mechanism has two rotating floor/cone systems and uptake ramps, separately controlled kickers, independent turrets and hood adjustment. The interview describes X44-driven indexer systems, 6-inch aluminum flywheels replacing heavy steel trials, an under-mounted battery on a pinned removable panel, and chassis-speed-dependent intake voltage bounded around 6.5–12 V.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: Aluminum flywheels were chosen after the steel trial proved too heavy. The battery mounting responds to crowded internal packaging. The retained interview account describes bristles, stacked wheels and shaped cones as successive feed iterations.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Two aiming channels do not automatically double match output. Fuel must be distributed to both cones, delivered through both ramps and accelerated without one path starving or overpacking. Moving-shot math must use the location of each turret rather than a single robot-center vector; angular chassis motion creates different local velocities at separated release points. Dynamic collector speed can match acquisition to chassis motion, but the exact speed signal and interpolation should be checked in code because the caption wording mixes angular and translational quantities. The removable battery panel is part of the architecture: dense packaging is only useful if the robot can still be serviced reliably.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test unequal hopper loading, one jammed lane, low battery, turning shots and underbody battery retention after bump contact. Verify the actual intake-speed input in source code before reproducing the controller.

technicalNotes.title: Rebuild removes feed compression and separates shooter readiness
technicalNotes.construction: The interview distinguishes a former divided two-lane/double-spindexer arrangement from the drum rebuild with a roller floor. A powered lower intake roller was replaced by two 3/4-inch aluminum shafts with reduced compression. Compliant wheels near entry feed a J-shaped path; a guide was added after WPI wobble. Four motors drive the drum/kicker/hood group, and feed is enabled only after aiming, speed and hood conditions are satisfied.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The team reports improved throughput after reducing collector compression, adds the guide to control observed motion, and describes reduced belt tension as a current-draw improvement. Driver controls were intentionally simplified around repeatable actions.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: This is evidence against treating maximum grip as maximum throughput. Too many opposing powered contacts can trap deformable fuel or make its entry velocity inconsistent. Removing a roller changes the entire force chain, so the improvement should not be generalized to a collector with different ground geometry. Likewise, the software shoot command is a sequencer rather than a simultaneous motor-on command. Feeding early can pull down wheel speed or create an inaccurate initial volley, while waiting unnecessarily long reduces usable shift time.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Compare feed latency, initial-volley accuracy, current and residual fuel with the actual readiness tolerances. Inspect the added guide over hood travel and repeat reduced-compression tests with worn fuel.

technicalNotes.title: Large inventory changes collector loading, frame clearance and drive gearing
technicalNotes.construction: The interview reports approximately 115-fuel capacity, a 33.5×21.375-inch robot envelope before the described extension, a wide 3-inch two-X60 intake, a load shield above the collector, and hopper structure changed from angle to tube. A two-position hood changed from pneumatic to linear actuation; wheel speed covers intermediate distances. Custom modules allow ratio changes and were geared down for the loaded robot.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The second collector motor and load shield respond to stalling and hopper pressure. Tube structure responds to racking and snagging. The lower drive ratio is explicitly tied to moving a heavily loaded robot across bumps with less stalling/current; the source attributes the actuator change to weight.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Capacity is useful only if it remains mobile and unloads reliably. A large stored column presses on its lowest contact surfaces, so a shield can be more valuable than another nominally faster roller. The hopper bar cutout and wheel sizing belong to the same route-clearance problem: a robot that can collect a full load but beaches on the bump loses the strategic value of that load. Two hood positions simplify mechanism travel, but the remaining range must be supplied by speed without creating unacceptable release-angle or recovery-time sensitivity.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test acceleration, bump traversal, braking, tip margin and current at empty/half/full inventory. Measure sustained unload rate rather than dividing nominal capacity by the fastest initial volley. Verify exact dimensions and the source gear notation in CAD.

technicalNotes.title: A drum rebuild shifts the problem to inertia, loading and inspection mass
technicalNotes.construction: The interview distinguishes the former turret from a four-X60 drum rebuild. A long kicker ramp maintains contact; a stub-roller floor pivots with the collector, with a jackshaft inside a roller. Passive hopper/net expansion is reported as roughly 50–55 fuel unexpanded and up to 78 expanded. A 1.5-lb steel flywheel with a stated 1:3 transmission supplements launcher inertia. The planned L1 mechanism was removed at inspection.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The team attributes the ramp to sustained compression, the added flywheel to speed droop while feeding a large load, and climb removal to a discrepancy between shop and event weighing. A revised hood ratio sought a compromise between actuation speed and resistance to disturbance.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: The supplementary flywheel stores energy in the motor-to-drum system; its contribution depends on the square of its speed ratio. That does not establish a sustained power budget, so a high first-volley rate may still decay. The pivoting floor improves access but introduces moving shaft/alignment interfaces. The source caption calls one small drum dimension ambiguously; do not infer diameter from that wording. Likewise, a removed climber is an unfielded feature for the filmed configuration, not an autonomous capability.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Measure speed droop over a complete hopper and repeated shifts, verify drive/driven ratio order, and calibrate scales before allocating the final mass margin.

technicalNotes.title: Surface contamination, inertia and power control interact
technicalNotes.construction: The collector deploy angle was flattened after first-event jams. The retained interview account describes surgical tubing replaced by grippier floor surfaces after fuel debris caused slip. The shooter uses a four-X60 aluminum drum, powered upper rollers and a compact geared steel flywheel; transfer is sequenced after launcher speed is reached. Current, voltage and temperature logging inform operating limits.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The team links the added flywheel to reduced speed decay and improved end-of-hopper accuracy. Floor/collector changes respond to observed jamming and contamination, while software limiting responds to the total electrical demand.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A material choice can work with clean practice fuel yet fail when loose surface debris changes friction. A flywheel can smooth a transient without fixing an inadequate recharge rate or a hot motor. The useful design reference is therefore a tested material/contact path plus an explicit electrical budget, not a motor count. Robot logging should distinguish commanded voltage, actual bus voltage, current limit, speed error and fuel flow; otherwise starvation and electrical saturation can look like the same shooting symptom.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Repeat full-hopper tests with used fuel and low batteries. Compare surface cleanliness, slip, speed recovery and motor temperature over multiple shifts rather than a single successful volley.

technicalNotes.title: Passive feed solved one jam while rack durability remained unresolved
technicalNotes.construction: The rack collector and belt floor feed an originally divided shooter that became one continuous drum. In the team’s later technical discussion, powered upper/lower indexing rollers overpacked the ramp; immobilizing the lower rollers corrected that feed issue. The static hood avoids an exposed powered-roller belt. The team separately reports repeated polycarbonate rack-tooth failures and a 45-A deploying/5-A deployed current-limit strategy at Worlds.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The stated priorities are simple, durable mechanisms and resistance to trench contact. The lower surface was made static to meter entry rather than forcing fuel into a congested ramp. The current-limit change aimed to let the intake collapse under impact; failures became less frequent but did not disappear.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: This example needs two distinct failure histories. A feed-path change can be successful while the deployment structure remains unreliable. Stronger propulsion is not automatically the fix for a packing jam, and a high-performing alliance run does not certify rack durability. Source-reported storage also has a useful distinction: almost 70 geometric capacity versus commonly 50–60 in play. Protected interior PETG vector wheels surviving a season is not evidence that the same prints would survive as exposed intake wheels.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Test the passive lower feed with full hopper pressure and varied fuel. Instrument deployment impact/current and inspect tooth-root damage. A proposed decoupling of intake sides is a future idea, not a fielded fix.
technicalNotes.limitations: Focused interview plus first-party technical replies 5, 8, 11, 13 and 15 in topic 521008. Tech-slide access returned Gone; the slides were not reviewed or counted as a binder.

technicalNotes.title: Trench access and speed-error feeding explain the rebuild
technicalNotes.construction: A slotted three-roller transfer provides adjustable compression before a two-X60 high-inertia launcher. The flexible Hopper Flopper compresses under the trench and re-expands afterward. The shooter was reversed relative to the original robot, and the feeder speed varies with launcher speed error. The interview explicitly reports no climb.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The team links trench access to losing neutral-zone fuel races, preserving capacity to avoiding a smaller fixed hopper, and reversed orientation to reducing the need to turn after acquisition. Transfer modulation is intended to give fuel sufficient energy transfer while maintaining accuracy.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: A compliant storage envelope changes which routes are available, so its value cannot be measured only in added fuel. It can change autonomous arrival order and the opponent’s available supply. Speed-error-dependent feed is a form of demand management: slow entry when the launcher is behind instead of allowing a nominally high feed command to create low-energy misses. The caption’s flywheel mass arithmetic is inconsistent, so preserve the qualitative high-inertia claim and seek a published mass breakdown rather than silently choosing one number.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Compare route arrival times, full-load trench passage, recovery after contact, and total scored fuel with fixed versus variable feeding. Measure sustained and initial BPS separately.
technicalNotes.limitations: Interview plus team replies in topic 515730. The first release reports about 15–16 BPS over a full roughly 80-fuel hopper versus around 20–25 initially; these are team reports for that configuration, not measurements of every later revision.

technicalNotes.title: A fixed-angle launcher deliberately shifts complexity elsewhere
technicalNotes.construction: The interview describes a passively deploying intake/hopper, roller floor explicitly inspired by 2017 team 254, a separate feed stage, a four-X60 launcher and added brass flywheel inertia. The hood is fixed; distance changes use speed and chassis aim. Intake motion agitates the stored fuel, and the aiming system has a manual fallback.
technicalNotes.team_stated_reason: The team explicitly credits the historical floor reference and identifies the fallback as a way to keep playing when automatic aim fails. No team-stated numerical optimum for fixed hood angle is established in this passage.
technicalNotes.engineering_analysis: Removing hood actuation reduces moving hardware, but does not remove aiming requirements. The usable trajectory envelope is now constrained by wheel speed, launch angle, release height, accuracy and the routes from which the chassis can point at the target. The passive deployment also makes initial orientation and autonomous motion part of the mechanism’s operation. A simple subsystem can therefore demand careful whole-match planning without being a poor design.
technicalNotes.recommended_validation: Map accuracy versus range and bus voltage, test deployment from plausible starting poses, and practice the manual-aim fallback. Do not interpret the caption’s repeated “8-inch tube” wording as a verified drum diameter.
